Consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 80 respecting the Grand Trunk arbitration.

Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Prime Minister) moved concurrence in the amendments.
He said: I can explain the amendments, I think, very briefly. The first amendment is to leave out all the words after "appointed" to the end of subclouse (a) and substitute the following:
"Directors; provided that the substituted board of directors of the company need not comprise more than five members; that until otherwise provided by the board a majority of the directors shall constitute a quorum; and that it shall not be necessary that any of the directors shall reside in England or be qualified by ownership of stock."
The whole purpose of that is to take care of a possible eventuality of resignations going in together, leaving not enough members to constitute a quorum to accept the resignations of those who have resigned. To cover that eventuality it was provided that the substituted board, first of all, should not comprise more than five. We believe that has to be legislated for because the present charter calls for more. The rest of it is merely to take care of the eventuality of directors resigning at once leaving not sufficient quorum to care for the situation and carry on, pending appointments. The change is designed to meet a legal point. After reflection it was felt this proceeding would be better and more safe than the other, but the effect is exactly the same.
The next change is that paragraph (c) is struck out. That paragraph provided that meetings of the board of directors of the company for the transmission of any business may be validly held in Canada or elsewhere. ^ Instead of that the following paragraph is substituted by amendment:
' (c) that the head office of the company and the meetings of its board of directors for the transaction of any business shall after the substitution of directors as herein provided for be in Canada."
It was feared that under the old wording the meeting at which the new board was appointed might not be legal. By the change it is intended to make clear that it may be legal, and that subsequently all meetings shall be held in Canada. In a word, that again just meets the intention of the legislation, but is considered by the draughtsman who draughted the Bill, and by the Justice Department, as better.
In paragraph (e) the words "the company shall not" in line 41 are struck out and a substitution made. This clause is intended to make clear what the effect of the old legislation was: that the Grand Trunk's costs of the arbitration shall be 
paid, not by the Grand Trunk, because if so it would ultimately be paid by the country, but out of assessments levied against dividends coming to the debenture and guaranteed stockholders, and the words "that the company shall not be bound to see to the application of the moneys requisitioned or otherwise responsible for or bear any of the costs of the arbitration" are amended to this extent: "neither the company nor the Government as guarantor of interest and dividends shall be bound," etc. Then, to make it still more clear that there is to be no liability on the country nr on the Grand Trunk for their share of the costs, the following is added:
"And moreover, after substitution of directors of the company as herein provided for, the company, and the (Government as guarantor of interest and dividends on the debenture and guaranteed stock, shall be entitled to deduct and retain from such interest and dividends as may thereafter become payable upon the said stocks any and all costs and expenses connected with the arbitration heretofore or hereafter advanced, paid or incurred by either the company or the Government, other than such as under the agreement of March 8, 1920, are payable by the Government."
That removes all possibility of legal doubt, as the Government is advised, as to the costs being collectible except out of dividends coming to the debenture and guaranteed stockholders.
In subclause (g) of clause 1 the word "arbitrators" is struck out and the word "arbitration" substituted therefor. That is merely to correct a clerical error.
The following is added as section 4 of the Bill:
For the purpose of carrying out the substitution of directors of the company herein provided for, any director of the company may vacate his office by resignation in writing submitted to the board at any meeting of the directors, and if one or more of the directors of the company, not exceeding five at any one time, shall in the manner aforesaid vacate his or their offices, the remaining directors of the company present at the aforesaid meeting or at any subsequent meeting, even although they do not constitute a quorum, may elect a director or directors nominated by the Government to fill the place or places of the director or directors so vacating his or their offices.
Up to that point it merely carries out the intent as stated by me in explaining the amendment in subclause (c). Then the new clause continues:
Moreover the Governor in Council may at any time appoint additional directors to the substituted board if considered expedient.

What is
that for?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Provision is made for a certain number of directors, and if later it should be decided to increase the number under this amendment, additional directors can be appointed.
What contingency has the Government in mind there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Government has not any contingency in mind, but the draughtsman, Mr. Tilley, in association with Mr. Newcombe, thought it would be unwise to restrict the Government in that regard; and, in fact, it was not known that they would be restricted until this was put in. It was not suggested by the Government.

On the face of it, it looks as though it were intended to give the Government power to appoint new directors in case the existing directors should not act sufficiently in accord with the views of the Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Canadian National Railways Act gives the Government similar power. Stockholders must be able to appoint directors or there is no control at all. The Government is responsible for the character and capacity of the men running the road, and with that responsibility must go the power of removal. You cannot have responsibility without that authority.

As the Prime Minister has said, these amendments seem largely in the nature of improvements of legal phraseology, to enable the Government to tighten their control a little on the Grand Trunk. I do not think they affect the principle of the measure in any way, and therefore no useful purpose can be served in offering any objections.
Motion agreed to and Senate amendments concurred in.
The adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Spinney for the second reading of Bill No. 122, to amend the Civil Service Act, 1918, was resumed.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that on Friday last I was out of the House when the motion for the second reading of this Bill was moved
by the Government. Had I been present I certainly would have protested against the procedure adopted from the beginning to the end. I think it is most peculiar. Nobody could help but be suspicious of the motive and purpose behind the Bill, particularly by reason of the manner in which it has been presented to the House. There has been an absolute absence of candour or frankness in the explanation upon the first reading of the Bill or upon the second reading. The purpose of the legislation has not been disclosed at all, in fact any explanation has been evaded, and apparently every step taken has been with the view of preventing the House gaining any knowledge of that purpose.
I do not say that I am right in that assertion, that will be for members of the Government to state themselves, but I do say that the procedure adopted in presenting such an important measure to the House is open to serious criticism indeed. In the first place, the Bill was introduced in blank when the first reading was moved. On Friday last, before the second reading, a committee was appointed without an opportunity being given by the House to hear from the Government as to the purpose and provisions of the measure or to express its opinion on the principle involved. In that respect the procedure has been most unusual. It might naturally have been expected that upon the second reading at least some explanation would have been forthcoming. I say that for the reason that the Bill affects fundamentally the main provisions of an Act which, after great deliberation Parliament adopted three years ago. That Act is difficult to understand at best, and most .members, I fancy, have never given to it that direct study which would enable them to understand the importance of	its main
provisions, to say nothing of its many subsidiary clauses. I would not object to a Bill being sent to a committee without a full discussion of its principal provisions, if the legislation being amended were well known to the House and if the amendments were of a trivial or unsubstantial character. But the Bill before us for consideration is extremely important. It is a reversal of every principle of importance contained in the Civil Service Act of 1918, it is a reversal of public policy as declared in the elections of 1917, and it is not a Bill that the Government should have contemplated sending to a committee without full and ample discussion in the House. It is a Bill that cannot be properly,



effectively and intelligently considered by any committee until the House has decided whether as a matter of principle they intend to revert to the patronage system as it prevailed prior to 1918. And that is the purpose of this Bill-a clear-cut, definite reversion to the practice of political patronage as it prevailed before 1918, with a few trivial and perhaps unimportant exceptions-exceptions which, I think, if the Bill is accepted by the House, might as well go along with the other portions of the Act that are being amended. Therefore I say that this measure should be discussed by the House; that it should not be sent to a committee before the principle involved is adopted by the House, and that the motion setting up this committee should be rescinded if only as a matter of respect to members of the House.
Now, when the Bill was introduced the other day the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Spinney), in presenting it, said:
If the introduction of the present measure, which proposes to amend the Civil Service Act of 1918, leaves the impression on the mind of any hon. member that the Government is receding from the main principles of that statute, namely, the abolition of patronage, he may at once dismiss that thought.
Now, with all due respect to my hon. friend I do say that that was hardly a fair description of the measure, because it is, without a scintilla of a doubt, a reversion to the patronage system as it prevailed prior to 1918. There are some exceptions, I admit, but they are unimportant, and, as I have already said, if we adopt this measure we might as well let these exceptions go with the other provisions of the Civil Service Act of 1918 which are being amended.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) sought to hasten the transmission of this Bill from the House to the committee upon the ground that the principle of the Bill had already been discussed upon a resolution of the member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes). Well, I do submit to my right hon. friend that that was hardly good ground for hastening the measure from the House to the committee. A discussion upon a resolution asserting abstract principles can hardly be regarded as taking the place of a discussion of the principles involved in definite legislation. On the resolution of the hon. member for Victoria many matters were discussed. While I was not present on the occasion of the debate upon that resolution, upon reading some few days later the speeches that were delivered, I was gratified to 
learn that the principle of the Civil Service Act had been supported by practically every hon. gentleman who spoke, no matter on which side of the House he sat. I was very much pleased at that time to read the remarks of the right hon; Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) whom I had always known to be a sincere and zealous supporter of the principles embodied in the Civil Service Act. He stated, as reported on page 844 of unrevised Hansard of March 11, 1921:
Now, in so far as there may be betterments in administration, I am open to the adoption of those betterments, but I am absolutely against putting patronage back either here or in the Outside Service, except under very exceptional circumstances.
Later on he said:
I do not want to go back to the old system of patronage. I felt my heart throb in response to sentiments expressed by the member for Ottawa (Mr. Chabot), when he faintly adumbrated the joy and the pleasure of living in Ottawa as a public man in these days as compared with the times-

I am coming to that later. It robs the Civil Service Commission of its principal duties;-it is doubtful whether it would be worth while retaining the Commission to carry on the duties left it under the Act if amended as proposed. It would foe worth while, I think, for the House to consider briefly the history of the events leading up to this legislation and to study carefully the provisions of the Bill-because, having regard to the remarks made by hon. members of the Government in support of the measure, it is evident that they themselves are not fully conversant with it.
I should like to recall the attention of hon. gentlemen to the fact that in the election of 1917, the then Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), in his platform, stated to the public that he proposed the elimination of patronage in appointments to the public service. That pledge was deliberately and fully carried out. I admit that it was a tremendous step to take in legislation of this character, and that we proceeded further than any other country in the world had up to that time. I can quite
understand how this might affect political organizations, how it might directly and indirectly affect members of Parliament and prospective candidates to Parliament.
I can understand what confusion it might possibly create, and it created some. But, nevertheless, this Parliament, after due deliberation, with the support of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, unanimously accepted the Civil Service Act of 1918 introduced into Parliament in fulfilment of the pledge which the then Prime Minister made to the country in 1917. I think I may assert without much serious criticism that when a measure is placed on the statute books of this country in such circumstances, no Government should attempt to violate the main provisions or principles of that Bill without at least absolute and due frankness to the House, without affording to the House an opportunity of discussing the Bill, and certainly there should be no evidence of an attempt to send it by a subterranean passage to a committee of this House without the House knowing what the Bill contains.
Further, I think every hon. gentleman opposite, who is now a member of Government, heartily supported the Bill of 1918, and all the amendments that have been made to it since then. I remember reading reports of speeches delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) and his colleague the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) on their western tour during the autumn of 1920, and I observed that on frequent occasions they solicited support for the Government upon the fact that the Civil Service Act of 1918 had been introduced and adopted, and evidently they were both seeking support from the western provinces upon this measure. It seems strange that, within a few months after soliciting electoral support upon this measure, they should become responsible for the introduction into this House of an amending measure	,	which	practicallydestroys the most vital principles of the Civil Service Act. I wish to assert the following proposition	as a sound	principle,applicable to the	question,	and tothe parliamentary	system	obtaining
in this country. In 1917, an election took place upon several issues, including the Civil Service Act, under circumstances which I detailed a moment ago. That platform or public pledge was converted into definite legislation. There has been no election since that date, and, therefore, no attempt should be made to destroy that measure without an appeal to the

country. Some hon. gentlemen opposite express dissent; but if those gentlemen opposite were elected on that platform and supported and assented to the principle involved in that legislation, by what authority can they openly and brazenly revert to conditions which existed prior to the passage of the Civil Service Act of 1918? I deny that constitutional authority rests with the Government or with Parliament to make such important amendments to the Act prior to a dissolution of Parliament and an appeal to the people. Of course, Parliament is all-powerful; it may amend to-day anything to which it committed itself yesterday. Parliament undoubtedly has the pgwer; but considering all the circumstances in which this legislation was submitted to Parliament and to the country during the election preceding the constitution of this Parliament, I say that this Parliament cannot very well now go back on the principle of that legislation.
This Act has been in force for three years. I concede that it has not been a very popular measure with certain sections of our people. It is not popular, it is quite true, with many members of parliament. I do not question their right to that view or to opposition to the measure. I appreciate fully the basis and reasons for their opposition to the Act and their prejudice against it. The measure was not popular amongst certain civil servants and I think the Act was made unpopular with the public by the unjustifiable attitude of many sections of the Civil Service at one time or another since the introduction of the Act. There has been much confusion, of course, by reason of the enactment of such legislation. That was to he expected; it was unavoidable; you could not cast away the Civil Service Act of 1908 and insert in its place the present Act, with the very important and almost violent changes which it includes, without creating con- ' fusion. But the present law has been in force for three years; it is beginning to be understood; it is becoming popular with the masses of the people; it is becoming more acceptable to the Civil Service than ever it was; and as the days go by, it should become more acceptable to members of Parliament and they should be glad to have upon the statute books of this country legislation which would do away with the harrassing and disconcerting duties attaching to matters of patronage in connection with appointments to the public service.
If it were not for the Civil Service Act of 1918, the're would be thousands more

people in the public service than there are to-day. It is true there are ten or eleven thousand persons more in the public service than there were in 1914, but it is not difficult to understand the reasons for this increase. The Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, the Soldiers' Land Settlement, the Income Tax Branch of the Finance Department, the Pensions Board, the Record Office, the Air Board, and sections of the Militia Department, are all practically new departments; they are war departments; they are incidents of the war. Their growth and development and the employment of many persons within those different branches of the public service was not due to the Civil Service Act, but was, as I say, one of the incidents of the war. I fancy that if one were to go through the various departments with a view to ascertaining the number of persons within the service, he would learn that there are no more persons engaged in the public service to-day than there were in 1914, and I say that the tendency in the future will be to reduce the number. Why? Because there is no incentive to-day to create new positions, for the reason that no person seeking appointment and no person seeking the creation of a new position or office, knows who under the competitive system will obtain the appointment. Now if Parliament and the country are serious in wishing a reduction in the Civil Service Staff to proper proportions, they certainly should not desire a reversion to the provisions of the Civil Service Act of 1908 and its amendments. The Civil Service Commission and the Act deserve credit for some of the things that have taken place in connection with certain departments of government. Great improvements are to bo made, so far as the number of persons employed is concerned, in the Post Office Department and the Customs Department. I have not personally seen the report of the Commission to the Government, but public rumour would justify me in saying that several hundred persons are to be retired from these two departments, and I believe I am right in saying that this can be done without injustice to the departments and without in any way lessening their efficiency. This means a saving of money, and surely this is a time, with our mounting expenditure, with our taxation now already at the breaking point, when we should restrict public expenditure for all purposes, but particularly should we protest against the creation of unnecessary

public offices and the appointment of persons unnecessarily to public offices.
Are not these retirements from the Post Office and Customs Departments due to Griffenhagen's investigation, and not to the Civil Service Commission?

My hon.
friend and a great many other hon. gentlemen have repeatedly stated that Griffen-hagen and Associates and the Commission were one and the same body. Now, for the purpose of my hon. friend, this afternoon, he is willing that they be regarded as separate entities. Griffenhagen and Associates were the employees of the Civil Service Commission; they were employed by that body; the Civil Service Commission were authorized by statute to engage assistance. Griffenhagen and Associates were not employed by the Government, and the work performed by these gentlemen in connection with the reorganization of the Post Office and Customs Departments was practically the work of the commission. If we revert to the position suggested by this bill, it will be utterly impossible to reduce the Civil Service staff in any department. On the contrary, you will see the staffs in several branches of the service in Ottawa and outside, immediately begin to grow.
I should like to refer the House for a moment or two to the splendid work done by the Civil Service Commission in connection with the Printing Bureau. I have in my hand a report made to the Civil Service Commission by Mr. A. L. Lewis, who was one of the members of a committee of three practical publishers who were invited by the Civil Service Commission to make, in the first instance, a preliminarv survey of the organization of that department. The reorganization of that department, I take it for granted, is pretty well known to hon. gentlemen of the House. It was put into operation partially in 1919 and completely last year. Early this year Mr. Lewis and one of the other gentlemen who, with a third, composed the membership of that committee, made another survey of the Printing Bureau, just for the purpose of ascertaining what improvements had actually been made. I cannot very well read the whole of this report to the House, but I wish to read a short extract to give hon. gentlemen an idea of the practical value of the work done by the commission in the reorganization of the Printing Bureau, and the economies effected. Mr. Lewis states:
There has been effected a reduction in staff over all three branches, from 1,171 on June 1. 1919, to 749 on October 20, 1920-a reduction of 35 per cent.
Some of the heaviest reductions: in the Composition end from 368 to 180, or 50 per cent; Bindery from 281 to 159, or 42 per cent; Stationery and Distribution combined from 160 to 94 ; or 40 per cent; Proof Room from 65 to 26 or 60 per cent.
The pay roll covering Printing, Stationery and Distribution Branches for the present fiscal year should show a decrease of approximately 30 to 35 per cent, or in the aggregate from $425,000 to $475,000.
I shall not ask the House to listen to a further reading of the report.

Who is Mr. Lewis, and
what connection did he have with the Civil Service Commission? Is not he to be given the credit?

As I explained a few moments ago, Mr. Lewis was a member of the committee appointed, I think, by the Governor in Council to make a preliminary survey of the Printing Bureau, and to report showing if any practical reform was possible in that department, and if so, in what respects it could be reorganized.
What was his business?

I stated before that he was a publisher or printer, and that the other members of the committee were also, I think, engaged in the same business. Mr. Slack, of the Montreal Gazette, now deceased, was also a member of that committee. They made a report which was submitted by the Government to the Civil Service Commission, requesting the commission to proceed with the re-organization of the department; and I do say-and perhaps this will be an answer to what is in my hon. friend's mind-* that the actual re-organization of the Printing Bureau could not have been carried out by Mr. Lewis and his colleagues because the work required men of special experience. I say that the employees of the Civil Service Commission who did the work are entitled to the credit. I admit that this committee, composed as it was of practical men, might very readily have perceived, as they did, the objections to the operations of the department, and suggest obvious reforms. That they did, and for it they are entitled to a great deal of credit.
Now, I venture the statement that if the Bill now before the House becomes law, that the economy of $450,000 effected in the Printing Bureau in the last fiscal year will be entirely lost, and we shall very quickly

revert to the condition of affairs when it will cost anywhere from half a million to a million dollars more to run that department than it does to-day. You cannot reorganize the public service, you cannot reduce the numbers therein, unless the whole force is entirely removed from political influence, and such is the great value of the Civil Service Act, because, the motive for the creation of new positions having been removed, positions will not be unnecessarily created.
I want to make this further point: we are embarking to-day upon the experiment of Government control and, practically, Government operation of railways, and when the Grand Trunk has been acquired, our railway system will probably involve a mileage of considerably over 20,000 miles. I think I can safely say to-day, to the credit of the Government and its immediate predecessors, that the railways, in so far as they were subject to the control of the Government, have been remarkably free from political influence. I have heard that statement questioned by some of my friends on this side of the House, but I do affirm, without any fear of successful contradiction, that the railways of this country have of late been remarkably free from political influence. Why? I say, Mr. Speaker, that this is due merely to the fact that the Civil Service Act of 1918 was passed and has since been in operation. The effect of that Act upon the public mind was such as to make it possible for the Government, or members of the Government, to permit the operation of our railways free from political influence and political patronage such as were known to exist in the years gone by. If that Act is destroyed, and if the Bill now before the House becomes law, then I declare that the railways of this country will become a machine of the political parties, in which case this country might as well get rid of the railway system which we own and control, and endeavour to make some disposition of it that might give it a show for its existence. Some hon. gentlemen may say that there is very little connection between the fact that the Civil Service Act is-in force,-and that therefore appointments and promotions are free from Government control,-and the operations of the railways, which do not come under the Act. But hon. gentlemen know the psychology of the public mind as well as I do, and they will readily perceive how easy it is to secure public approval of the operation of the railways without political 
influence, when you have the great body of civil servants of the country under the Civil Service Commission and altogether free from any political influence or control.
There is another reason, I think, why the Civil Service Act should be allowed to stand as it is,- for the present at least, and why this Bill should not pass. I refer to the matter of preferential treatment given to returned men in appointments to the public service. Hon. gentlemen will remember that back in 1916 an Order in Council was passed making all appointments. to the Civil Service, whether in the inside or the outside service, subject to a certain qualification, in regard to returned men. I think I had better read the Order in Council:
In making all appointments to the Civil Service, whether in the inside or in the outside service, preference shall be given to those candidates who have served overseas in His Majesty's Forces during the present war, and who have been honourably discharged therefrom, especially to those who, through disability occasioned by active military service, are unable to fulfil their previous occupations.
In 1918, a further -Order in Council was passed, as follows:
In all competitive examinations held under the Civil Service Amendment Act, 1908, persons who have been on active service overseas in the military or naval forces of His Majesty, or of any of the Allies of His Majesty, who have left such service with an honourable record or who have been honourably discharged and who obtain sufficient marks to pass such examinations, shall, irrespective of the marks they have obtained, be placed in the order of merit, on the list of successful candidates, above all other candidates.
Such was the position of affairs in relation to preferential treatment of returned men in appointments to the public service in February, 1918. Naturally, these provisions, as contained in the Orders in Council, would be incorporated in the legislation following, namely, the Civil Service Act of 1918, and I shall read section 39 (a) of the Act, which is as follows:
Provided, however, that in all examinations for entrance into the Civil Service, persons who have been on active service overseas on the military or naval forces of His Majesty, or of any of the Allies of His Majesty, during the present war; who have left such service with honourable record, or who have been honourably discharged; or, when any persons who have served as aforesaid have died owing to service overseas, the widows of such persons, and who in either case obtain sufficient marks to pass such examinations, shall, irrespective of the marks they have obtained, be placed in the order of merit, on the list of successful candidates, above all other candidates.
I submit that this provision of the Civil Service Act in respect of preferential treat-

ment for returned men, can operate only under that Act as it stands to-day. The Bill before the House repeals it, I would say, as regards fifty or sixty per cent of the total service. It is actually impossible to carry that section into effect if the Bill before the House becomes law. Further, no means are provided in the Bill for giving preference to returned men, and I doubt whether means can be so provided, for the reason that appointment upon competition is very largely done away with by the Bill, as is also promotion upon the competitive basis. I do not see how the Bill could be amended to safeguard that provision as contained in an Order in Council passed in 1916, and further supported by an Order in Council passed in 1918, and later by the legislation-
Will the hon. gentleman permit me a question, because he seems to have a brief for the Civil Service Commission and of course he will have all these facts-
No, no.

-would he be kind enough to inform the House what percentage of the returned soldiers appointed have been appointed as permanent civil servants, as compared with the other appointments that have been made by the Civil Service Commission? That is the point at issue.

I am sorry but I cannot answer my hon. friend's question. It is altogether too big an order for me to answer offhand and I would need to have access to the records of the Civil Service Commission to inform myself. But my hon. friend knows, just as well as I do, that thousands of returned men have been appointed to the public service.
Nearly every one of them has been fired by the Civil Service Commission.

I say this
to my hon. friend, and I say it to the Government:	If they desire to restrict
the operation of that section in relation to the appointment of returned men to the public service, if they wish to withdraw the preference given returned men in whole or in part let it be said so; that may not have been the intention of the framers of the measure, but very largely it is the effect of it. Now, as I say, if it is desired to amend section 39 (a) of the Civil Service Act let the Bill make provision for it
17 9i
clearly so that we can understand the possible effect of the thing if it becomes law. I do not say that this section should always remain in the Civil Service Act. We may be approaching the time when it should be amended somewhat, there probably will come a time when it should be stricken out entirely from the Act; but it has been a provision of the Act highly regarded by the returned men, it has done a great deal towards the rehabilitation of many of them, and it should only be cut out, or amended, or restricted in any way, after due deliberation.
Will the hon. member tell us what percentage of the higher appointments, if any, have been given to returned soldiers?

I cannot
answer that question either.
Practically none.

I should say a great number of men have been appointed to the higher positions but exactly what number, of course, I cannot say.
Now, further, Mr. Speaker, I want the House to understand this point. It may be that the Civil Service Act of 1918 proceeded too far, I can quite understand any hon. gentleman raising that point, but when it is raised I should like the privilege of debating it, I should like to see it come before the House in a clear-cut fashion so that we may be faced with a definite issue. It may be that the rural postmasters should be excluded from the operation of the Act; it may be that manual labour should be excluded from the operation of the Act; but there is no necessity of introducing a Bill for that purpose. If hon. gentlemen will turn to clause 38 (a) they will find a section framed with that express design; I am in a position to speak with some authority upon this point. That section is as follows:
-the provisions of this Act shall not apply to positions in connection with the Government railways or any railway owned or controlled by His Majesty, or to any position on any ship of His Majesty until the Governor in Council
otherwise directs	in any case where
the Commission decides that it is not practicable to apply this Act to any position or positions, the Commission, with the approval of the Governor in Council, may make such regulations as are deemed advisable-
Now, Mr. Speaker, when the Act was drafted it was foreseen that it might be difficult or impracticable to carry out certain of its provisions, and that it might

some time in the future be desirable to remove certain classes of public servants from its operation, and, that was the purpose of that section. For some reason or other which I have never been able to understand, the Civil Service Commission undertook to make appointments to His Majesty's Ships-I do not mean the naval ships but the ships controlled by the Marine Department. For a certain time they made appointments to this part of the public service; I do not know why they did, or where they got their authority for it, but at least they did it. Last July they submitted to the Governor in Council a recommendation to withdraw this class from the operations of the Civil Service Act and they were withdrawn. Now I am sure if the Government feel that rural postmasters and manual labourers, for example, should be withdrawn from the operations of the Act, and they ask the Civil Service Commission to meet them face to face to discuss the suitability and practicability of such a suggestion, the commission would meet them in a fair spirit and I have no doubt they would reach a right conclusion upon it. I do not hesitate to say that very many strong reasons could be given for the elimination of these two classes from the operation of the Act, although I do not say that I would so change the law at the present momment. And my reasons for not doing so now would be these. In the first place the Civil Service Commission affords the best safeguard that the returned men will be given the preferential treatment required by the Act and which I think represented the judgment of Parliament and the wishes of the country.

Will the hon. member
show me where, in any single instance, any body representative of the returned soldiers has passed a resolution endorsing the Civil Service Commission?

The returned men will have an opportunity of making their views known to Parliament and the country. I cannot speak for them; but I say I would object to making that change at the moment for two reasons: First, the Civil Service Commission affords a safer assurance for preferential treatment in the appointment of returned men to the public service than would be afforded if the appointments were made by the Governor in Council. For the wellbeing, comfort and happiness of my 'hon.

friends opposite who are members of the Government I would like to see the Act remain as it is. In these difficult and trying days when there is so much unemployment, is not the public treasury better safeguarded by the intervention of the Civil Service Commission in the appointment of manual labourers, than if that duty were thrown upon the departments of government who inevitably would be influenced-I know I would be myself and I believe they would be-by demands from constituents for employment of one kind and another? And, Mr. Speaker, the House knows just as well as I do that the creation of public positions, merely for the purpose of affording employment, will never solve the difficulties which are presenting themselves to us today. Therefore let me make this suggestion, Mr. Speaker, that if the Government really desire to withdraw certain classes from the operation of the Act, let them invoke section'38 of that Act; let them request a conference with the Civil Service Commission. I am sure they will be met in the proper spirit and that both parties will endeavour to do what is right in the circumstances.
Now, I purpose to briefly go over some of the provisions of the Bill. It is for me at least a difficult measure to understand, and I am not clear what the draftsman intended when drafting the Bill. I would ask hon. gentlemen to accompany me as I go over the several clauses, which are few in number. Subsection 1 of section 1 states that the Civil Service Act:
-in respect to organization and changes in organization, changes in classification, appointment, transfer, promotion, salaries and increases of salaries-
Shall not include:
Manual labourers. . . . post masters. . . . professional, scientific and technical officers.
I desire to add another word to what I have already said in respect to manual labourers, and that is that the lexicographer will have to conjure up a new definition of the term "manual labourer" if they would include all who would be appointed to the public service under subclause (a), if it became law in its present form. Manual labourers to-day are, after all, controlled by the Government or the departmental heads, and there is really no purpose to be served by the amendment. Casual labourers employed for less than thirty days are selected by the heads of departments without regard to the Civil Service Commission. If em-

ployed for more than thirty days those heads of departments must submit a list of the same to the Civil Service Commission, accompanied by a certificate which reads as follows-this is the form used in the Public Works department:
I certify that the employment of the above person is necessary for the efficient carrying on of the work of the department. The selection has been made without reference to personal or political consideration and strictly on the merit principle, as between persons applying or available for such positions. The appointee has satisfied me as to his qualifications. The appointee is suitable as to age, character and habits. The salary is fair and reasonable and does not exceed the rates approved by the Department or prescribed by the Civil Service Commission. The above-named civilian was employed only after efforts were made to obtain the services of a returned soldier and none were found to be available.
In Ottawa the Civil Service Commission have an employment bureau, and heads of departments requiring any short-time employees or manual labourers go to that bureau, where they are furnished with a list of those available. That list is practically given to the Civil Service Commission by the Great War Veterans' Association. If manual labourers are required outside of Ottawa the practice is to use the employment bureaus established under legislation of 1918 or 1919 and directed by the Minister of Labour. There the Great War Veterans' Association also list those of their men requiring employment. Those bureaus are co-operating with the Civil Service Commission and departmental heads, and so far as manual labourers are concerned the situation is very satisfactory; nobody is complaining, the returned men are protected according to the spirit of the Act, there is no loading of the Civil Service because of the watchfulness of the Civil Service Commission, and the departmental heads do not want to go back to the old conditions.
Subsection 1 also refers to postmasters. I think if ever the time arrives when certain of these positions should be excluded from the operation of the Act, the exclusion should not be so wide as is indicated in this section. I think it would be quite sufficient if it were merely extended to appointments to rural post offices; and, of course, I am not admitting that even that should be done.
Subsection (c), however is the very objectionable portion of the proposed enactment. It covers:
Professional, scientific and technical officers employed for the performance of duties as such.
Proceeding with subsection 2 it will be found that it provides that these three classes shall thereafter:
-be appointed, promoted, transferred and otherwise regulated-
As they were before the passage of the Act in 1918. Now, just imagine what would come within the classes of "professional, scientific and technical officers." I fancy it would include one-half of the Civil Service in Ottawa. All lawyers, doctors, engineers, architects, draughtsmen, actuaries, accountants; technical men of the Mining Department would come within its scope; also a great portion of the staff of the Department of the Interior-all within the Reclamation Service, the Natural Resources Branch, the Parks Branch, the Water Powers Branch, the Topographical, Geodetic and other branches of that department; technical men in the Marine Department; technical men in the Naval Department; all the Air Service; a large proportion of the Militia Department, and a great portion of the Finance Department as constituted at present.
We had experience of the equivalent of this in the Act of 1908, where under section 21 it was provided:
If the deputy head reports that the knowledge and ability requisite for the position are wholly or in part professional, technical or otherwise peculiar, the Governor in Council, upon the recommendation of the head of the department based on the report in writing of the deputy head, may appoint a person to the position without competitive examination.
Large numbers improperly got into the service through that clause, and one can readily see how it could be greatly abused. That was our experience. But taking this sub.-C section 1 literally, which provides that all professional, scientific and technical officers in the Inside and Outside Services are to be employed by the Governor in Council, nothing would be left but practically the clerical and stenographic services. Now under subsection 2 of section 1 the salaries of these persons are to be fixed by the Governor in Council making the appointment, which doubtless will be out of alignment with the remuneration to that part of the Civil Service which remains under the operation of the Civil Service Act. The result would be great variations in remuneration and consequent discontent in the Civil Service; there would really he a recurrence of the position which we sought to avoid in the Civil Service Act of 1918, that is, of paying different salaries to different persons for doing the same class of work.

Mr. Speaker, I do not
wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman but I do not think it is customary in this House to go into an analysis of a Bill on its second reading.

I am not

Provided that, except in the case of manual labourers, and professional, scientific and technical officers as above described, no person appointed shall be retained in employment-

Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The custom of the House is well established, that an hon. member should not upon the second reading of a Bill attempt to discuss in detail its several clauses. It must, however, frequently occur that it is impossible to discuss the principle of a Bill without referring to the different principles involved in its different clauses. I hope that the hon. gentleman will not depart from the custom of the House by going into the intricate details of any particular clause. On the other hand it has been held many times that some license should be conceded to hon. members addressing the House and that they should not be precluded from referring to the different clauses of a Bill in so far as they may affect the principle of the Bill itself. This doctrine is laid down in May's Parliamentary Practice at pages 356 and 351

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the House that this is a second reading debate and, therefore, questions and comments by other hon. members are not in order.
Under the Bill which we are discussing the recommendation for promotion is made by the minister on a written report from the deputy.
For merit.

For merit,
and the recommendation will be only in respect of one person, it could not be for more; whereas under the statute as it now stands anybody in the particular branch or department can take the examination for promotion. Human nature is what it is and we all know, particularly those who have had political experience, that ministers and deputy heads in many cases will

not recognize merit and make promotions purely upon merit. Further, we all know that deputy heads are very impressionable to the representations of the political head of the department and the principle of the Act as it stands should not be departed from.
The other clauses of the Bill in respect to transfers and the establishment of new classes are absolutely unnecessary, and though they would not change the exact position of affairs at the present moment, still, it would be much preferable to allow those particular provisions which are proposed to be amended by these sub-clauses, to remain as they are.
If this Bill becomes law, the matter of establishment of rate of salaries would rest with the Governor in Council. The Government proposes by this Bill so to amend the Act that only as regards appointments which are clearly left with the commission, would salaries be fixed by the Civil Service Commission and as provided under the legislation passed in October, 1919. The result of the passage of the Bill will be that all manual labourers, postmasters as designated in the Bill, and all professional and technical men, inside and outside, are withdrawn from the operations of the Act. Practically the only persons who could be appointed to the public service at Ottawa by the Civil Service Commission would be the clerical staff. As regards the Outside Service, the only appointments to be left with the Civil Service Commission would be the customs and post office branches,-that is, such as do not come within the definition of scientific, professional and technical classes. This Bill, if it were ultimately enacted, destroys the fundamental principles of the Civil Service Act of 1918. It practically destroys the Civil Service Commission. I hope it will not become law; I hope Parliament will decline to accept it. This vis not the time to amend the Act in this way, and if it is to be so amended, that might very well be done later when we have a little further experience with the Act.
After the next election.

I am not now interested in the next election. In the interest of the country and without detriment or injury to any political party now or in the immediate future, the Act might well be left as it now is until we have further experience with its operations. Therefore I move, seconded by Mr. Reid (Mackenzie) :

That the word "now" be left out, and that the words "this day six months" be added at the end of the question.
Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister
of Justice) : Mr. Speaker, I was somewhat surprised to hear the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) open his observations by complaining of a lack of candour and frankness in the manner in which this Bill was laid before the House. It seems to me that to whatever criticism either the form in which the action was taken or the substance which it was intended to lay before the House, may be open, certainly the manner of laying it before the House is not open to the reproach addressed to it by the hon. member. He has chosen to ignore entirely the explanation that accompanied the introduction of this Bill-it was, however, sufficiently clear-and he has attached himself to a minute discussion of the terms of the Bill as it is now before the House. And this in face of the clear and unmistakable declaration of the hon. minister who introduced this Bill that he laid all its provisions before the House as tentative, with a view to the entire measure going to a committee of this House in order that that committee might consider it, and might come to such conclusions as they would be advised were proper conclusions upon the whole subject of the desirability of a modification of the existing Civil Service Act, and if they reached the conclusion that modification was desirable, then, what particular modifications were required. It was pointed out that the particular list of officers referred to there was not in-, serted as being anything more than by way of example, that it was not intended to send this Bill to the .committee with the Government proposing that those particular classes should be the classes, if any, to be exempted from the operation of the Civil Service Act. Nor, in like manner, was it intended to put before the committee as the Government's proposals, which the Government intended to insist upon, the other particular proposals contained in the Bill.
There is behind the introduction of this measure-I am only repeating what has been said already-no purpose to depart from the fundamental principle that inspired the enactment of the Civil Service Act as it stands. That fundamental principle was that such a method of appointment of public employees should be found as would at the same time be most conducive to the efficient carrying on of the business of Government, and consistently
with that, as would assure, as far as that was possible, that in the making of selections of persons to fill positions and carry out the duties I have referred to, there should be the minimum influence of any consideration other than the fitness of the person concerned.
May I ask if the Civil Service Commission has asked for this legislation, and if not, if it has been asked for by anybody?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Civil Service Commission have not asked for these amendments.

They are opposing
them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In some respects, I believe it would be fair to say that they were opposing them. I would judge by what I have seen of newspaper utterances that the Civil Service Commission take the position, which, after following the hon. member (Mr. Maclean, Halifax), seems also to be his position, and that is that whatever complaint may be made, whatever suggestion of possible improvements may be made, the Civil Service Act stands there like the Ark of the Covenant upon which no man especially no member of Parliament, and least of all, the Parliament of Canada, must lay an unholy hand. I do not think that is any unfair description of the position taken by the Civil Service Commission.
If I might digress for a moment I will take up at this stage a point of the hon. member for Halifax, because these observations seem to make it appropriate. The hon. member practically admits that with regard to the suggestion as to rural postmasters and manual labourers their appointment ought to be taken out of the hands of the commission. He admits that there is a very strong case for taking them out, but his position is that the Civil Service Commission could take them out if they wanted to-notwithstanding the fact that for three years they have not wanted to, and that there is no indication in any of the public utterances at all events of some of its members that the commission would give one moment's consideration to taking them out. The hon. member tells this House that because there is power for the commission to decide that matter, it must not be free for this House to consider it or even to think about it-because, Mr. Speaker, it must be borne in mind that the legislation as it is now before the House, with the explanation that accompanied its

introduction proposes in substance, that this House should sit down, in the first place in its committee, and then by itself upon the report of that committee, and make a study of the Civil Service Act, to see whether or not that Act has attained those two purposes which I pointed out at the outset as being the purposes for which it was enacted. Now, however perfect in the opinion of its authors that legislation may have been when enacted, and however perfect it may be found to be upon examination at the present time, surely there cannot be reasonable objection to its being carefully examined. I think the hon. gentleman himself would admit that, whether rightly or wrongly, there has grown up in the minds of a very large proportion of the public of this country

we had evidence in a recent debate in this House that there has grown up in the minds of a large proportion of the members of this House, the representatives of the people of this country, members sitting on both sides of the House, members occupying leading positions on the opposite side as well as upon this, a very strong impression that the authors of the Civil Service Act (we have all got our responsibility, I am not repudiating it) had overshot the mark. That belief naturally generates a discontent upon the part of those who believe that the public interest is injuriously affected by that overshooting of the mark, and also upon the part of those who believe that it may work injustice to themselves. Now, of course, the first consideration is the great consideration. We must not, in dealing with questions of Civil Service, run away with the idea that the occupancy of positions in the Civil Service is a competition between individuals to get a job, and that the one great consideration is to see that there shall be absolute and minute carefulness in the weighing, even to a grain, of one individual as against another. I would be the last to deprecate the doing of fair justice as between individuals, but that is not the great purpose of Civil Service legislation. Its great purpose is to assure efficiency in the public service. Now, it has been put forward very strongly from different sources, and men of experience in the public business of this country, men competent to judge, men long years removed from any political action, men above the suspicion of using their positions to favour individual friends, have expressed in strong and clear terms the opinion, that the public service of Canada, the business of this Government, and

therefore the business of the people of the country, was suffering by reason of the enforcement of certain provisions of the Civil Service Act. I am not here to say that that opinion is well founded; I merely say that it exists-and I may add that that opinion operates to create a very strong pulblic sentiment throughout the country adverse to the particular Civil Service Act that is now in force and operation. What is proposed to be done in that existing condition of affairs? It is proposed to ask the House to sit down and study the question to see whether the objection to the Civil Service Act is, or is not well founded. Surely the hon.- gentleman, who is so strong an advocate of the present law, should welcome an opportunity of addressing such eloquent pleas as he has offered in defence of it to a body that would be appointed for the purpose of hearing both sides of the question, a body that will have authority to go into the facts, and ohe that will not be, as we are, powerless in the face of contradictory statements of fact, -in short, a body that will be able fully to verify all the facts and finally reach a conclusion based upon those facts; and submit such a law as may commend itself to their judgment. When that is done this House will be in a position to take the report that is submitted to it, with the evidence that will have been gathered, and then decide as to who is right and who is wrong in reference to these divergent views concerning the operation of the Civil Service Act. If the hon. gentleman's faith in the Act is justified, why does he not look forward with confidence to the vindication of that faith by this method? I think he will admit that, if his view be right, an immense advantage will be gained if, by the report of the committee and the subsequent action of the House, there is brought home clearly to the people of the country, to those who believe that the Act is not operating satisfactorily as well as to those who are convinced that it is, the conviction that the Civil Service Act is all that he claims for it. On the other hand,-because, after all, I am satisfied that the hon. gentleman does not assume the impossibility of his being mistaken-if the result of careful examination of the whole question establishes that he is mistaken, and that there is room for improvement in the existing law, improvement that will not abrogate the fundamental principle of the law, but will furnish machinery that will operate more smoothly and more efficaciously so as to enable the wheels of

the Government business to run as they ought to run, then I think it will be conceded that it is only proper to have this matter thoroughly investigated. That is the question that is put before the House to-day with the perfect frankness and candour that characterized the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Spinney) in introducing this measure on behalf of the Government.
Now, I realize that the form adopted to arrive at this result may, from the point of view of strict regularity, be a proper subject, perhaps, for justifiable criticism. The action taken might have been taken, certainly, and perhaps better taken, by a simple resolution looking to the appointment of a committee of the House to go into the whole question and report a Bill if that committee thought proper to do so. The only reason why the House finds itself face to face with this tentative Bill is that it was considered to embody the more important objections that have been raised against the operation of the Civil Service Act as it stands. Those important objections having been raised, it was thought that if the matter came to the committee in the shape of a Bill which, upon its face, would propose to deal with those objections in the manner set forth in this Bill, it would bring the whole subject before the committee in a more concrete form and would serve to call to their attention in a specific way the principal suggestions made for modification, looking, of course, to improvement in the law. It was felt that the Bill would provide the committee with a starting point in their operations, putting before them in a concise form the principal questions that have arisen in the public mind as well as in the minds of members of this House with regard to the operation of the Civil Service Act. As has been said and repeated, certainly with perfect frankness, there has been, and is, no intention on the part of the Government to put these particular provisions forward as a policy upon which they have decided; and with perfect candour I admit that the form in which this matter is brought forward may perhaps be open, as I have suggested, to justified criticism. But surely the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) and other hon. members do not desire to deal with a subject of this kind as a pure question of formality. Surely we all want to sit down and take up this grave question seriously and deal with it as practical men. For myself, I am not here to express any opinion in advance as to what modifications if any, should be made in the present Civil Service Act. But certainly no one could listen to the discussion that took place in this House the other day without at least recognizing that there arose a question, with which we were all face to face, as to whether or not, in the adoption of the Act which we now have upon the statute book, Parliament had not, to use the expression of certain hon. members on the other side, overshot the mark. After all, I think I may fairly say that the sole principle underlying the whole speech of the hon. member for Halifax is that this particular Act is as irrevocable as the laws of the Medes and Persians,-that not only it is susceptible of no change, but that ic is so sacrosanct that Parliament must not even consider for a moment whether or not it is properly open to improvement in the public interest. May I be pardoned if I say that the hon. member (Mr. Maclean), could, with better advantage have reserved the very earnest arguments which he made in support of the Bill just as it stands, to be addressed to the committee, at the proper time and in the proper place, when the representations which he and any other hon. gentlemen who advocate the retention of the present Act in its entirety may desire to make, it will be open to them to make.
I have said that all of us have our share of responsibility for that legislation, and I have no desire to disclaim mine, but I think we might all of us wisely see-in the wide divergence, at all events, that has arisen in public opinion as to the wisdom of many of the provisions of that Bill-an admonition to its more immediate authors, as well as to the rest of us who took the responsibility of supporting it, that the Bill, at the time of its introducing and passing through the House, might have been the subject of more careful study and more profound consideration, and, perhaps, of a more thorough informing themselves on the part of those who had to deal with it as to the real facts and the real results to be expected from certain provisions.

May I ask my right hon. friend a question: Does he seriously suggest to the House that this Bill, involving amendments which are vital to the Act of 1918, should be sent to a committee, without the House discussing the principle and deciding whether that course should be adopted? I was very clear to say that I, at least, would not have objected to this Bill going to a committee if the proposed amendments to the Act had not been

such a substantial character. Surely my right hon. friend will not argue here in the presence of intelligent men that this Bill should go to a committee in its present form.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The best evidence that I am not asking that the Bill should go to a committee without discussing it is that I am discussing it at the present time. I have not suggested that the Bill should go to a committee without discussion, I am endeavouring to discuss whether it should go to a committee.

I have no desire to offend my right hon. friend. I understood him to say that he is not going to discuss the principle of the Bill, and I understood his remarks to be in criticism of myself because I object to the Bill going to a committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is quite right. I do not know that I would qualify it as criticism but I was endeavouring to make a reply to his argument-and what is embodied1 in this amendment-that this Bill should not go to a committee. I was trying to demonstrate just why the Bill ought to go to a committee; I am not arguing that it should go without the discussion of the real principle involved. The hon. gentleman apparently desires to argue, in the face of what has been said and repeated, that this Bill is not put before the House as involving any other or greater principle than this-that the time has come when it behooves the House to sit down and look over its work of three years ago and endeavour to ascertain which of the very divergent views as to the satisfactoriness of that work is the well-founded view, with the purpose of taking action according to the decision that may be reached. That, as I understand it, is the real question of principle that is presently before the House. I have admitted that if more importance be attached to technical form, to printed words, than to the real substantial thing that is intended to be laid and is laid before the House, it may be technically argued that printed words, admittedly put forward as tentative, may lead to an inference as to the adoption of a principle which is perhaps one that this House would not be right in adopting. But I do not think that I can make more clear than I have endeavoured to make it that this Government is not asking the House to adopt such a principle as may be inferred from a literal adherence to the words that are in 
the sections of the Bill. Now, taking the view that I have taken, and which I ask the House to take, it becomes quite useless for me to follow the hon. gentleman through his somewhat prolonged arguments-I do not complain of that, however, because to defend the whole Civil Service Act would necessarily take a very prolonged discussion,-through his somewhat prolonged, I will even say, forcible, arguments, in support of the principle provisions as they now exist. Let me only repeat this once more: The purpose of the Bill is not to subvert the fundamental principles of the legislation which it is suggested may be susceptible of amendment. If there be anything in this Bill which is subversive of those fundamental principles I for one, and I am sure the Government, do not ask any committee, and do not ask the House, to adopt it. That is one of the things that the committee will consider. As I have said, the problem that goes to the committee is this: Is a modification of the existing Act both' possible and desirable which, while it will not be inconsistent with the fundamental principles which I have indicated as underlying the Act, will be more conducive to efficient administration of the public business and more conducive to prompt and proper selection of those who are to perform that public business? If any of these particular provisions goes too far in one direction or the other it will be for the committee in the first instance, and for this House in the last instance, to correct it.
Now the hon. gentleman made some reference to an endeavour to get at results through "subterranean passages." I trust he will reconsider that suggestion. I am at a loss to see what "subterranean passage" is suggested to anybody. I hope we will all keep to the upper air and at the same time avoid "getting up in the air," and be able quite sanely and on terra firma to deal with the problem which presents itself.
The hon. member seemed to devote himself with particular energy to the proposition that something in this measure involved a possible deprivation of the returned soldier of the right which he is entitled under the existing law. He seemed to think that for any purpose for which a competitive examination disappeared, with that disappearance at the same time went the possibility of preference being given to the returned soldier. I do not think the hon. gentleman was particularly fortunate in the special provision which he selected

as the particular object of attack. It is not the competitive feature of the present law that gives the preference to the returned soldier. On the contrary, in order that the returned soldier should have the preference it was, and is, absolutely necessary to insert a special provision to say that in these cases the competitive principle shall not apply, because though there be men who have surpassed the returned soldier on the competitive examination the returned soldier, having * gathered enough marks to enable him to qualify is to be entitled to the position. The danger to the returned soldier came from the competitive system, and that danger was removed as I have stated. Now the hon. gentleman argues that it will be impossible to provide that safeguard in a law which may possibly do away entirely with the competitive system in respect to certain positions. I am sure his anxiety is quite unnecessary. I venture to say that the claim of the returned soldier to a legitimate preference will be as safe in the hands of a committee of this House as it possibly can be in the hands of the Civil Service Commission. And let me point out to him that in regard to certain positions which this Bill is intended to cover, if it should pass there would be absolutely nothing impossible in providing adequate methods for the perfect recognition of the right of the returned soldier to preference in the filling of those positions. It is just as easy, if the appointment be in the hands of the minister or of the Governor in Council, to make provisions looking to the protection of the right of the returned soldier as it is under the present existing legislation. The section then referred to and which, as I pointed out, need not necessarily disappear under this Bill, is section 39a, dealing with the returned soldier. We had then a special insistence on the right of the Civil Service Commission to deal with these classes,-classes which, almost by the hon. gentleman's admission, ought to be taken out of the Civil Service Act. I have already dealt with that part of his contention.
Now, the hon. gentleman says that he objects to this Bill going through without privilege of debate. As far as the question now before us is concerned, he has had the fullest possible privilege of debating it. This committee will assure him an additional opportunity of debating upon the * merits the existing legislation and any suggestions that may be made to modify it, and he will have before the,committee,
or certainly upon any Bill which the committee may report to this House, the perfectly clear-cut issue which he desires.
The hon. gentleman has indulged in verbal criticisms of the Bill, telling us that the term "manual labourer" according to any dictionary would cover practically the whole Civil Service. There will be opportunity for verbal correction of that kind either in committee of the whole House or in the committee to which the Bill has been referred. All the apprehensions which arise in the mind of my hon. friend I think will vanish after a little reflection. With regard to manual labourers, the hon. gentleman tells us that this provision is not necessary because that is the way they are appointed now. Surely if that is so it is at least more honest to say to the world: Why, the way that it is being done shall be in accordance with the law. Can there be a better justification for the suggested modification?
The hon. gentleman has great apprehension as to the operation of the provisions dealing with promotion. I do not propose to discuss those provisions now. I do not suggest that they are perfect, and, as I have said, I am not putting them forward as the last word upon the subject. They are put forward in order that a question which has given rise to serious differences of opinion among competent and disinterested people may 'be thoroughly threshed out. I confess that personally I do not sympathize with the hon. gentleman's distrust of the deputy heads in this matter. I do not know if my personal experience is different from that of other ministers of this or previous Governments, but I have not found, in dealing with the deputy head with whom I am particularly concerned, that he was prepared to yield his opinion to mine upon any question where the performance of his duty was involved. I noted that the hon. gentleman when dwelling upon the danger of political influence entirely omitted from his reading of the clause, whether intentionally or not, the proviso that the recommendation of the deputy head and approval of the minister must be accompanied by certification of qualification from the Civil Service Commission itself.

It would
not amount to anything, because the Civil Service Commission could only deal with the one appointee recommended by the political head of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What this committee
will have to consider, and the House

ultimately will have to deal with, is the question whether in the light of experience the principle of promotion, subject to examination by an outside body, works in the interests of a better administration of the public business. But when the hon. gentleman talks about political influence, he should remember that no man is to be appointed whom this disinterested body does not certify to be perfectly qualified. In view of that, what is the serious danger to be apprehended from the operation of political influence? So far as the Civil Service Commission can bring us any guarantee under any system, there would be a guarantee under this section that no man would hold office who was not perfectly qualified. So that under that system every appointment will be subject to the absolute veto of the Civil Service Commission. Now, that is no small restriction, for that power of veto is, after all, the last word. With his unbounded confidence in the commission, I think the hon. gentleman would find in that veto a very material guarantee of the protection of the public interest.
In resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, let me repeat once more that the purpose of this Bill is not to subvert the fundamental principles of the Civil Service Act. The purpose is to study whether or not it is possible, consistently with those principles, to ameliorate, in the interests of public business, certain conditions in respect to the service as they presently exist and to provide a method which will act more promptly, more effectively and just as usefully in the public interest as does the present system, without presenting certain of the objections which have been made to the working of the present Act. There is on the part of persons who look at the matter disinterestedly, persons competent to judge, a very strong prejudice against the method of application of the principle that underlies that Act, which has generated a strong prejudice against the principle itself. We would like, if that be possible, to remove that prejudice, and the best way to remove preconceived and mistaken ideas on either one side or the other of this question is to have the question thoroughly threshed out in the presence and to the knowledge of the public of Canada by a body that shall have opportunity to hear, and whose duty it will be to hear, all that is to be said from one point of view or the other. Parliament' may then, in the light of the knowledge so obtained, determine what action, if any,

it ought to take, determine what modification the existing legislation is susceptible .of to the public advantage, and expressly what form any such modification ought to assume.

I think that no one on either side of the House can find very much fault with the Opposition for taking up the time that has been occupied in the discussion which has proceeded this afternoon on the second reading of this Bill. A very meagre programme was set forth by the hon. member who introduced the Bill (Mr. Spinney), who said:
In this Bill there are incorporated in italics some tentative restrictions which cannot he considered as final, hut rather on account of the Bill not 'being allowed to be presented in blank.
That is not a very considerable bill of fare; it is not very much of an indication of what the Government do or do not intend to do. The Government do not tell us why amendment of the Civil Service Act is desired; they do not tell us wherein the Act has failed; they do not tell us what amendments are deemed necessary. They simply say: You shall take this holus bolus; the matter will go to a committee,-in order, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) has just said, that the committee may suggest modifications. The Minister of Justice said also that the modifications suggested ,in sub-clause (a) of clause 1 were "only there as an example." Well, how far may it go? If the classes set out in section 1-manual labourers, postmasters, professional, scientific and technical officers-are only "examples," where, I ask in all fairness, will1 these amendments take us? To my mind there is no doubt about the answer to that question, in view of what we heard the other day in regard to the census enumerators. Talk about rending the veil of the ark of the covenant so far as the Civil Service Act is concerned-hon. gentlemen would leave it absolutely exposed, without a shred of covering. To my mind, Sir, there is only one conclusion that the House and the country can come * to, and that is that it is the intent of the Government slowly to strangle the Civil Service Act, in connection with which such promises were made prior to the last election, and to go back to the old system of patronage.
Sir, I supported most heartily the amendments made to the Civil Service Act made in 1918, because I believed that the Bill then introduced was in the interests
