of the country. I believe that so far it has worked well, and 1 am sure that there is not one single member of the House who desires to go back to the old importunities of the patronage system. It was a ease of men here and men there until the stress of politics became so strong that appeals could not be withstood and positions were created in order to take care of influential party men. Are we to have a recurrence of that condition? Are we to go back to conditions as they prevailed prior to 1918? The provision in italics referred to by the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Spinney) covers the following classes:
(a)	Manual labourers whatever may be the
character of the work upon which they are employed and whether they are paid by the hour, the day, the week, the month, the job, or the piece ;
(b)	Postmasters whose remuneration consists In whole or in part of a percentage on the receipts of the office.
(c)	Professional, scientific and technical officers employed for the performance of duties as such.
So far as the first two classes go, I am free to confess that I do not think the Civil Service Act has worked out well. I did not see at the time how it could possibly work out well, because these appointments must be made on the spot. But I would like to ask hon. gentlemen who are much more familiar with the meaning of the English language than I am-the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), for instance-what he would say to this: "professional, scientific and technical officers employed for the performance of duties as such." Why, Sir, if you go down the calendar with this list where do you stop? Who is nbt professional? Who is not a technical officer? As I understand it, any officer is a scientific officer who is applying his best energies and his best intellectual ability to bring about the best results from the work in hand. The one who does that, has attained some degree of scientific accomplishment. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), astute lawyer that he is, would argue any judge and jury into acceptance of the principle that under subclause (c) of section 1 you could appoint any one on earth to anything at all. It is patent; it is self-evident. I say without fear of successful contradiction that if you take the classes mentioned in italics and follow that idea out to its logical end, so far as the Civil Service and the Civil Service Commission are concerned we are absolutely back to
where we were and the Civil Service Act might as well not have been passed.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the Civil Service Act has been only a short time in operation-a matter of three -years. Does the Government think it is fair that the Act should be looked upon as unworkable, looked upon as calling for such fundamental changes, after so short an experience? Surely three years is hardly sufficient to enable the various officers to get shaken down into their positions and to know just what or what not to do under various circumstances. No precedents can arise in the short space of three years. I say that the Civil Service Commission should be given a chance; they should be given a further opportunity to work out this Act. The Act should not be in effect repealed at this stage and another substituted in its stead.
It is proposed that the Bill shall be referred to a committee. That committee will be a partisan committee, the majority consisting of government members. Any recommendations or suggestions made by government members on that committee will ultimately be carried. And what will the Government do? The Government will simply hide behind the skirts of the committee and say: "the committee have found that this provision or that provision is not working properly and the committee have made this recommendation we feel, as we have appointed this committee and have provided for modification-as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) has remarked-"that we must carry out those recommendations." Therefore, any change which the Government desires to make will be made by that committee, and the Government will have an opportunity of hiding itself behind the skirts of that committee.
This Bill ought not to be proceeded with now for two reasons. With the exception of a very small percentage of the people, the country is absolutely satisfied that political patronage has been done away with. The country heaved a sigh of relief when it knew that appointments were not being made here, there and everywhere, a position sometimes being created for the purpose of giving it to a needy supporter of the Government. The people heaved a sigh of glad relief when this Act came into force; they are perfectly willing to stand by it; they want to see it tried out; they feel that in these times of extravagance, the Civil Service Commission is a bar as between them and the Government, and they

know that only those men who ought to be appointed will be appointed for positions that should be filled. For those reasons, I thoroughly and heartily support the amend-' ment of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). This is not an opportune time for the enactment of such a Bill as this. - The people do not desire the proposed legislation, and I believe that if the real truth were to be spoken, there are not many members of the House who desire to see this Bill passed.
I will not go into the Bill clause by clause. I could not improve on the explanation given by the hon. member for Halifax. All that he has said is, in my opinion, absolutely and entirely right, and I, therefore, have much pleasure in supporting his amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know that any one has made a demand in this House that the motion which is at present before it-I do not mean the amendment-should be passed and that the matter should be sent to a committee which has been appointed, without an opportunity being given for discussion. I have not heard any one make that demand. It is open to question where the brunt of the discussion had better come, whether we should have it after we have the matter looked into by this committee and have its views sent back to the House, or whether we should take the discussion now and reduplicate it and more after the committee has made its investigations and has given back its report and its recommendations to the House. As a mere matter of business, probably we would get further ahead and accomplish the result in quicker time if, with the explanations that have been made, the committee should receive this Bill in its present form, a tentative matter all through, and should do its work upon it. In that way we shall have the benefit of the information received in the committee and the views as expressed by the committee. There is no disposition on the part of the Government, nor, I am sure, in the House, to send this matter direct to a committee without allowing members, if they so desire, to express opinions with regard to it.
As regards the whole question, there is one view which makes me favourable to the reference to a committee, and I will tell the House just what that is. The Civil Service Act has been in operation in its present form for some two years or more, and 
during that time it has operated, I am bound to say, under difficulties more than ordinary. It has been subject to misapprehensions and to prejudices and to lack of information more than would have ordinarily occurred in times which were less troublesome and less filled with labour and work by the House and by members of the House, than times of war. It must not be forgotten either that the Civil Service Commission had to do a very large and difficult work in the matter of classification of the Inside Service, and when afterwards the Outside Service was added, the commission did a still more extended work in classification and in appointments outside of Ottawa. No three men, however appointed, however diligent and however capable, could have undertaken and have progressed through that period of classification, with both of those branches of the Civil Service thrown upon them, and given complete satisfaction either outside or inside. But the fact that they had to do it, and under the somewhat troublous conditions under which it was performed, has, I think, made them subject to more criticism and opposition than they otherwise would have received. I have had a good deal to do with the commission itself and with those who have been watching and observing and helping to carry out the work of the Civil Service Commission as applied to the different departments, and I have very great sympathy with that commission, with all its three members, in the *work that has been placed before them and the difficulties with which they have had to labour. I never have wanted, nor do I at present want, nor am I at present in favour of having, the Civil Service Commission and the Civil Service law as it is to-day bowled out of existence in so far as its principles and work are concerned, without some more investigation than has been given to it already. With an adverse opinion in the Civil Service at first, which adverse opinion, I am bound to say, is at present very largely if not entirely overcome; with an adverse sentiment on the part of those who favoured and who had worked under the old system; with an adverse sentiment from certain methods employed and certain agents which it has used -a sentiment which has been pretty strongly expressed-in the interest of the working of the Civil Service Act itself and of the working of the Civil Service Commission, I believe it is better that an opportunity should be given for those who have misjudged the commission, for those who have lack of information-as most of

us have-for those who are opposed to particular instances about which they may or may not know the facts, to get all together before a small committee of both sides of this House, with the Civil Service Commission there as well, and get the information which is vital and true. What has happened this afternoon? One hon. member gets up and says: To my mind, so far as my information goes, there is not a returned soldier who has received one of the higher positions; maybe there is one, but not many, and I doubt if there is one. Another member says: I have not the information, but I think I am correct in my impression that several of them have been given high positions. So there is scarcely a thing that comes up on which there is not a lack of information on the part of the individual member or person. Now a Civil Service Commission, and the system itself, does best when it has the clearest foundation of information, and of approval upon the basis of that information, to go upon, and rather than have this opposition from lack of information continued, opposition from certain particular instances which may be explained, or because of some particular lines upon which the commission works and where a better method might be followed'-rather than have all this backwater, this continued and uniform opposition to the work of the commission, is it not better that we get together in a small committee of intelligent men from both sides of the House, and get down for a few days to looking into the exact facts and circumstances?-so that if our information has been wrong, if our impressions have been false and our prejudices unwarranted we may relax our opposition and say: Yes, we understand better now the workings of this commission, and consequently we will raise our hands for it rather than against it?
While I am in favour of the principle of doing away with political patronage- always have been, am still, always shall be-I am not so bigoted in the matter as to say that any certain incarnation of the principle of no patronage in the Civil Service Act is the final word which may be said on the subject and that no improvement of method is possible. So I am not at all averse to having the matter reviewed by members of Parliament, who certainly have a first and vital interest in it, and who also have the public service at heart. Whatever you may say when you want as a partisan to attack another partisan, I believe it is a fact that members of Parliament on both sides have the public interest as the first thing in their minds, though, of course, they may have different ideas as to how that may best be served. I believe, that sentiment being there, that it will be a good thing to put this matter before a committee; let all parties meet together. If we have had misinformation, if we have had prejudices, if we have had a lack of apprehension as to what was actually being done, we will have the benefit of finding out the facts, and our action will be different afterwards. When that committee finds and reports to the House, this House will take into consideration any points which may be brought to its attention as to deficiencies in the Act, as to what things might better be done in another way, as to certain employments that might very well be exempted from the Act entirely.
My hon. friend (Mr. Pardee) who spoke last said, very frankly, that with regard to two of these classes he was of opinion that they might better have never been undertaken by the Civil Service Commission, and he mentioned my own name in connection with the census enumerators. Now, if country postmasters and manual labourers, temporary and casual, might very well be exempted from the Act, what plea would my hon. friend put in for the census enumerators, some 10,000 or 12,000 of whom have to be selected for temporary employment of a month or even less, in every part of this Dominion from the Yukon down to Sydney, with the liability of a large percentage of them falling out at the very last moment and with no possible means in the hands of the Civil Service Commission to fill those vacancies which occur? With reference to the census enumerators, when the matter came up I talked the matter over with the Civil Service Cimmission, and said:	There is the census; there is what
we are to do; does the commission feel like taking that on? The commission, after they had thought it over, sent in their decision, that they would give that up as a part of the Civil Service work, and that they would confide it to the department itself. I believe there are some things in which that might be done to the advantage of the working of the system as a whole, but I would be very careful how far that went
My hon. friend (Mr. Pardee), and my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) say that with regard to scientific, technical and professional men you may so extend that as to eliminate from the Civil Service Act maybe three-fourths of the whole Civil Service. I do not believe you

can do it. I do not believe that any Civil Service Act would be a decent Act if it was so framed that that could be done. I do not take the definition of my hon. friend's of a scientific man. If I understood him, you could include in his definition of scientific man every man who applied the best that was in him to get the best out of the work he was doing. I do not think that that definition would suit the thing at all. I do not think that is a definition which could be applied under that clause. But I do say that if you allow technical, scientific and professional men to be exempted from the Act under certain conditions, you will make easier and better and more efficient that part of Civil Service work which is, without doubt and honestly technical, professional or scientific. But in any Civil Service Act which included that as a portion of the Act it should be put in such a definite manner that it never could be abused in the way my hon. friend has suggested.
Therefore, in conclusion, I say that I am impelled to this action, not because I want to get rid of the Civil Service Act, not because I do not believe-I always have believed-in the principle of the elimi-ation of political party patronage from the Civil Service of the country, but because I believe under all the circumstances a review of the whole matter by a small committee of both sides would result in an actual and positive benefit to the working out of the Act. Afterwards, when what they give us as the result of their investigations comes here, the House can exercise, its own j udgment-and certainly the Government will exercise its own judgment-upon it.

Does not the minister think it would have been better to have had that investigation before the Bill was introduced? Is it not an unusual thing to introduce a Bill of this sort and then have the investigation afterwards?

My hon. friend has heard what his lord and master, in a legal sense, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) has said with reference to that, and it is not necessary for me to make that argument as well.
At Six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I wish to say 
a few words in support of the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). In doing so I might direct the attention of the House to the circumstance that possibly no hon. member in this House is as well qualified to speak on this measure and the significance of it as my hon. friend. He was the member of the Government who introduced the legislation embodied in the Civil Service Act of 1918, and, having been the one to introduce that legislation, he naturally is better informed than any other member can possibly be as to its importance and the significance of any amendment that may be offered. For that, amongst other reasons, I think the House may assume that every argument the hon. member has put forward is one to which it should listen with a great deal of attention. Indeed, I might say that every argument presented by the hon. member against the present Bill, with its proposed amendment, is practically the same argument which as a member of the Government he urged in support of the original Act in 1918.
The Act of 1918 was one which purported to extend the powers of the Civil Service Commission and to lessen the powers of the Governor in Council with respect to appointments, promotions, transfers, and matters of classification. The legislation which we have now before us in the form of a proposed amendment to the Act of 1918 is intended to lessen and restrict the powers of the Civil Service Commission and to increase the powers of the Governor in Council in all those particulars. If there are any gentlemen who should be careful in amendinents they propose to the Civil Service Act, in view of the professions which they have made throughout this country in regard to the part which the Government has played in Civil Service reform, they are the members of the present Administration. I shall not repeat to the House-the matter has been mentioned in a previous debate-the professions respecting Civil Service reform which were put forward in the Conservative Party platform of 1911 and advocated by the then leader of the Opposition, subsequently Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), and the gentlemen associated with him. One of the outstanding features of the so-called Halifax platform was the reform of the Civil Service which it was intended to introduce if the hon. gentleman came into power. In 1917, at another election, a great deal was said

about what should be accomplished in the way of Civil Service reform, and still more about what would be accomplished in view of the fact that the Government which was seeking power was a Union Government composed of members of both political parties. It was urged that, having in the Union members of both political parties, that the Union Government was in a position to do, in the matter of Civil Service reform, what it would be practically impossible for any strictly party government to do.
The Unionist administration was returned and a measure of Civil Service reform was introduced by the hon. member for Halifax, as a member of the ministry, and it received the support of all members of the Government. After the measure had met with this support, a great deal was said throughout the country, from one end of it to the other, as to the significance of what had been achieved. I shall not attempt to review the many assertions, made by members of the Government as to the measure of credit to which the Government was entitled in virtue of this reform, but I should like to refer to one or two speeches made within the last few months by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Calder), who accompanied him on a tour through Western Canada. Hon. members will recall that in the fall of last year the Prime Minister and the President of the Council addressed a large number of meetings in the western provinces. It would take too long to go through the different speeches delivered on that occasion; but, having looked over the press reports of some of them during the short recess between six o'clock and the present hour, I find that, in practically every meeting addressed by these hon. gentlemen, they took great credit to themselves for. being members of a government that had abolished party patronage in this country. They claimed that there was no longer such a thing as party patronage in Canada, and that as a consequence, we had now a measure of Civil Service reform which had completely changed the public service.
I have in my hand a report of a speech which was delivered at Winnipeg on October 25. It is an account of a meeting addressed by the President of the Privy Council in the course of that trip through the West; the Prime Minister was also present at the meeting. In the Winnipeg Free Press of the next day-October 26-
the President of the Council is reported as follows, under the caption "Party Patronage":
Tou ask what has been done. I would say that 99 per cent of party patronage is gone-There may be a shade of it to-day, but you will have to look mighty hard to find it. Prior to 1917 under both the Liberal and Conservative Governments, Ottawa was filled with patronage hunters all the time. They were hanging around the Parliament buildings day and night. No, they are not there now.
We also had to deal with the question of Civil Service, and again the Civil Service has been lifted out of politics. Now, I don't say that things are entirely altered in the Civil Service. In putting our new law into force there have been mistakes here and weaknesses there, but we have undertaken a great reform on behalf of the people of Canada, and I hope also this reform will stick and that we will never get back to the old order of things. Is that what the people want? Do you want us to go back to the old order of things?
That was the kind of profession with which my hon. friends opposite started their campaign of political meetings. I find that at meetings at Vancouver on October 29, and at New Westminister the same day, similar statements were made. For example, in a telegraphic despatch of the Canadian Press which appeared in most of the newspapers of October 30, the President of the Privy Council is reported as having said:
Party patronage was practically a thing of the past in Canada.
Then, again, at Lethbridge on November 20, in a special despatch to the Montreal Gazette giving an account of the meeting held in Lethbridge that day, the following appears:
Patronage was practically gone, said Mr. Calder, and he gave the Union Government credit for its extinction.
But the President of the Privy Council was not the only one who gave credit to the Union Government for the complete abolition of the patronage system. I have here an account of a meeting held at Medicine Hat on November 10. This report, which appeared in the Toronto Globe of November 11, and which is similar to reports in other Canadian papers, has the following from my right hon. friend the: Prime Minister:
Patronage in the Federal Service is gone. Down at Ottawa, and in Ontario, where they watch us more closely nothing has brought us more criticism than our course in this thing. There were more workers in the Government Service because Government activities had been greatly extended, but they were not party workers.
Now these are the professions which my right hon. friend and his colleague were

making through the West, with regard to Civil Service reform.
When was that?

That was in November of last year, after my right hon. friend had become Prime Minister. He and his colleague were taking the credit for having abolished party patronage. Under these circumstances. I think the House was entitled to more accurate and definite explanation of the principle involved in the Bill which is now before us than the one which was presented by my hon. friend from Yarmouth (Mr. Spinney) who, as one of its members introduced the Bill on behalf of the Administration.
Reference has already been made to the manner in which the Bili was introduced. On its first reading, as has been pointed out by an hon. gentleman on this side, practically nothing was said as to what the Bill involved. All that my hon. friend from Yarmouth mentioned was that there were certain italics, or italicized words, in the Bill which was to be introduced, but that they were really to stand for nothing-they were put in as a kind of blank form and later on if a committee had occasion to consider them, the House would see their significance. Nothing, Mr. Speaker, was before us to denote what the Bill might contain when it was brought down, or what these italicized words might be. Now we discover the whole measure is to afford a return to party patronage. I think it was on Thursday of last week that the Bill was introduced, on Friday before the Bill had had its second reading, my hon. friend (Mr. Spinney) moved that it be sent to a select committee, a course of procedure to which you,
I think, Mr. Speaker, directed the attention of the House as being, to say the least, somewhat irregular. However, we were given at that time two positive assurances from the Ministry-one from the hon. gentleman who introduced the Bill, as to what purported to be its principle, and the other from the Prime Minister who also gave what from his point of view, was the principle or significance of the measure. Let me read to the House what was said by the hon. member for Yarmouth with respect to the principle of the Bill. My hon. friend said:
If the introduction of the present measure, which proposes to amend the Civil Service Act of 1918, leaves the impression on the mind of any hon. member that the House is receding from the main principles of that statute, namely the abolition of patronage, he may at once dismiss that thought.

There, Mr. Speaker, was a statement from the ministry that the Bill which is now before us was in principle in no way receding from the principle of the Civil Service Act of 1918. What was the principle of the Civil Service Act of 1918? It was to give to the Civil Service Commission certain powers with respect to appointments, promotions, transfers and classifications, which had therefore been exercised by the Governor in Council and which had been a matter of party-patronage. That was the principle of the Act of 1918. What is the principle of the present Bill? It is precisely the reverse. The principle oi this Bill is to take away from the Civi Service Commission certain powers whicl were given to it in 1918, and to transfei these particular powers-powers wit! respect to appointments-powers with respect to transfers, promotions and classifications-to the Governor in Council. 1 say, Mr. Speaker, that in the statement which I have just quoted the Government completely misled the House in regard to the significance of this measure.' What did the Prime Minister say? He, I regret to say, was equally misleading. He rose in his seat and gave as a reason why the House should not even look at the Bill, that it was simply a skeleton. My right hon. friend used the word two or three times. "This is simply a skeleton and there is nothing to it," or words to that- effect. It was simply so many dry bones as it were. Well, now that we have the Bill and have begun to examine it we find, so far as the skeleton is concerned, that the purpose is to reduce the powers of the Civil Service Commission to a skeleton. That is the purpose, not to present to the House a skeleton measure which it shall fill' out, in accordance with the recommendations of the so-called committee which is to investigate it.
Mr. Speaker, if there is one step above another which it has been difficult to accomplish in this country, it has been that of getting rid of party patronage with respect to the vast majority of appointments to the public service. Reference was made to the effect that the Civil Service Act has only been in force for a short time, that it has not had a very long trial. May I point out that the Civil Service Commission has existed since 1908. The original Bill to reform the Civil Service was introduced in that year by the administration of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. From 1908 down to the time of the introduction of this Bill we have had no move for a lessening of the powers of the commission.

We did not have until after the Act of 1918 the kind of criticism of the administration of the Act by the Civil Service Commission to which we have listened of late. We had a measure which was so generally approved that hon. gentlemen opposite said: "We will extend the principle of this Act so as to embrace the Outside Service as well as the Inside Service," and they have taken credit to themselves for so doing
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, in speaking this afternoon, said virtually that the purpose of referring this Bill to a committee was to take account of criticisms which had been made of the Civil Service administration, to take account of the prejudices that existed in the mind of the Civil Service and of the general public against the Civil Service Commission and its work. He said he thought it was in the interest of the Civil Service Commission itself that there should be this inquiry by a committee of the House to remove prejudices and doubts, and to help to give the Civil Service Commission the standing which it should have before the country. Well, Mr. Speaker, if that is the purpose which the Government has in mind, why does the Government not go about it in a regular way? If it is necessary to have an investigation into the working of the Civil Service Commission, and desirable to have a committee of Parliament to show the strength of that institution, why does not the Government appoint a committee for that special purpose? Let a committee of the House be formed for the purpose of inquiring into the workings and methods of the Civil Service Commission. The Government has appointed many committees for different purposes, let it appoint a committee for this purpose; and then, if the committee finds that the Civil Service Act is in need of amendment in any particulars-and no doubt it is susceptible of amendment in many particulars-let the committee make suggestions of its own initiative and bring these suggestions forward for the action of the House.
I submit, Sir, that this measure cannot be construed as a measure for the protection of the Civil Service Commission. It is not a Bill advantageously to amend the Civil Service Act of 1918, but in reality it is a Bill to destroy that Act in very large part. Let me repeat as respects the Act of 1918 that it gave the power of making certain appointments to the Civil Service Commission.	-<
This Bill specifies three classes of appointments which are to be taken out of the hands of the Civil Service Commission and transferred to the Government, thereby permitting the Government's followers, in all certainty, to make recommendations which the Governor in Council will act upon. That is a step entirely in the wrong direction.
I wish to direct the attention of the House to the fact that these classes do not include all classes of appointments that may be brought within the scope of the measure. We.have been told by hon. gentlemen opposite that the blanks or italicised portions of the Bill are only inserted for the purpose of amplification by a committee. Now we have a committee named, and if we look at its personnel I think we shall find it is not a little partisan in its nature. It is open to that committee to add any further classes of appointments it pleases.
With regard to promotions, members of the service in doing their duty faithfully feel a sense of security by virtue of the fact that when promotions are now to be made, examinations must be held by the Civil Service Commission, they know that those best qualified in any particular branch or department will in all likelihood receive appointments on merit. This Bill proposes to take away that power of examinations from the Civil Service Commission and give the power of promotion to the minister of each department in consultation with his deputy minister, and without any action on the part of the Civil Service Commission other than approval of the appointment when recommended. I am told that within the last few months, in connection with appointments in the post offices of some of the larger cities, among others Hamilton, Toronto and Vancouver, men who had worked in those offices faithfully and skilfully received the appointments on merit after recommendation by the commission, but that tremendous pressure was put upon the Government to waive the power of the Civil Service (Commission and to allow appointments to be made by the minister of the department on the recommendation of friends of the party. I believe, and I think with a good deal of justification, that the pressure which came from that direction, as well as pressure which has come from all directions on the other side of the House, to return to party patronage, is the real cause and explanation of the measure which is now before us.
The same thing is true in regard to transfers between the different departments. Under the Civil Service Act these trans-

fers can only be arranged by the Civil Service Commission on merit. This Bill proposes to take away that power from the commission and give it to the minister of a department acting with his deputy minister and in conjunction with the minister and deputy of some other department, and leaves the commission with nothing to do but approve the transfer made. We know well enough that the most unfortunate think that can happen to the Civil Service is to bring the Commission and the Government into constant conflict, as will be the case under this Bill under such a policy. The whole purpose of Civil Service reform was to remove altogether the possibility of ministers acting in a partisan way, this Bill simply attempts to restore the old conditions.
Another feature which has not been mentioned this afternoon, and Which I think in some respects is possibly the worst of all, is that the Bill gives to the Governor in Council power to undo all the work that has been done by the Civil Service Commission and by the various expensive commissions which the Government have appointed from time to time to classify the Civil Service along lines that seem to be in the public interest. I will not refer to the specific section of the Bill, but hon. members will see that the Government has taken to itself the power as respects classification in different departments to change, divide, amend and even to abolish any existing classification, and the only power that the Civil Service Commission has in respect to abolitions effected in this manner by the Government is the right to present a report to the Government for its consideration. It does not reserve to the commission even the right of approval, but simply gives, its members power to report to the Government, and of course on this report the Government is to be at liberty to take such action as it may think fit.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these facts make it wholly apparent that if a measure of this kind is permitted to pass even the second reading it is setting back in a very real and substantial way the efforts of the past few years in the direction of Civil Service reform, and I therefore hope that the House will support the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and, by preventing this Bill being advanced a stage further, destroy that possibility altogether. If there is need for consideration of any amendments to the Civil Service Act, let it be undertaken by a committee of the House formed

for that particular purpose, but do not let us proceed with a series of destructive enactments in the form of a Bill every one of which tends to weaken the scope, the authority and the usefulness of the Civil Service Commission.

Mr. Speaker, it would not be proper for me to enter into a defence of the various sections of the Bill now before the House. The only question for consideration is the principle of this Bill, and that, putting it in the plainest language, is: Has the time come when it is necessary for this House to review the legislation passed during the stress of war dealing with the question of Civil Service reform? The Civil Service Act created a commission, and the members of that commission have undertaken the appointment of civil servants from one end of the country to the other. The general impression given to the public through the propaganda established by this commission is that the commission is indispensable to the efficiency of the service. I must say it is a very clever propaganda, equal to that of any organization I know of, and even members of the commission are not afraid to stand up at meetings and defy this House, of which without a doubt they are the servants.
There is no other country in the world where a body of this kind is permitted to make appointments to the Civil Service. The impression has been created that we are following in the footsteps of Great Britain. Such is not the case at all. The Civil Service Commission in Great Britain is purely an examining and not an appointing body. I have never heard of the Archbishop of Canterbury being appointed by the Civil Service Commission, nor the Commander of the Grand Fleet, nor ambassadors, nor the heads of the British Consular service,-none of these important appointments are made by the British Civil Service Commission.
Now, our Civil Service Commission has not only arrogated to itself the right to appoint everybody, from a stevedore, on a steamship, up to the commander in chief of the militia, but it seems to resent the suggestion that Parliament has any control whatever over its own actions. A great many complaints have been made to members and to the Government with reference to the manner in which this commission is carrying out its work. We have given it its fling for three years, it has not been interfered with by anybody,

and to my mind the time has arrived when this House should appoint a committee to consider whether this commission is doing its work in a proper manner and whether some amendments should not be made to the Civil Service Act.
In the first place, a commission of this kind is entirely contrary to British principles. We know that Germany has set up commissions and bureaux to carry on the work of civil government. The cities there are administered by commissions over which the .people have very little control. This commission is nothing but a bureau. It has all the ear marks of a Prussian institution, and it sets itself over its masters. After all, we cannot have representative or responsible government in Canada if there is any body of men above the law or above the will of the representatives of the people in Parliament. It is folly to say that you are going to give higher powers to a commission than you are going to give to the Parliament of Canada. The Parliament of Canada, if it is to retain its self-respect, must come to this conclusion, and support this idea, that no commission and no body of men in this country is greater than Parliament. The grandfather of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) fought against the principle of setting up some clique as supreme and above the people. His grandfather fought for responsible government and for representative government as well, and the result has been seen in the growth and development of our constitution. Now we are asked to turn back the pages of history; to go back to the old idea. I am very much surprised to learn that the leader of the Opposition supports that view, because it is quite contrary to Liberal and to reform principles as I understood them and as I followed the leaders of that party for very many years in their speeches and in their declarations. This body sets itself above Parliament, apparently, through its spokesman and they seem to take an attitude hostile to the members. Now, a great many complaints have been made against this commission, and the easiest way to have those complaints threshed out is by referring the matter to a committee of this House.
The hon. member from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) who spoke this afternoon, made a great plea on behalf of this commission so far as its attitude toward the returned soldiers was concerned. I remember very well that when the amendments to the Act
were before the House in 1918 I pleaded with the Government to place a returned soldier upon that commission. I fought almost alone on behalf of this proposal;
I wanted the returned soldiers to have a say. I failed to notice on that occasion that the suggestion received any support from the hon. member from Halifax. He was against the returned soldier then, so he must have seen new light, or he is simply trying to get the support of the returned soldiers to his claim on behalf of this commission. Before this commission began functioning the returned soldiers were getting their share of the appointments. I do not know of one single returned soldier who has applied to me for a recommendation to this commission who has been given an appointment-not a single one in three years, so that personally I cannot speak of the commission as supporting the returned soldier in any way. It is quite true that there is a small clique of returned soldiers in Ottawa who are called in to pass on boards and so on, and who get five or ten dollars a day for their services in this connection; and of course they are very strongly in favour [DOT] of this commission. But there are thousands of returned soldiers throughout the country who are not in favour of this commission because the commission has not given them a fair deal. When I say that I refer particularly to the permanent appointments. It is quite true that a lot of returned soldiers have been put into the service, but so far as permanent positions are concerned the returned soldier has been passed over by the commission. So far as the commission is concerned, the men who are made to quit their jobs and who are thrown out of employment in Ottawa are, as everybody knows, the returned soldiers. I say that the commission has not given the returned soldier, so far as I personally know, a square deal. I am going to sit on this committee, and I do not want any one to think that I am prejudging the Bill and that my mind is not going to be open on all these questions. But I say with all sincerity that the commission has not, so far as I personally know, dealt fairly with the returned soldiers and has no intention of doing so. The fact that there is no soldier on the commission itself speaks against the returned soldier in the first place, and everybody knows that the members of the commission have fought right from the beginning against having a returned soldier sit on the commission.

Now, this is a very serious question for the country, and I trust that members on both sides will consider it carefully. When all the railways except the Canadian Pacific are brought under government control, fully seventeen per cent of the positions available in Canada will be held by civil servants-between seventeen and twenty per cent. Jt is true that at present the railways are not under the commission. If the commission is such a holy body; if it is of such a high order, why do we not have the railways under their control? Why is the Pension Board taken from under their control? Because the men who are at the head of the Pension Board know very well that the sympathies of the commission are not with the returned soldiers or the pensioners, and that is why they fought against getting under the control of this commission. And if seventeen to twenty per cent of the people draw money from the Crown, surely Parliament should have some say. In addition to that, every effort is being made to unionize these bodies. There are already several unions in the Civil Service at Ottawa. The railways will always be doing something of the same nature, and unless the Crown adopts some such method as France had to adopt -that of compelling everybody in the service to take the oath of allegiance and join the army reserve-the country might at any time be turned over by the Civil Service to a foreign body, a soviet or something of that kind, because the number of people who will be available under the regulations of organizations of this kind will be very great. Apparently this commission speaks on behalf of the civil servants as against the Government and the people of Canada. That is the sad thing about it. I was very much surprised to see members of the commission take that attitude. I am sure that no one in Canada desires to take positions away from any person in the service, but every kind of obstacle has been put in the way of anybody inquiring or considering anything in relation to that service. Now, it is a very grave reflection on the former Liberal administration to contend that members are not capable of making recommendations for these appointments. I see before me a number of gentlemen who were members of the House during the late Liberal regime. The Government of that day, under the leadership of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, appointed a great many persons to the Civil Service and kept a firm hand on that service-because it needs a 
firm hand. I have not yet heard of a single officer appointed under the Laurier regime who 'has disgraced the appointment then made-and all those appointments were made on the recommendations of members. The same applies to the Conservative regime. The men who aie now running the service, the' deputy heads of departments, are all appointees not of the Civil Service Commission but of ministers and members of the House of Commons. What finer body of men is there in the world to-day than the men at the head of the Canadian Civil Service? Take the head of the Post Office Department, Colonel Ross, the most highly efficient officer that I know in any service in Canada, private or public. The same is true of the Department of the Interior, the head of which is Mr. Cory, and you can go over the whole list and find that these gentlemen were not appointed by this Civil Service Commission that goes around feeling peoples' bumps, and seeing what they know about conic sections and differential calculus. If men have energy and industry and common sense it counts for a great deal, and no Civil Service Commission can ascertain the quantity or the quality of a man's common sense. In England before the Boer war all, the appointments in the army were made by examination. A young man could not aspire to a staff position unless he was thoroughly conversant with higher mathematics, that is to say, unless he was well versed in algebr? and trigonometry and differential calculus and all these things. Well, when these young men went to South Africa it was found that with very few exceptions they were not capable of leading their men in action. Therefore, the method of examination was changed after the South African war, and questions of leadership, ability, common-sense and good judgment were taken into consideration as well as a man's ability in the higher mathematics.
The system of promotion that has been carried on by the Civil Service Commission and that has been so highly spoken of, is not a system of promotion at all, and I think when the committee investigates the matter, they will ascertain that most of the promotions that have been made during the past few years have been made without examination; that hundreds of people have been promoted in the service over people who had the qualifications. For instance a young man takes a qualifying examination for a higher grade than he has and he holds the certificate, and he has

paid his fee. When the time comes for him to be promoted to a higher grade, I will warrant that not one-quarter of young men like him who have passed those qualifying examinations have been promoted and that the balance of those who have been promoted have received their promotion without passing any qualifying examination whatever. What right has the Civil Service Commission to do that? The question will, of course, be discussed in the committee, and we will ascertain the numbers of such promotions then. Three or four weeks ago I put on the Order Paper a question in reference to the number of persons in each department who were promoted without qualification, and I have so far failed to get an answer from the Government. There is not a department that could not have given that answer in twenty minutes, but the answer has not been given because it would reflect upon the Civil Service Commission. We will, however, obtain that information when the committee takes the matter up.
When the commission appoint people in a member's riding, in most cases they appoint people without any qualification or not the proper people for the positions, but nobody can get out of the mind of the electorate the idea that the member is responsible. In my riding, I have not had an appointment for months since the commission began functioning under the new Act. I might say that when I came to the House in 1911 and there was a Conservative Government and I had a little say as to who might be appointed to positions in the service, I made inquiries to ascertain how many people in the service had been appointed from my riding during the last twenty years. My riding was represented for many years by the late Dalton McCarthy, a very able, intelligent man, and I think we have as intelligent and independent a body of men in my riding as can be found in any riding in Canada. The answer that I obtained was that only one solitary man had been appointed in my riding in 1888. Why should my riding be ignored? Why were most of the other ridings in the province of Ontario ignored? The reason was that most of the appointments were made from Ottawa, and to-day the Civil Service Commission is appointing three people from Ottawa to every one from outside. For that reason, we should investigate this matter and find out whether boys in outside ridings are not just as capable of filling positions at Ottawa as persons who sit around and have a family
pull with the commission. The trouble with the commission is that it is personal, family pull with them; it is not political pull. This applies to hon. gentlemen opposite just the same as to those who sit on this side. If there was any fairness to be shown as regards appointments, I would say: "Let the member, regardless of whether he is Grit, or Tory, or Progressive, nominate the candidate for the Civil Service." The member would surely know the best person in his riding. But that is not the way in which appointments are made. The appointments are all delegated to one authority, and if you are going to delegate such a tremendous power to one authority, you are going to have corruption and rascality and everything of that kind. I do not see the wings of angels sprouting on the shoulders of the members of the Civil Service Commission. They are human like everybody else and just as liable to go wrong.
I fail to see why they put people up in this House of Commons with briefs to fight their causes. If there is nothing wrong with them, they can afford to be investigated. If there is nothing wrong with them, why are they so anxious?
Who is to-day appointing people in the constituency from which I come? In the last election I defeated the man who is now leader of the Government in the province of Ontario, Mr. Drury. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), hon. members will bear in mind, told the House that the Civil Service Commission, when it wants to appoint anybody in a province, applies to the labour employment bureau. Who runs that bureau in my constituency? Who appoints it? Mr. Drury, whom I defeated. If a man is to be appointed from the Riding which I represent, the Civil Service Commission sends to Toronto; they make inquiry in my Riding, and who do you think bosses the job? Mr. Drury and his satellites make the appointment. Instead of my having some say in the matter, we have all gone to work and by self-denying ordinances, as they used to call this away hack in the history of England, we have deprived ourselves of the right of recommending anybody, and we have given the party in power in Ontario the right to pick and choose everybody who is appointed by the Civil Service Commission in Ottawa whom we are paying. The same thing holds good in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick; it holds in every province in Canada to-day, with this result, that none of the good old Tories and Liberal-Unionists are appointed

by these labour committees that have charge of things locally. Supposing I recommended a Liberal who voted "wrong " as they would say, in 1917, to a position in the service. Why, he would have no more chance to pass that Labour Employment Bureau at Toronto that is bossed by Mr. Drury than a chunk of ice has in a hotter climate

not a chance in a thousand. That is what is taking place, and we might as well face the issue openly, fairly and justly. This is something in which the members of the House will, I am sure, recognize that we ought to have something to say. They say: " Take the service out of politics." Is that taking the service out of politics? Why, that is giving the service over to the worst form of politics, to irresponsible politicians. Everybody knows that the Dominion Government has endeavoured in every possible way to be nonpolitical, especially in its appointments, and the result should be correct and right. What has happened? The appointments have all gone to the local governments, and there are some men sitting opposite waiting to hand in a name to them for some position. The appointee is always a strong supporter of the U.F.O. The Civil Service Act was not intended to be worked out in that way. If that is the case, and the investigation before this committee, shows that to be the case, we shall be quite justified in taking a number of the appointments away from the present body.
The facts of the matter are that we cannot de>] rive ourselves of responsibility in this Parliament. We have taken away our responsibility as far as we can and endeavoured to turn this House of Commons simply into a rubber stamp to pass appropriations to be spent by commissions and other people without any control by Parliament. That is quite contrary to constitutional usage. Constitutional usage means that this House is responsible for every dollar that is spent, for all appointments and for everything that this commission does. Therefore it ill becomes anybody to stand up for the commission and say: "Oh, the commission is so very great and holy that nobody shall touch it or find fault with it." It will be a sorry day for this country when we can establish a commission greater than the Parliament of Canada, and to do so is to lower the dignity of members of this House. This way of acting has proceeded far enough. Under the stress of war we were prepared to forego many things, in order that there might be efficiency; we deprived ourselves 
of any right as regards promotions or appointments of any kind that might interfere with what? With the efficiency of the service because we were fighting with our backs to the wall and we wanted nobody but the most efficient to be put into office. But those days are gone and we have been finding out that we have been very much deluded by the commissions we have appointed. We have found out that in many cases where we have trusted them, we have trusted them in vain. When this committee comes to investigate, no doubt the Government will be able to furnish cases that will surprise the House in reference to the operations of this commission, and I say that members on both sides of the House should have no hesitation whatever in voting for the second reading of this Bill so that it may be sent to the committee. If the evidence taken before the committee proves that the hands of the commission are clean, and that it is functioning in a proper manner, we will not interfere and no Bill will be passed. Nobody wants to interfere and have the appointment of petty officers all over the country. We want to be relieved of that as much as possible. But we do not want these appointments, and all the political influence and power that goes with petty appointments, to be handed over to our political enemies, to people sitting up at night wondering how they can destroy this Government. I may not agree with this Government all the time, but I think it is the best Government in sight, and I think the future of this country, its power and prestige, depends on the continuation of this Government for a great many years to come. For that reason I do not see why the House should be asked to indulge any more in these, as I call them, self-denying ordinaces, where we deny ourselves the right to appoint anybody or even to recommend anybody for appointment. A number of members know that if they recommend any person to the commission for appointment that act simply signs the death warrant of that party with the commission.
I say that the commission has failed to function on two counts. In the first place, they have failed to function in promoting people on merit. That will be proved to the committee without a doubt. One of the reasons why the commission was appointed was to see that promotions were given fairly to the people who had the qualifications. It will be proved that the commission has appointed hundreds with-

out the necessary qualifications; I do not hesitate to say that.
In the second place, the commission was intended to deal fairly with returned soldiers. Evidence will be produced before that committee to show that the returned soldier has got the worst of it right from the beginning. There are returned soldiers in the service who have had the necessary qualifications for three or four years and yet they have not received permanent appointments. Why? Because the commission just keeps a screw on them, and if a soldier looks sideways he is thrown out, and another man, a follower of this commission, who is generally a relative of one of the officials, is given the job. I know how it works out very well, and I could name cases if desired. Therefore, I say that the commission having failed to protect the soldier, we should investigate to find out why they do not protect him.
In the third place, one of the commissioners should be a returned soldier undoubtedly. For these reasons, and having no confidence in the commission as it stands,
I am quite willing, and I think the members of this House would every one of them be fully justified in standing up and seeing that this Bill gets its second' reading.

Do I understand that
my hon. friend considers that the Civil Service Commission is hostile to the returned soldier?

Not openly, but I say
that covertly they are hostile to the returned soldier. Why did they withhold the permanent appointment of hundreds of returned soldiers? If the returned soldiers had got their permanent appointments in proper order there would not have been 400 or 500 of returned soldiers thrown out of employment a few weeks ago, and no civilians. The civilians are not thrown out; it is always a returned soldier. We want to find out how and why that occurs. I have the interests of the returned soldiers just as much at heart as anybody here. Until this power was handed over to the commission, all the appointments in the service went to returned soldiers, but the minute the commission started to function, it appointed civilians, and leadslingers. Men who never went to the war got the pick of the appointments. That is the charge made by the returned soldiers, and we want to investigate and find out if it is true. For that one reason alone, I think this Bill should go before the committeee.
My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) made a long and discursive speech.
I never saw him deal with a brief so long before, although I have often seen him at it when he stood up for a poor case. He wants his friends in Halifax to get all the appointments; that is why he wants the committee to function. The making of appointments has only been transferred from my hon. friends around me to the local employment committees. I do not think even my hon. friends opposite like these committees to carry on, that is the U.F.O. I believe that the Liberals in Ontario are just as much against this system as the Conservatives.
What committee does my hon. friend refer to?
To the employment committees that each province has. ,

My hon.
friend is wrong in this case, for the province of Nova Scotia did not establish any.
I am creditably informed that these employment committees or commissions are in Nova Scotia.
They are, but they are appointed by this Government, by the Minister of Labour.

I am informed to the contrary. But let the committee investigate. I think the hon. gentleman, having made that charge, should withdraw his motion and see whether Nova Scotia has these committees. But my hon. friend does not want any investigation. He wants to sit on the lid absolutely.
No.

We can easily see whose ox is gored in this case. He is up to his old tactics as a blocker; he is one of the best blockers in this House; many a committee I have been at with him. My hon. friend from Halifax is a great stickler for constitutional usage. I am going to say a word or two in reference to his conduct in this House and elsewhere, which I think should be taken into consideration when he stands up to oppose a motion of this kind. I have a distinct recollection when I was a boy of a case where an hon. gentleman of this House, Mr. Dalton McCarthy, differed with his leader Sir John A. Macdonald, in his views. Instead of jumping over into an independent opposition and saying nothing about it, to his electors, Mr. Dalton McCarthy had the courage and

honesty to go back to his constituents. I was at the meeting, at the convention. There were close to 150 delegates there from the county I represent; and Mr. McCarthy said to them: "Gentlemen, this is one of the most memorable days of my life. I have called you together in convention because I have found that I cannot agree with the Government in its policy. There has been a vital difference of opinion between Sir John Macdonald and myself. I am following the constitutional practice. You gentlemen nominated me, picked me out to go to Ottawa as your representative, and then elected me. I am now placing my resignation before you, and it is up to you to say whether you approve of my conduct or not. If you, in convention, do not approve of my conduct in my difference with the Government, then I shall have to place my resignation in the hands of the Speaker, and another election will be held at which the people of the whole riding will express their views." Well, the convention debated for an hour-and-a-half, and then they passed a resolution approving his conduct. But if . the resolution had been to the opposite effect, he would have resigned, as a man of honour, and as a member of this House.
What has the hon. member for Halifax done? He has left the Government and jumped to the other side. Did he do that without consulting his friends in Halifax? They sent him here, and they should be consulted as to whether they wish him to oppose the Government without putting in his resignation. If things are to be carried out in his way, political honour is going to be absolutely destroyed; it will become a dead thing. How can the people have any confidence in a man whom they send down here to represent their views, if he is permitted to bolt the very next day, without consulting them, if he is going to backtrack on them in every possible way, and vote against their views and their whole position, without any reference to their political views. Now he is asking us to violate another constitutional principle, and that is the principle that asserts the right of Parliament to investigate the operations of a commission. There is no department of Government which should not come under the scrutiny of a committee of this House, and the Government has a perfect right to bring before Parliament, for investigation, any department or part of a department, which it is felt should be inquired into. The manner in which a department's activities are sub-
mitted to the consideration of Parliament is immaterial. It does not matter whether the subject comes up in the form of a Bill or otherwise.

Does the
hon. member, by this lengthy speech, wish to convey the impression that some one has opposed the appointment of a committee to make inquiries into the operations of the commission? No one has suggested such a thing, because that would be a fair proposition.

And that is exactly the proposition that is put forward in the Bill. The Government, in this Bill, have outlined certain reforms. They have frankly admitted that they may possibly be wrong, and therefore want the whole matter to be thoroughly discussed by a committee of the House, by whom evidence can be taken and all the necessary witnesses heard. But the hon. gentleman does not want any investigation; he wants to carry on independently, above the law, so far as the Civil Service Commission is concerned.
Not at all.

I do not think he will receive very much credit from the people of the country by trying to stifle investigation in regard to the operations of the commission, and prevent an inquiry to ascertain whether amendments to the Civil Service Act are desirable or not. I think that a period of three years is ample time for any commission to function without interference on the part of Parliament, and it is about time that the House of Commons took cognizance of the statements and reports we hear all over the country regard-try regarding the Civil Service Commission. I trust, therefore, that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, including my Liberal friends on the other side, who are supposed to stand for the principles of responsible government, will support this Bill. I have heard the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) repeat again and again that we must have responsible government. Well, here is his opportunity right now for ensuring the vindication of responsible government. I hope that he and his followers will support the Bill, send it to the committee and have the whole question thoroughly investigated. I am a member of that committee and I, at any rate, will take care, that fairness will be shown to all concerned. I do not wish to express now any view as to whether I approve of the Bill or not. E

believe that in some respects it might be open to amendment. Nevertheless, I must say emphatically that any attempt to gag the House, to shut off discussion, and to prevent investigation of the Civil Service Commission, does not look well coming from the quarter from which it does, and I hope the whole House will vote down the amendment proposed to the Bill.

I have listened closely to the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie), and I wish to say before going any further, that his arguments have produced on me an opposite effect to what they were intended to have. My hon. friend the senior member for Halifax (Mr, Maclean) was asked this afternoon to state a specific case in illustration of his contentions, and I may say that a case in point came to my notice to-day. In my western mail this morning I found a letter from the provincial secretary of the Great War Veterans' Association of Saskatchewan, which I desire to read to the House. It bears date April 28, and is as follows:
Dear Sir,-It has been noted for some little time that an attempt was being made to return to the patronage system insofar as i.t affected part of the outside services which, at the present time, are under the control of the Civil Service Commission. In view of this fact, I have gone into the matter with our branch secretaries, who have discussed the matter locally, and it appears that, without a single exception, our branches, backed by local opinion, are against any change in the Civil Service regulations which would allow a reversion to the patronage system, as apparently is intended in a Bill which is coming up in the Dominion House. It is noted with grave concern that it is intended taking about seventy-five (75%) per cent of the services in which returned soldiers, partially disabled, and otherwise, who have been able to obtain employment, out of the control of the Civil Service Commission (in which these men have been able to obtain employment so long as they had a minimum qualification in preference to civilians) and putting there branches of the Dominion Civil Service under the control of Patronage. This would undoubtedly throw thousands of returned men out of employment.
I would ask my hon. friend from Simcoe to note that.
What was the question; I did not hear my hon. friend?
The gentleman whom I am quoting says that this Bill would undoubtedly have the effect of throwing thousands of returned men out of employment.
Who is that?	[DOT]
He is the secretary of the Provincial Command Saskatchewan, Great War Veterans' Association.
Likely he has a government job.

Well, I hope that many of them have. According to my hon. friend, it seems to me that very few of these men are in the employ of the Government. To continue where I left off:
Notwithstanding that they have not been properly re-established in civil life, owing to the extremely high cost of maintenance and the casual state of employment since demobilization. The Special Parliamentary Committee have refused to reopen the matter of further gratuity, and as an enormously large percentage of the soldiers are not re-established we look with grave concern on any attempt by the members of Parliament to react in a matter apparently under .proposal which would create a serious situation, which at the present time is at least ameliorated owing to the fact that the partially disabled men have at least a chance to obtain employment under the Civil Service.
We would very strongly urge that you assist in every way possible in opposing any Bill [DOT]having to do with a reversion of the patronage system, and would thank you for a statement of your views in this connection.
Yours sincerely,
T. S. H. Lovis.
I wish to point out that during the 1917 campaign I was an ardent supporter of the Unionist party, and I have no regrets over my action at that time. The one big issue before us then was conscription, and the successful prosecution of the war, and to my mind the next big issue was the plan put out by the Unionist party then that patronage would be abolished and Civil Service reform instituted. As I view this Bill, it is the voice of the Government, and that being the case I feel truly thankful that I have withdrawn from the Government, and am now in no way called upon to support the motion before the House. I will give my most hearty support to the amendment that has been moved.

I have listened with a great deal of attention to this discussion, particularly to the speech delivered by my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie), and I must confess that I have been greatly surprised in some respects. The greatest surprise came to me as I listened attentively to the hon. member, because, as a Tory dyed-in-the-wool, he was upholding the principles of self-government, the rights of the people and the privileges of Parliament. As one of the most extreme Tories, he was expressing opposition to bureaucracy which, as we all know, is the cradle of Toryism.
Was it not a Tory Government that gave responsible government?

My hon. friend is all wrong. A Tory Administration may have proclaimed responsible government in Canada, but it was applied by the Reform party after much trouble in the country. But that is not the point. I fear there is something sinister behind this display of Liberalism on the part of my hon. friend. I am afraid that under cover of the rights of the people, the privileges of Parliament, and such other assertions, there is lurking the old system of political patronage so useful during a general election for the friends of a discredited Government. My bon. friend had to make his own confession. He said: "True, during the stress of the war we had to make certain reforms. We had to amend the Civil Service Act, which was passed by this Parliament in 1908 under the leadership of the late Hon. Sydney Fisher. We had to do our duty here in Canada, whilst our boys were fighting and dying for us in the trenches at the front." That is what my hon. friend said in so many words, but he qualified his statement:	"Those days are gone." of
course they are gone and with the days have also gone, like bubbles, the election promises and the sacred pledges of the hon. gentleman. The most sacred pledge was taken by the Nestor of the Tory Party in this Parliament. Perhaps it 'will bear repetition, Mr. Speaker, so that the people of the country may well know what a versatile Government is ruling Canada today-all sanctimonious during the war but bound to the patronage evil after the war. Now let me repeat the words which were quoted the other day by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding)
[DOT]-words which took the House by surprise and the right hon. gentleman himself more than any others. Those words will bear repetition, they were uttered by Sir George Foster during the session of 1916 and will be found at page 907 of Hansard of that year:
Now, as to patronage, I have been thirty-four years in public life ; I have been a pretty close student of political parties and political history in this country, and I have simply this to say-I give it as my individual opinion-I have long felt it and I feel it now-that in the whole course of my political life I cannot point to a single instance where political patronage ever raised the status of the bench, ever promoted the efficiency of the Civil Service, ever helped to economy in administration or enhanced the status of public administrators, no matter what functions they performed, ever helped a member of Parliament in reality, or ever strengthened a Government in reality.' On the contrary it almost always causes the dry rot and disintegration that break up government after government and party after party, and X

wish now, in the white heat and light of this great contest and struggle and the self-sacrifice that we are called upon to make, that we might speak from the heart out, and make an agreement in this country between both parties, that hereafter patronage shall not be applied by political parties in the administration of our public services. Now, that is a frank admission. Some may say to me that I have no right to make it. I presume upon my grey beard and thirty-four years in public life, and I make that statement for what it is worth. I will just append to that one single sentence, and it is this: that if there is any laxity in the public virtue of this country to-day, if there is any canker of public corruption, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred you can trace it to the baleful effect of political party patronage.
Mr. Speaker, the same right hon. gentleman this afternoon said exactly the contrary, and he will vote exactly the contrary when the vote is taken this evening. You have there, Mr. Speaker, an object lesson of the honesty of purpose of the present Government and the leaders of the Tory party. And in 1917, as was stated this afternoon by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), what was the platform of the Unionist party? On October 1917, Sir Robert Borden, after consultation with his colleagues, gave out to the public the policy of the new Union Government. The first article related to the prosecution of the war. The second, considered as only second in importance, was Civil Service Reform; and let me quote here the language used by the Prime Minister on November 12, in his manifesto addressed to the electors:
But there are other reasons why the Union Government should be entrusted with power. It has pledged itself to the extirpation of the old abuses and to a wise and bold policy of constructive reform. The system of patronage in the distribution of contracts and offices, which has prevailed in Canada for generations) has been the root of many political evils. It has fostered local and sectional interests incompatible with the national welfare and injurious to the efficiency of the national service. It has troubled representatives of the people, permitted the ascendancy of organized minorities in the constituencies and affected the independence of Parliament itself. It may be that these evils should have been overcome long >ago. Censure may lie upon successive Governments, which have tolerated the system. But inveterate diseases succumb only to heroic treatment.-and heroism has not distinguished Canadian parties in dealing with patronage. Generally, Governments have lived long in Canada, and when for many years distribution of patronage has been confined to the party in power there is a natural disposition to adjust the balance when at length the other party succeeds to office.
Once committed to the system, influences are recognized and interests created that are not easily resisted or dislodged. It is believed that a Government derived from both political parties and strengthened by special representation of agriculture and organized Labour can act with greater freedom and independence than a Gov-

ernment which held office under the old conditions. Hence the resolution to abolish trading in patronage, to fill public office by merit and not by favoritism, and to establish honest and open competition in awarding contracts and buying supplies.
There have been many breaches in that sacred pledge since it was taken in 1917, but the most brazen, the most outstanding is that which is presented to the House to-day in the effort to force through Parliament the present Bill sponsored by the member for Yarmotfth, !(Mr. ISpinney). He is an honest man I know, he has had many years of public service and he has enjoyed the respect and confidence not only of his province but of the members of this Parliament who have known him since he was elected. Does he realize what game he is made to play on behalf of the wirepullers of this party, against the will of the people as expressed in the elections of 1917? The hon. gentleman was elected against the very legislation he is now propounding and I am sorry to see that at this stage of his ministerial existence, of his political life, he should come before the House, and, because of his well-known honesty of purpose, be made the tool of unscrupulous politicians.
