If we had any love of tradition in this country, Mr. Speaker, we would cling to the system which Great Britain instituted eighty years ago. There, no member of Parliament ever dreams of appointing or recommending any one to the Civil Service. Every appointment is made after a competitive examination.. That is why Great Britain has the best Civil Service in the world. And the United States offers us another inspiring example. There for many years patronage was indeed a great evil, and the well known slogan of, To the victors belong the spoils, was acted upon by both Republicans and Democrats. But twenty years ago the public men of that country becoming alarmed at the abuses inseparable from patronage, boldly advocated the adoption of the British system, and to-day the Civil Service of the United States is second only to that of the Mother Country. Canada followed twenty years after the United States and in 1908 Parliament adopted the beginning of a great reform-the principle of a competitive system or appointment by merit in the Inside Service. But as the Hon. Mr. Fisher said at the time, that was only the thin edge of the wedge, and the day would come when the Outside Service would be brought under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. Then in 1917 the electors of Canada gave this Parliament a direct mandate to deal drastically with the whole of the Civil Service, and it dealt drastically with it, Mr. Speaker.
In 1918, when my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax became a member of the Union Cabinet, he introduced legislation which brought under the Civil Service Commission both the Inside and the Outside Service. I grant that such a great reform is bound at the outset to create some difficulties and some troubles, but what are those troubles and difficulties considering the merit of the reform itself? Is there a member of this Parliament with any self respect who of his own free will would return to the days when lobbies were filled with office seekers who made parliamentary life almost unbearable by their importunate demands? I say there is not one member of this House who would return to that system. Yet because of the approach of a general election, and because some believe that patronage will attract supporters at the polls, they are attempting to destroy the legislation unanimously adopted in 1918. I protest against such a retrograde step. No such legislation was ever mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. We were not called upon this session by His Excellency the Governor General, speaking through the inspiration of his ministers, to restrict the authority of the Civil Service Commission.
The Civil Service Commission was reorganized when the Civil Service Act was amended, a few years ago. The majority of its members were selected from among friends of the Government, and for my part I am pleased to say that I have the fullest confidence in the honour and patriotism of the personnel oT that Commission. We may differ as to some of their methods, but having sat in this House with the Hon. Mr. Roche during nearly twenty years, I say that he possesses in an eminent degree the qualifications necessary to preside over that Commission. I know Mr. Jameson, who also was one of our fellow members during two parliaments, and I have the fullest confidence in his integrity and ability. The same remarks apply also to Mr. Larochelle. Mr. Speaker, has the Commission been consulted about the Bill which is now under discussion? On the contrary, this legislation is brandished as a weapon against it, notwithstanding that the majority of its members were friends of the party which now holds office. Therefore I say there

must be something suspicious if not sinister behind this legislation which is introduced by my genial friend from Yarmouth. Further, the great body of civil servants is opposed to a return to the patronage system. There are men in the Civil Service who belong to the Conservative party, there are also men in the service who were no doubt rewarded as they had distinguished themselves during the campaign of 1917 against the Liberal party. Are they clamouring for this legislation? No, they have sent a circular to the members of this House protesting against a return to the evils of patronage. But not only have those two bodies been discarded, but public opinion as expressed in the newspapers is ignored. With the exception of a few rabid Tory papers, it will be found that the great mass of public opinion is opposed to this party legislation.
My hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie), himself a returned soldier, had the audacity to make a veiled charge against the Civil Service Commission. He stated in so many words that the Hon. Mr. Roche, Mr. Clarence Jameson and Mr. La-rochelle were prejudiced against the returned soldiers, but on what he bases his accusation, I do not know. Mr. Speaker, I have had some business with the Civil Service Commission. I have received letters from constituents and from friends all over the country making inquiry as to how they should apply for positions. I have always directed them to the Civil Service Commission, and invariably they have been told that they might make their application as the positions would be advertised but that they should bear in mind that returned soldiers had the preference. Not later than this morning-and I am sorry not to see my good friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie) in his seat-I received a circular issued by the Civil Service Commission with respect to the appointment of veterinary inspectors. This circular, which is dated at Ottawa, April 25, 1921, and signed by Mr. Foran, the secretary, describes the nature of the work to be performed by these inspectors, their qualifications, the examination to which they are subjected, etc., and then there is the following paragraph:
According- to law, preference is given to persons who have been on active service overseas in the military or naval forces of His Majesty, or any of the Allies of His' Majesty, during the late war. The age limit does not apply to persons who have seen active service overseas, but returned soldiers must furnish a certified copy of their discharge certificate, or in the case of

commissioned officers, a certified statement of their military service.
By order of the commission,
W. Foran,
Secretary.
Is that showing indifference to or prejudice against returned soldiers? Mr. Speaker, I make the statement that no circulars are issued without that provision in favour of the soldiers. The accusation, therefore, made by the member for North Simcoe is absolutely baseless. He himself served gallantly on the other side, and I hope he will make it a point to withdraw that charge at the first opportunity, because it might create discontent in the ranks of our returned soldiers.
My hon. friend said that he was a supporter of the Government and that in his humble judgment it was the "best government in sight"-I use his own words. Well, it may be the best government in sight, but not in foresight, Mr. Speaker. It may be the best government according to the tenets of the Tory gospel, but I have some evidence of what the Government is already doing in the matter of patronage with its opponents in a county which at present is open for by-election. I refer to the county of Yamaska. The other day, as the writs were issued, the postmistress of St. Thomas de Pierreville, one of the large parishes of that county, suddenly received a visit from a post office inspector, who was the bearer of a telegraphic order received from the Postmaster General. He said to the lady, Madame Boucher, who happens to be the mother of the Liberal candidate in the county of Yamaska: Madame, it is true that you have served the Crown and the public faithfully for twenty-five years, but here are my orders from the Postmaster General; hand me your keys and your equipment; you are dismissed as postmistress- Sir, that is the Tory method. I was told very gently the other day by the right hon. Minister of Justice-of "Justice", mark you-that a charge had been made against the postmistress and that she had admitted the charge. He did not explain what the charge was against the postmistress. Madame Boucher lives in the same house with her son, a notary public, and when the- mail bags arrive in the morning, in the afternoon, and in the evening, fresh from the train, the ungrateful son helps his aged mother to unlock the bags and to sort the letters in the post office. That is the charge, Mr. Speaker; that is the crime; that is the outcome of the patronage evil now sponsored by the Government.

Sir, I fear the Greeks even when they hear gifts. My hon. friend wishes to restore the right of Parliament, a right which is fraught with so many wrongs that I for one care not for it. The right to dismiss and appoint according to the fancy or the temper of the minister is not a right which should be exercised by a politician. I would rather leave it in the hands of a commission which stands by the principle of competition, a commission in which Parliament three years ago placed its confidence. Every one admits that the competitive system has made of the Civil Service in England the exemplar of all other civil service systems of the world. Canada has adopted that principle; let us maintain it. As the right hon. gentleman once said of the principle of a Canadian navy, we should root it to the soil, root it so deeply that it will never be uprooted. Mr. Speaker, I have confidence in the Civil Service Commission. I have not the least confidence in the Government; it is not the best in sight; it is the worst in sight, and if you put this lever into their hands, I say in all sincerity: God save the country and the Civil Service.

Mr. Speaker, I have never been able to see any merit in the Civil Service Act because I believe it strikes at the very foundation of responsible government. As it has worked out I think it might very well have been described as "An Act to Destroy the Discipline of the Civil Service and Promote Inefficiency". If I were disposed to-night to go over all the cases that have been reported to me it would take a much longer time than I am prepared to speak. But I am going to present one case for the consideration of the House which is typical of the way the Civil Service Commission carries on its work. My hon. friend from Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) said, in reply to the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie), that the soldiers had been well paid. I stated a case in this House in a former session where a man was brought from Calgary in December to fill a position in this city. In February the position was advertised and returned soldiers applied for it, one of them, to my knowledge, being a man of fifteen years' experience in the very work that was advertised. But the man who had been brought from Calgary in December, of course, received the appointment. He had been brought down here; the expenses of himself and his family in coming down here were paid, and yet the Civil Service
Commission advertised the position as vacant in February. I have, however, given that instance to the House before.
I stated, in a letter which I wrote in reply to a communication from the Civil Service Federation, that patronage had not been abolished and that it could not be abolished. All that this House or this Government can do is to transfer the patronage from the members who formerly exercised it to somebody else. Some say that it has been transferred to the Civil Service Commission. My judgment is that it has been transferred to the secretary of the Civil Service Commission, and I am going to submit to my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) some evidence that will establish the fact. The Civil Service Commission is ruled by the secretary, and many important matters are dealt with in the name of the commission about which the commissioners know nothing at all until the thing is all over.-Therefore, What we have done by the Civil Service Act is to transfer all the patronage of the Dominion of Canada to one man, and that man a paid official of the commission. As a matter of fact, this Civil Service Act has been tried and found wanting, and there is not a man on this or that side of the House who does not know of grave injustices that have occurred under the operations of this commission. It should not be tolerated that injustice should be done to any citizen of this country; but there is no recourse; the commission does as itjikes; it is superior to the ministers. No minister can nominate even an assistant deputy minister; that is a prerogative taken out of his hands by this Act. I never could imagine why a group of otherwise sensible ministers should be parties to depriving themselves of one of the gravest responsibilities that rests upon any government, the expenditure of tens of millions of dollars, and should place it in the hands of the Civil Service Commission. It was a piece of idealism. There are a number of idealists on this side as well as elsewhere in the House, and the Civil Service Act is the product of the minds of idealists, but it is a form of idealism that requires perfection in the personnel of the commission to make it effective. You canndt get perfection, and you certainly do not have perfection in the present commission.

Would my hon. friend
abolish the commission?

I have stated before
what I would do. All you can get in the way of Civil Service reform is, first, that

no man shall be appointed to a position unless that man's services are required. The next thing to he sure of is whether that man is qualified. You cannot get any more than that, no matter how you try, and you do not need any more than that. If a position is vacant, I would have the deputy minister declare that a man is required for the particular office. If it was an appointment to the Outside Service, I would have the member for the constituency recommend a man for the position, and then I would have that man submitted to an examination by the Civil Service Commission. If he could not pass the examination, he would not get the position: he would be set aside and another recommendation would come up. That at least puts the responsibility for the appointment, as regards recommendation as to the character of the man, upon the person who is responsible, who is elected to carry such ' responsibility. It puts the responsibility for his qualifications upon a group of men supposed to be specially fitted to determine that one fact. That is the way in which I would fill the public service, and I venture to say that I would get much better service under that plan than you could possibly get under the present one. It has been stated around this House-I do not know whether it has been stated in the House- that there is a back door to the secretary's office. Everybody in Ottawa will tell you that. You must be personally friendly to this friend or that friend or some other friend, and having that kind of influence with the secretary, you are sure of an appointment. I have gone over many cases before that I do not intend to repeat tonight. A piece of legislation that depends upon securing a group of men who are perfect is not likely to be successful in Canada or anywhere else that I know of in this world. We must wait for a civil service commission of that kind until the millennium comes.
Do I understand that the hon. gentleman is making a charge against the secretary, and on what-ground? Is it corruption, favouritism, or what?
I say, favouritism.
Has the hon. gentleman any concrete cases?
Yes, I have concrete cases. I want to give the House one story and that will be enough for to-night.
Stories are not facts.

I want to give the House a case of injustice. I want to show that the chairman of the commission does not know what positions are advertised, and that after a position is advertised and an unsatisfactory man gets a position or is the successful candidate, the position is abolished because the man whom it was desired to put into that position did not succeed in the examination. I have a communication that is somewhat lengthy, written by Mr. Roy Fraser, who resides at Fitzroy Harbour. Mr. Fraser is an expert in agriculture. He was head of the Arbuckle Institute in the state of New York. He is one of the most highly qualified men in his line that you could get anywhere. He had resigned his position because he was ill and he came home for a rest. While he was at home, he got in touch with some of the staff of the Civil Service Commission, and he was encouraged to write for an examination. This is his story that I want to put upon the record. He writes:
In view of the grossly unjust treatment which I have received at the hands of the Civil Service Commission in the matter of the abovenamed competition-
That is for the position of Principal Civil Service Examiner in Agriculture.
-I am setting forth the facts in the following statement. I respectfully submit this statement for the consideration of the members of Parliament in the hope that in the interests of fair play and responsible government, parliamentary action will be taken toward preventing any future recurrence of a similar injury and toward curbing the arbitrary and unreasonable empowerment which makes such an injustice possible. .
About the second or third week of October, 1920, I had a conversation with a member of the commission's staff. I stated that while I had access to opportunities of higher remuneration in the United States, it was my very strong conviction that Canadians should stay in their own country and have a part .in its upbuilding, and that I therefore desired to devote my training and experience in technical and educational fields to the service of governmental or institutional work in Canada.
The staff member was both courteous and cordial. He informed me that the commission was looking for men of the calibre of academic and practical experience which I possessed. He stated that the position of Principal Civil Service Examiner in Agriculture would shortly be created, and after giving me an outline of the qualifications and duties involved, asked me if I would care to apply for the position. As a result of his statements I became greatly interested in the matter and answered that as I possessed the necessary qualifications and would like the nature of the work very much I would apply for the position.
He welcomed and commended my application and informed me as to the necessary procedure of application. He was also kind enough to

give me an order on another office to provide me with copies of previous examination papers, and stated that while the examination for the principal examinership would naturally be more difficult, it would toe very much along the same lines as these papers. He was further kind enough to suggest text-books and references which, he said, would be of use to me in preparing for the examination. He then introduced me to another staff member of the commission. Some time later he sent me a letter accompanied by an application form. I take this opportunity of expressing my sincere appreciation of his courtesy and helpfulness.
In view of the encouragement I had received I immediately started to prepare for the examination and to devote all my time towards familiarizing- myself as far as possible with the structure and functions of the Civil Service Commission, so that if I was successful in the competition I would be more fully qualified for the duties of the position.
The position of Principal Civil Service Examiner was announced in list No. 65, on November 8, 1920, with announcements of Senior Civil Service Examinership and Junior Civil Service Examinerships in the same list. I filled out my application at once. Before I could send it in, I received a letter from the office of the secretary of the commission stating .that as I "possessed qualifications which would be very valuable in a senior examinership they had taken the liberty of entering an application for me in the competition for Senior Civil Service Examiner." I wrote immediately to the secretary's office thanking the commission for entering an application for me of their own accord, but that I was a candidate for Principal Civil Service Examiner and not for senior examiner. I requested that the application be therefore entered in competition No. 1731, Principal Civil Service Examiner.
The necessary applications and recommendations being filed and receipt acknowledged I continued with my preparation.
In December I received a notification that the examination for Senior Civil Service Examiner would be held, stating place and date, and an order admitting me to the examination was enclosed.
This gentleman did not want to write on the examination for senior examiner, but for principal examiner. The secretary knew that^ yet he sent him the papers for the senior examination.
I immediately called -Mr. Foran on the longdistance phone and directed his attention to my letter on entering application in proper competition. I asked that he correct the error of his office, cancel the senior entry, and enter my application properly, and to send me the admission order for the Principal Civil Service Examiner's examination.
In answer, I received orders of admission to both examinations, and a letter stating that they had entered me in both examinations.
Why was the secretary so extraordinarily anxious that this man, with undoubted qualifications, should not write on the examination for principal examiner, but should write on the examination for senior examiner? Even after this man had told him that he did not want to write for the examination of senior examiner, the secre-
181J
tary sent him the papers for that examination. If the secretary had not some person in his mind whom he thought would be fit for the position of principal examiner, I cannot conceive any reason why he should not accede to this gentleman's request. The letter goes on:
As this was directly contrary to my expressed wish I did not pay any attention to the senior examination, but wrote on the principal examination on the following day, December fifteenth.
Under date of December 28 I was notified that I was successful in the examination, and to appear at the commission's office on January 7 for oral interview. The date was postponed to January 8, and on that day I was examined orally. At the close of the examination I was told that I would hear the result in a few days.
After what seemed to be a reasonable length of time I expected to hear the decision of the commission. When the lapse of time increased considerably I telephoned long-distance to Mr. Foran and was answered by Mr. Bland, who stated that no decision had been reached. A second similar call some time later received a similar answer.
A month after he had been notified that he was successful in the examination he went to Ottawa, and called Mr. Foran's office. Mr. Foran made the following statement:
I thought that that Principal Examinership position was all settled. You are the best man in the competition. Mr. Bland then came in. He said: "I believe that Mr. Fraser would be an excellent man for the position. We would like to get the matter settled as we need a man in the position as soon as possible, for there Is a very great deal of work to be done.
That is a very striking statement in view of what follows a little later on:
Mr. Foran asked Mr. Bland the reason for the delay. Mr. Bland replied that it was due to a difficulty in obtaining certain information i.n regard to one of the other candidates.
Remember this man has already been notified that he was successful in the examination.
The statements made by Mr. Foran and Mr. Bland concerning my standing in the matter naturally gave me a great degree of encouragement.
Weeks passed, then a month, and no further word came. Under date of March 7, I wrote to Mr. Foran. I asked him for .some more definite indication as to when a decision would be made known. I made it clear that as all my affairs and the affairs of those dependent on me were being held up by the delay, that it was only reasonable that I should be given a more definite assurance as to the future of the matter.
Mr. Bland, under date of March 9,-
This was four months after.
-answered my letter to Mr. Foran. He said he was sorry that there had been so much delay and that he hoped to advise me "within a day or so as to the successful candidate."

Four months after he had been notified that he was the successful candidate: You will notice that up to this time the position was still in existence and that it had not been filled:
It was now five and one-half months since the position had first been brought to my attention. I had exerted every effort, led the competition, and endured the long delay as patiently as possible, as the delay had now gone past any endurance I decided that I was entitled to some definite and final assurance.
I came to Ottawa on March 30, and went to Mr. Poran's office. Mr. Bland met me in the hall. Then, out of a clear sky, he stated that the commission had abolished the position!
This was after he had been notified that he was successful, after Mr. Bland had said: "We need a man in the position as soon as possible for there is a great deal of work to be done." Then, when it comes down to the final thing, they say, "the position is abolished." Is not that extraordinary? Is that not an unbusiness-like way of doing things? Is there not a nigger in the fence somewhere? Is there any other conclusion? You can talk as you like about the high standing of these men, but there is something wrong with a body of men that will keep a man waiting around five months for a position, and then tell him they have decided not to fill the position.
I pressed him for a definite statement of the commission's action, but his statement was not definite not were his explanations lucid. I gathered that the commission, through some Parliamentary action bearing on the outside service, was being forced into a policy of reduction of staff and a retrenchment of expenditures. I expressed my amazement that, after all that had passed, and without the slightest intimation of such a development, I was to be thus abruptly ousted. He said "You'd better see Mr. Foran."
And then there is a most interesting case of passing the buck all round on the part of the commission:
I went into Mr. Foran's office. Mr. Foran said "You had better see Mr. Bland." I replied that Mr. Bland had just referred me to him. Mr. Foran said that "he (Mr. Foran) did not know the details of the matter,-that Mr. Bland looked after everything like that, and Mr. Bland was the man to see." Mr. Foran was obviously ill at ease, and had none of the cordiality of my previous conversation with him. I pressed him to make a definite and final statement of the commi-ssion's action and the reasons therefor. He said "There is almost nothing for a principal examiner to do."
What do you think of that, Mr. Speaker? Only a few days before he was told "We need a man in the position as soon as possible, for there is a very great deal of work to be done". And now Mr. Foran comes along and says there is almost nothing for a principal examiner to do.

"The agricultural service is in a stagnant condition,-
I wonder if the minister would admit that.
-and there are so few appointments In demand that we would not be warranted in maintaining a principal examiner. Here was a new and amazing explanation, totally different from the one Mr. Bland had given. I said: "Mr. Foran, in the conversation between you and Mr. Bland and myself a few weeks ago, Mr. Bland said most emphatically that the commission needed a principal examiner in agriculture at once, as there was a very great deal of work to be done. How can your statement be reconciled with that? Can such an abrupt change have occurred in the agricultural service?" Mr. Foran evaded the question; he merely said: "Well, that ds the condition anyhow". I said: "Is it fair that a technical man of standing, having entered this competition in good faith, spent five months' hard effort and hard waiting, should now be put out of the matter in this way? His only answer was: "You had better see Mr. Bland; he looks after those things". I went to Mr. Bland's office, and waited until Mr. Bland returned. Mr. Bland intimated a very vague possibility that later on, "when we knew what Parliament is going to do-
They evidently knew what Parliament was going to do on November 8, when they advertised the position.
-the principal examinership might materialize after all,-
It might materialize after Mr. Fraser has gone back to New York; I have no doubt it will.
-and that it might be a good thing for me to go on an eligible list and-just keep on waiting.
This man had come home and waited five months, studying and preparing for this particular position, for which he undoubtedly was qualified, and was then told that he would have to go on an eligible list and just keep on waiting.
I said that I expected a more definite answer, and Mr. Bland said:-
Again passing the buck.
-"You had better see Dr. Roche." So I went to see Dr. Roche and Dr. Roche said: "The commission have not had the matter before them until yesterday" (March 29).
What do you think of that, Mr. Speaker? Here was a position advertised on November 8, and the chairman of the commission, on March 29, said that the matter had never been before them until then, and that he had not known anything about it. Is he running the commission, or is the secretary? Four months, after the examination had been advertised, and the whole process had been gone through from beginning to end, the chairman confessed that he had never heard anything at all about it. Is that the kind of body from which

you can expect efficiency in the Civil Service? Is that the kind of body which the hon. gentleman from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) is prepared to defend?-a body in which the chairman does not know what is going on from one day to another. Let me proceed:
The position of Principal Civil Service Examiner had not come before the commissioners until then, and then it came in the form of a recommendation from Mr. Foran that the position be abolished.
It was advertised, as I say, on November 8, all the procedure had been gone through regularly and carefully, the candidates, a great many of them I have no doubt, were all examined and the successful man was notified accordingly. Yet the first thing that the chairman knew about the position was a recommendation from the secretary that it be abolished. That is the way they do business in the Civil Service Commission. The chairman did not abolish the position; the commissioners did not abolish it; the secretary abolished it. That is what happened. Am I not right, then, when I say that patronage in the Dominion is handed over to one man, that man the secretary of the Civil Service Commission? I think I am right when the chairman will make such a statement to a disappointed candidate who had been treated so badly. The first the chairman knew about the position was when Mr. Foran recommended to him that it be abolished. The situation is certainly most extraordinary.
He said:	"Mr. Bland is to have charge of
the examination branch, and to add those duties to his own."
Now, Mr. Bland was not the man picked out in the first place for this position, because he was there and could have been appointed; but Mr. Bland, at the beginning was not satisfactory, so they advertised for candidates, and when Mr. Fraser applied for the papers to write, he was told "You had better write for the senior examiner." He replied that he wanted to write for the principal examiner, but again he was told "You had better write for the senior."
Is the position of senior examiner abolished also?
No.
He should have written for that.

I will tell you about
that; it is quite interesting. Mr. Bland was in the department, but evidently Mr. Foran did not think he was qualified so they advertised for some one else. Then, when a man comes along that they do not want and they have not some one to put in the position, he says: "We will put Mr. Bland in." Whether Mr. Bland is the man there or not I am doubtful. I have a suspicion that there is another nigger in the woodpile. To continue:
He said: "Mr. Bland is to have charge of the examination branch, and to add those duties to his own. It has been hinted in Parliament that our staff was reaching large proportions-
Well, I am sure that hint was heard by the commission because it was voiced very loudly in this House on more than one 'occasion, and when you look at the Estimates, there can be no getting away from the fact that the staff certainly is reaching large proportions. This document goes on to say:	,	:
-"Owing to what may happen in Parliament any day now, we are concentrating our staff. This position was a scheme of Mr. Muddi-man's-
Whoever he may be; the whole thing is pretty dark to me.
"He has left us. Yes, the position was created by Order in Council."
Here is a position created by Order in Council and the secretary of the Civil Service Commission abolishes it. That is interesting.

Does my
hon. friend know as a fact that the position was created by Order in Council?
He says so.
That does not prove it.
Well, Dr. Roche says so.
It is not so stated by any one in this House who knows the facts.

It has been so stated by Dr. Roche, and I have a letter from this gentleman who is just as reliable as my hon. friend from Halifax, in which he says:
If it becomes desirable that a statement be sworn to before a notary I will be glad to come to Ottawa to do it.
The only reason that this communication is not iri the form of an affidavit is that there is no lawyer near this man, and he would have to travel to Ottawa to swear to it.

Will my
hon. friend give me a little further evi-

dence as to what the position was which he alleges was created by Order in Council?

Dr. Roche said to Mr. Fraser: (reading):
"This position was a scheme of Mr. Muddi-man's. Yes, the position was created by Order in Council, but we don't have to put it into operation, and don't want to."
happen in other departments, but this is the first time it has ever happened in the cornmis-sion. '
Dr. Roche's utterv indifference to the injury done me was a very plain indication of tne commission's sense of fairness.
I then said-
And this my hon. friend from Marquette
will notice.
Now that may be the case, that may be the law, but I submit that if it is the law then the law ought to be changed, or that part of it anyway. If we are to have a Civil Service Commissioner over-ride Orders in Council we certainly are further away from responsible Government than even I imagined and I am bound to say I thought we were a long way from it. But if this commission can set aside an Order in Council, as Dr. Roche said to Mr. Fraser, and I am taking Mr. Fraser's word for it, then that is an extraordinary state of affairs.
There are quite a number of members of the Government in the House at the present moment and my hon. friend might direct a question to them.

I rise to a point of order.
I would like to know if this recital is relevant to the principle of the Bill we are discussing.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will recall that I have only recently resumed the Chair. The Bill before the House is in amendment to the Civil Service Act, and I think it i3 highly questionable as to whether detailed information of this character is germane to the principle of the Bill. I think the hon. member for Toronto will be better advised if he directs his remarks more closely to the subject immediately before the House.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I
have read it all. There is only one thing that I did not reach and that is the point as to which the hon. member for Marquette asked me a question-if the other positions had been filled? The positions of Senior and Junior Examiner were filled by Mr. B

and Mr. M

.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think what I have laid before the House-
Were they competent?

I do not know, I presume they were. The point, Mr. Speaker, is that they entered a man of their own accord against his desire. He passed above everybody else and then they put another man in the position and abolished the one that he desired.
Were these two appointments made without the knowledge of the commission?
Yes, evidently. If Mr. Speaker will give ane permission to read further I can show that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will be good enough to indicate how his remarks bear upon the subject before the House?

I am trying to show the necessity, Mr. Speaker, for a revision of this Act. I submit that I can prove that the operations of this commission are unfair and lead to inefficiency and ill-treatment of candidates writing for examination. I can prove that if I am in order; as to that I do not know.

I would have waited to
speak after my (hon. friend but I want to give him a chance to answer a question. Does he realize that he is making an ex-parte statement with respect ito the Civil Service Commission, and that according to all ideas of British law and British fair play he cannot do that unless the commission is called upon to defend itself? If my hon. friend wants to make a charge against the commission, in order to be fair towards them, he should make his charge and if .the charge is found to be right such action can be taken as the case calls for. In the next place Mr. Fraser, in this matter, is finding a mouthpiece in my hon. friend while the commission have no one to say whether the statement is right or wrong. There is no solemn declaration or affidavit in support of my hon. friend's statement.
