This is my question-

Order. When the
Speaker rises the hon. gentleman should sit down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I fear the hon. member is really making an argument when he is only at liberty to submit a question by leave of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken).
Mr. Speaker, I have not yet spoken on this Bill and only intended to put a question to the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I will
answer the question all right. You give us the committee that the Bill proposes, and we will have Mr. Fraser here to meet the commissioners, who can then give their side of the case. But this is something that ought to be cleared up before a committee of the House.
I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that the Civil Service Act has destroyed the efficiency and discipline of the service, particularly the discipline. There is no discipline in the service to-day. The Civil Service Federation is more important in the eyes of the civil servants than the ministers of the Crown. Is that responsible government? Is that a state of affairs that this House should be satisfied with? Surely, we ought to remedy such a condition, and the Civil Service Act ought to be reviewed in that regard. This Civil Service Federation assumes, I might almost say, authority to determine the conditions under which its members work and

the salaries that are to be paid to them. ' We know they have been bombarding the Prime Minister because he proposed to reduce the bonus by twenty-five per cent-a proposition that rests on the most solid grounds because of the reduction in the cost of living. Yet they bombard him and every member of the House, and while now they try to get us interested in their cause, at other times they display nothing but contempt for us. If any member is willing to take that contempt he deserves it, but as far as I am concerned I will not take it. I object to a federation of civil servants trying to place themselves in a position of superiority over the heads of ministers of the Crown in settling questions concerning their employment. They regard the commissioners as their employers, not the Government. This Government and this Parliament have made Civil Service Commissioners virtually the employers of the service, and the ministers can go away back and sit down; they do not count for much, and members of Parliament count for less.
But, Sir, that is only one particular case. I am credibly informed that this commission, against the report of a Commissioner of Customs and in spite of the recommendation by the member for the riding, saw fit to appoint a man to the public service who had been a confirmed drunkard for fifteen years. He could not stay there, of course. But when the Civil Service Commission will make an appointment of that character, I submit that it is not the proper body to look after appointments to the Civil Service. You have only one step farther to go-hand over to this commission the appointment of the judges, the lieutenant-governors and the senators. That is all the commission lacks now from being in complete control.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill under consideration is one of the most important, in the principle underlying it, that has come before the House this session. If I read the Bill aright, it proposes a very radical departure indeed from the principle at present governing appointments to the Civil Service. It proposes in very large measure to revert to the condition of affairs that obtained prior to the passage of the Civil Service Act three years ago. The manner in which the Bill has been introduced has been criticised, and I think perhaps it is open to some criticism. The Government apparently are not very sure themselves what they desire to do in respect to it, for they have introduced

this measure in a skeleton condition and they propose to send it to a special committee in order that this special committee recommend the legislation that should be enacted.
The principle upon which the Bill is founded, and the principle that will almost certainly be reported back from this committee after it is inquired into, is that the control of appointments to the Civil Service shall be taken in very great measure out of the hands of the Civil Service Commission and put back into the hands of private members of this House. This is the actual purpose of the Bill. It is true that it does not go to the full extent to which this flagrant evil of patronage existed prior to 1918, but it does in very large measure. Take subsection (b) for instance, it is proposed to exempt from the operation of the Civil Service Act all postmasters whose remuneration consists in whole or in part of a percentage of the receipts of their office. If I am correctly informed, the only postmasters that are on straight salary to-day are those in cities of more than 12,000 population and where the revenue exceeds $20,000 per year. In the overwhelming number of post offices, not rural post offices alone, but those in towns up to a population of 10,000 or 12,000, what does the Bill propose so far as appointments are concerned? Simply to go back to the old order of affairs and have the appointments made on the recommendation of the sitting member or the defeated candidate of the party in power. Objection has also been made to the proposal that professional, scientific and technical officers employed for the performance of duties as such should be exempt from the operation of the Civil Service Act. And that objection also is well founded. There is one thing that the people will not stand for again, and that is a reversion to the old order of political patronage that existed prior to the passage of the Civil Service Act in 1918.

They are standing for
it in Ontario. [DOT]
Not yet.
Yes, sir.

The evils inherent in
patronage were apparent to every one. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) laid down a principle that two factors should guide in appointments to the Civil Service. He said that the service should have no more employees than were needed. With that I agree.

He says the second condition is that they should be qualified for their work. With that also I agree. But if my hon. friend from West Toronto knows anything of the condition that existed in the service before 1918-and, indeed, that exists in it yet in large degree as the result of the method under which appointments were made prior to that time-he knows that these two principles were constantly violated. We find in the service to-day people who have been in it for fifteen, twenty or twenty-five years and who got their positions as the result of political pull-because they had friends at court; because the minister of the day or some one near the minister wished to have them placed. Now, you cannot get efficiency in your service under such-conditions. I have taken advantage of the opportunity afforded me of asking members of the Civil Service in all parts of Canada, as I met them from time to time, how they regarded the new order under which patronage had been abolished as compared with the old order under which appointments were made upon the recommendation of the sitting member, and without exception they have in most unequivocal terms expressed their disapproval of the old method and their hope that we shall never revert to it.

May I
ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.
How were these members of the service appointed?

The members of the
service to whom I am alluding have been in the service for years, some of them for fifteen or twenty years.
How were they appointed in the first instance?

They were appointed
under the patronage system. It is true that you have in the service a certain number of good men who were appointed under the patronage system. But under that system what incentive was there to a good man in the service to do his work faithfully? What hope did he have of getting reward by promotion? It did not exist; there was no incentive at all.
Sure.

None whatever. If a
vacancy occurred, how was it filled? On the recommendation of the sitting member, who would put in some of his friends, as had always been the case.
Will the hon. gentleman-

My hon. friend will
please keep his seat.
Will the hon. member answer a question? I am allowed to ask a question in this House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member may
put a question if he has the permission of the hon. gentleman who is speaking.
Well, I am putting a question to him. Was it not the case formerly that all efficient officers in the Civil Service were promoted when vacancies occurred?
No.

The men at the head of
things now were promoted from lower down in the service.

All that I have to say
is that my hon. friend from Simcoe is not very familiar with what happened in the old days in the Civil -Service if he makes that assertion. There were cases and hundreds of cases yearly in which worthy civil servants did not get promotion. Promotions were not made on merit. Take the case of the post office in the city of Winnipeg, in which I happen to live. Within the past year the postmaster in that city died. What would have happened under the old order of things which my hon. friend from Simcoe and the member for Toronto West wish to get back to? The party managers, the party supporters of the Government in that city, would have been called upon to make a recommendation for the position of postmaster in the city of Winnipeg. But under the new order of things, what happened? The assistant postmaster, who had given years of faithful service, was promoted to the position of postmaster and every one in the city was satisfied that the best man available had been appointed. That is the spirit that the people of this country want to see manifested in the Civil Service, only in that way can efficiency be secured.
Now, who is asking for these changes?' I asked my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) this afternoon if the Civil Service Commission had asked for these amendments to the Act. Apparently they have not. Have the civil servants asked for them? I do not think so; I have heard nothing to that effect. Who have asked for them, Mr. Speaker? The Government have introduced, this measure, I venture to say, in response to the pressure

that has been brought to bear upon them by some of their supporters sitting behind them in this House. Some of my hon. friends opposite wish to be in such a position that they shall have an opportunity to dispense little favours; it may be valuable and useful when an election is on. I ask my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Hen-ders) what he thinks of that.
If my hon. friend wants an answer to that question, I shall tell him as soon as he has finished, or some time later in the evening.

Well, I am very glad that we shall hear from the hon. member from Macdonald. I imbibed my early ideas on civil service reform from that hon. gentleman; I trust that he has not gone back on the principles he so strongly and so firmly believed in in the days before he came to Parliament.
My hon. friend from West Toronto, (Mr. Hocken) raised considerable objection to the Civil Service Commission. He indulged in a very severe criticism of that body, particularly of its secretary, basing his whole complaint upon an alleged wrong that had been done to a gentleman named Mr. Fraser, whose long recital of trouble and woe the hon, gentleman related to the House. But that was an ex parte statement. It is one side of the story; I would like to hear the other side of it. I can imagine that the Government, in their desire to bring about a greater degree of economy in the public service, gave instructions to the various commissions operating under Government control that they must reduce their expenditures. It is quite likely that on the ground of economy alone the position which had been advertised and for which this Mr. Fraser wrote an examination was dispensed with. It may be that some criticism is due the commission because Mr. Fraser was not promptly notified; because he was kept waiting for several months before learning his fate. Well, if rumour is correct there are many gentlemen in this country just now who have been kept waiting for several years for senatorships. I do not know whether or not they will eventually land them, but the fact that these positions have not been filled should not necessarily bring criticism to the Government simply on that account.
The criticism has also been made by my hon. friend from Simcoe that the returned soldiers have not been fairly treated by the commission, and inferential^ he would lead one to believe that the returned sol-

diers desired to have these changes made. Well, my hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) read a letter this evening written by the secretary of the Great War Veterans Association of Saskatchewan stating that he had consulted all the local associations in that province and that without exception they were opposed to the very Bill which the Government has brought down, and opposed to it on the ground that they objected to a reversion to the old condition of patronage. I am convinced that there are no people more anxious than the returned soldiers to see the public business of this country put upon a plane of efficiency and made free from the evils of political patronage, I venture to say that my hon. friend from Simcoe does not speak the sentiments of the returned soldiers of Canada when he endeavours to lead the House to believe that they were desirous that this legislation should pass.
I do not intend to deal at any greater length with the evils of the patronage system. I think those evils are apparent to every one. You can take this country from Vancouver to Halifax and you will not find anywhere any considerable body of opinion in favour of reverting to the old conditions of political patronage in this country, when government positions were filled as a reward for party service. You can get neither efficiency in your public servants nor morality in your public administration when that condition obtains. There is nothing more certain than that, and if this step is taken, it will be a backward step as regards efficiency in the administration of Canada's business.
I do not for a moment say that the Civil Service Act is perfect; in fact, there are places where I believe the Civil Service Act can be improved. I agree with my hon. friends opposite that in some respects the Civil Service Commission may have too much power. It has too much power and control over dismissals of public servants. But the principle underlying the Act and the whole principle of the administration of the Act are thoroughly sound.
I would suggest this to the Government, and I would be very glad if they would adopt the suggestion, although I do not expect they will. I think not merely the particular matters that are referred to the committee under this Bill, but the operation of the whole Act might very well form the subject of an inquiry by a committee, with a view of seeing what changes could be made in the Act to remove the weak-

nesses and strengthen the whole administration. That should be, however, absolutely consistent with this, that the fundamental principle underlying the whole Civil Service Act, the abolition of patronage, which was promised to this country in 1917, and which was carried out by the Government of the day, shall not be disturbed in the administration of the service. In that way I think some good might be done by a committee. We are getting on pretty well now with the session, and I would suggest to the Government that it would be a good idea to let this matter stand over and take it up at the next session with a special committee. If it is found that there are spots in the Civil Service Act that can be strengthened as regards the administration of this country's business, let us by all means strengthen them. I am, however, convinced that the people of this country will not stand for any interference with the fundamental principle underlying this Act, which is that patronage in the carrying on of the country's business shall be abolished and abolished forever.
I think the rules of the House prevent his being placed, or acting, on the committee.

I do not know anything about that, but I would not like to sit on a committee if I had stated beforehand my views as to what my findings would be. I have been endeavouring to find the names of the members of the committee. I see one sitting up there in whom I have absolute faith and who, I know, will act with very great care and judgment in framing the recommendations of the committee. Therefore, I am in favour of appointing that committee and letting them investigate this question. They may make recommendations that would be very much to the benefit of the Civil Service Commission. If the Civil Service Commission are as weak as some members say they are, and if they are not carrying out their duties properly, it is the duty of Parliament and the Government, which represents Parliament, to place on the commission men who are perfectly capable and who have the wisdom and knowledge to carry out the views of Parliament.
I never dreamed that what we would call labour men-I am afraid we are all labour men to a certain extent anyway-men working by manual labour, were under the control of the commission, and when I discussed this question before the electorate, I never dreamed that purely rural postmasters would also be under the commission. I am not saying that I wanted to appoint them, because the only one that I had ever any voice in appointing in olden days, perhaps, won me one vote, but

he lost me five. Therefore, I was not in love with the job in any way shape or form, nor am I now. But my experience with the commission very recently has been thai they promote in accordance with service and most justly, and I have, therefore, nothing whatever to say against them. I can only repeat that I think, under the circumstances, after all the discussions that we have had this afternoon, it would be very wise for my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) to withdraw his amendment and let the committee be appointed, because I am sure there are on the committee men from both sides of the House who will see that absolute justice is done to this question.

Mr. Speaker, the Government of which I was a member was defeated on September 21, 1911. On the morning of September 22, 1911, I walked up the street, from my house to my office feeling that for the first time in about three years I was a free man. I walked up the street that morning having the feeling that I was one of the victors rather than one of the vanquished, and the feeling, Sir, was due to the fact that I realized I was free from the curse of patronage. Now it is because I see in the Bill which has been introduced by the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Spinney) the possibility of returning to the condition to which I have alluded, that I am opposed to its adoption by this House.
Before addressing to the House the few observations that I propose to offer, may I commend to my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) the sage and judicial principle laid down by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) that a member of a committee should not pre-judge a matter to be investigated by that committee.

The hon. gentleman cannot mention one word I said to show that I pre-judged the case at all. I discussed the principle of the measure, and endeavoured to show the House that the measure was necessary.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I am not proposing to
enter into any argument with my hon. friend. In the best-natured way in the world I was merely suggesting for his consideration the judicial principle laid down by the member for North Oxford.

If the hon. gentleman
had listened to my speech, he would have heard me lay down that very same principle.
[M. Nesbitt.!

If the hon. gentleman
will possess himself in patience, he will see that I not only listened to his speech, but made a few notes regarding it, to which I will advert in a few minutes. The longer this discussion lasts, the more apparent becomes the reason for introducing this measure, and the more speeches that are delivered from the opposite side of the House in support of this measure, and in opposition to the amendment of my h*on. friend the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) the more in the open do we see the influences behind the Government that prompted the introduction of this measure.
Before dealing with these latter phases of the matter may I be allowed to refer to one or two things connected with the way in which this measure was introduced. In the first place we had a somewhat Delphic utterance from my hon. friend the member for Yarmouth. When he asked leave to introduce the Bill, he said:
In this Bill there are incorporated, in italics, some tentative restrictions which cannot be considered as final, but rather on account of the Bill not being allowed to be presented in blank.
I confess, Sir, that when I heard those words uttered in the House I did not understand them, and I am obliged to admit that I do not understand them yet. I doubt, in fact, whether any hon. gentleman who heard these words understood them. The statement of the hon. gentleman left the House, as it left the public mind, in a state of confusion. However, the statement reminded me of a somewhat similar pronouncement by the hon. gentleman last summer on the occasion of his entry into the Administration of which he is a respected member. The Halifax Herald of July 14 last published an interview with the hon. gentleman in which he was credited with having said this:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman would be in order in reading the interview. It is not germane at all to the principle of the Bill under discussion.

What I was going to
say was this: An interview with the hon. gentleman was published on July 14 last in which he said that he believed that the old parties were dead. Another interview was published on the following day in the Toronto Globe in which the hon. gentleman was reported to have said that he was in the new Government as a Liberal. My difficulty was how to reconcile those two statements. If, as the hon. gentleman is reported to have said in the first interview,

the old parties were dead, how could it be possible for the hon. gentleman on the following day to say that he represented one of these dead parties in the new Government. That is my difficulty, and I am in a similar difficulty in view of his pronouncement on the introduction of this Bill. That,
I submit, Sir, makes the observation germane to the principle we are discussing. Beyond that, I do not intend to go.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I can hardly see how the previously expressed opinion of any hon. gentleman of this House on another matter can have any hearing on the question that is now before the House.

I regret that any observation of mine should leave any hon. gentleman or your Honour in a state of confusion, because I endeavour to make myself tolerably well understood. However, I do not wish to refer further to that phase of the matter. That was really all I had to say about it. I might comment that all this creates a very Strange atmosphere in connection with- this Bill-an atmosphere very different from that which surrounded the utterances of the right hon. gentleman who led the Government in 1917, an atmosphere very different from that which surrounded the utterances of several gentlemen who accepted his invitation to become members of his Administration. In 1917, the right hon. gentleman who was then leader of the Government, now the member for King's (Sir Robert Borden), said on December 13 of that year:
First, we have abolished patronage and no Government will dare to bring it back.
Who said that?

The then Prime Minister, now the right hon. member for King's.
First, we have abolished patronage and no Government will dare to bring it back. Second, the Civil Service Act has been made applicable to the Outside as well as the Inside Service.
So spoke the Prime Minister of this country on December 13, 1917. But, Sir, I submit that the Bill now before the House is a complete reversal of the declarations made by the right hon. gentleman on that occasion. There was another interesting pronouncement made by the hon. member who became Minister of Immigration in the Cabinet of the right hon. the member for King's. My good friend the present Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), speaking on October 22, 1917, on the subject of Civil Service reform, said this:
We believe that the time has come when an honest and sincere effort should be made to improve the Civil Service of Canada. Our Civil Service should be taken out of party politics and men appointed to the service on the grounds of efficiency and necessity, and not on purely political grounds. I am talking sincerely to you men and women to-night, arid voicing the opinions of every member of this new Government. We mean business.
Listen to that, Mr. Speaker.
We mean business. Parties in the past have issued their programs and their policies, and made promises, but I want to tell you people to-night that, so far as I am concerned, unless these things are done which the new Government calls for, I will not stay in the Union Government. iS-cx far as I am concerned I mean business. I know what party politics are. I have been in public life for twelve years, and know that our public men have been hounded day in and day out by job seekers and grafters looking for some special privilege to which they are not entitled.
So spoke my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, on October 22, 1917. Now, in view of that high-minded and patriotic pronouncement, which does him infinite credit, surely the hon. gentleman to-night will of necessity have to support the amendment introduced by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and oppose the Bill that is now before the House. If he does not do so, then he must be a victim, for the time being, of what is sometimes referred to in law-and my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie), will appreciate the significance of this,- as force majeur.
Then this afternoon we had a speech from my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). The right hon. gentleman said, at one stage of his interesting address, that there was very strong objection to the whole principle underlying the Civil Service Act. Now, we on this side of the House had a very strong suspicion that that was the case. We had an irresistible suspicion that this "strong objection" to the principle underlying the Civil Service Act came from quarters very close to the Minister of Justice. Strange to say, however, the right hon. gentleman proceeded with his speech and actually concluded without telling us whence those objections came. He did not give us the names, nor did he refer to individuals; but that omission has unintentionally been supplied by several hon. gentlemen who made speeches from the minister's side of the House later on in the discussion. That statement of the minister's was very interesting; but still more interesting was the declaration of the

right hon. gentleman when he said: " I am not here to express what modification, if any, should be made in the Civil Service Act Well, what is he here for? What is a member of the Government here for, if not, when he rises to support a measure, to express his candid views upon it and give to the House the benefit of his opinion? My right hon. friend took that position this afternoon, and I made a note of the statement because it struck me, with all due respect, as a most extraordinary one for my right hon. friend to make. If the right hon. member and his colleagues are not here to say what modification, if any, should be made in the Civil Service Act, a measure which, as it stands to-day, is a piece of legislation of their own enactment, then, Sir, I ask, what position does the Government take? What lead is the Government prepared to give to the House in connection with such an important matter as this? The Government and its followers take, and deserve, credit for having placed all these public positions outside of the bounds of patronage, and for having passed the Civil Service Act of 1918, and subsequent legislation. Now my right hon. friend tells the House that there is a very strong objection to the whole principle underlying the Civil Service Act, but, at the same time, he declares that he is not here to state what modification, if any, should be made in the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend intends to misrepresent what I said. I did not say, or, at all events, I did not intend to say, that there was any strong difference of opinion with regard to the principle that underlies the Civil Service Act. What I did say-at least, what I intended to say-was that there was a very strong divergence of opinion as to whether the Civil Service Act had worked out in the best manner to attain the purposes for which it had been enacted, and to give effect to what I understood to be the fundamental principle of the Act.

I unreservedly accept
what my hon. friend says, and that just enables me to anticipate a comment which I was going to make a little later on. If that is the position my right hon. friend took this afternoon and now takes-and I do not question that it was and still is- then I say that if the Government desire to investigate that aspect of the matter they should send the whole question before a committee and not submit to that body merely a few phases of the matter, to

which the committee will be shackled in their consideration of the measure. That, I urge, is the position the Government should have adopted; they should have referred the whole question to the committee, and not limited the committee to a few things specified in this particular Bill.
Now, my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), also spoke this afternoon, and in the course of his address he enumerated some reasons why, in his judgment, the Bill should be sent to a committee. He detailed for the House the extensive and difficult work which the Civil Service Commission has had to do in connection with classification and what he styled the troublous conditions during the last two years. He said, and said truly, that the work of the commission had produced criticism and opposition, and added that he had sympathy with the commission under the circumstances. My right hon. friend proceeded to say that he did not want the Civil Service Commission or the Civil Service law to be bowled out of existence without further examination. Well, I take it that that is the pass which we have reached in connection with this reform. We are on the eve of witnessing the Civil Service Act and the Civil Service Commission "bowled out of existence;" but my right hon. friend interposed the hope on his part, that this would not occur. I submit that this observation of the right hon gentleman shows the force of the pressure behind the Government which has compelled it at this stage of the present session to bring in the measure now before the House.
I repeat, if it were intended by the Government to ascertain how the Civil Service Act had operated, and how the general principle had been applied in that operation, the proper thing for the Government to have done would have been to refer the whole matter to a committee. Instead of that, however, they have brought in a Bill which, by its terms, limits the operations of the committee to three matters specifically mentioned therein, and beyond that the measure does not go. However, within the compass of what it is proposed to refer to the committee, a great deal of danger lies,- so much danger, in fact, that if the committee adopt this Bill, and if it comes back to the House and is passed, then we may bid good-bye to Civil Service reform as well as to the Civil Service Commission, and we shall hail again the return of patronage in all departments of the Government

in this country. Now, I told my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie), that I had made some notes of what he said. My hon. and genial friend, after about half an hour's speech in favour of the Bill and against the Civil Service Commission, concluded with the statement that he did not want to express any opinion at the present time. Well, my hon. friend was always a joker, and I took him to be in good form to-night when he made that observation. After having spoken for half an hour in favour of the Bill, and in Criticism of the Civil Service Commission, he said that he did not want to express any opinion. Well, for the life of me, I could not see what he had been at during that half hour if he had not been doing that very thing, and I had been paying special attention to the hon. gentleman because I always listen to him with a great deal of interest. Prior to that, however, ihy hon. friend said the trouble with the commission-whose secretary seems to trouble the dreams of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken)-was that there were too many appointments made from Ottawa, and he asserted that this is what is to be investigated by the special committee. If that be the fact that is a new reason for this committee.

The hon. gentleman says
I am prejudging the commission. I have a perfect right to say what I like about the commission.
Certainly.

I do not prejudge the
Bill. The hon. gentleman cannot separate the Bill from the commission. He seems to think the commission and the Bill are the same. I am not expressing any view on the Bill except that there are some provisions in it which I do not quite agree with.

Mr. Speaker, the admissions named toy the hon. gentleman make it unnecessary for me to elaborate my argument. My hon. friend did prejudge what is going to be done by the committee, and he has confirmed that by the observation he has just addressed to me so that I need not pursue the point-he and I are in perfect agreement. The other day the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) had a few remarks to make about the Bill and he referred to it as a skeleton. At the time that struck me as ominous, and listening to the observations of his supporters this afternoon I realized that the word was well chosen. This Bill is
evidently one of the party skeletons in the Government cupboard. That is why the rattling of the bones has occasioned so much trouble here this afternoon and this evening. Well, the attempt on the part of the Government to return to old conditions has attracted a good deal of attention outside this House, and only this morning a letter appeared in the Citizen newspaper of this city in which the writer, after enumerating the provisions of the Bill before the House, says this:
These sweeping changes have undoubtedly had their origin, first of all in the desire of certain politicians to revert to the "spoils** system, tat least in some measure, and secondly, in the dissatisfaction of the deputy heads with the many changes and frequent delays occasioned by the inauguration of a completely new system. Were the present merit system to be given another year in which to put classification upon a really satisfactory basis and to organize the necessary system for appointments in government offices far distant from Ottawa there is no doulbt but that the deputy ministers themselves would be satisfied with the situation.
This is the thin end of the wedge in returning to the "spoils" system, and, if it becomes law, Canada will be the only country in the world to have made [DOT] such a retrograde step. The fact that the thinking public, the civil servants themselves, the public press and the prominent men of Canada, Great Britain and the United States have repeatedly expressed themselves in favor of the merit system as opposed to the "spoils" system, makes it inconceivable that the Parliament of Canada should approve of the vicious and retrograde proposals included in the present measure.
The statements in that letter, Mr. Speaker, I am quite satisfied will be the considered judgment of the people of this country when they become aware of the proposals embodied in this Bill. Now, Sir, the Bill, I submit, is either a sop to the opponents of Civil Service reform who desire a return to party patronage or, if it is not that, then it is an instrument to destroy the Civil Service Commission, and in either case the result will be the same. If it is the first-that is if it is a sop on the part of the Government to those who are opposed to Civil Service reform and who desire a return to the patronage system-it is quite plain what will happen in this connection. The committee will dawdle along, it will kill time, and prorogation will arrive without anything having been done. If, on the other hand, it is not that but is a design to kill the Civil Service Commission the fact will be made known sooner or later, and the sooner the better. I say-better sffoner than later, because one of the first effects of the enactment of this legislation will be seen in the appointments that will follow soon

after to influence the pending by-elections. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, what may be done when this class of public appointees is once more placed at the disposal of the Government. Take manual labourers, whatever may be the character of the work upon which they are employed, whether they are paid by the hour, day, week, month, the job or by duties and you can visualize, Sir, what will happen if all that class of public) employees is once more placed under the discretion of the party in power, of the ministers of the day. And then, Sir, the full effect of this Bill, if it becomes law, will be seen in the by-elections that now cannot be very long deferred. Already we have had the Minister of Trade and Commerce announcing and defending in this House the appointment' of 24,000 census enumerators. A further army will be appointed by the Government-

My hon. friend will allow me to ask him, even though it was in reference to a statement made by myself, to reduce that 24,000 by one-half. The number of enumerators will, I am informed, be upwards of ten or twelve thousand.
I accept the right hon. gentleman's statement and I sympathize with him in the fact that he had to disappoint ten or twelve thousand others who were expecting jobs.
My hon friend sympathizes with me.
Well, even the corrected figures given by my right hon. friend represent a fair sized army.

A little later on an army far in excess of that number will, in all probability, be appointed by the Government .to prepare the voters' lists. Then, as was the case in the West Peterborough election, there will be contracts given and jobs opened up at the psychological moment. They will happen to synchronize, as an old friend' of ours used to say, with the dates of holding the by-elections in the different constituencies. In these constituencies other armies of ten or twelve thousand

or less, or more as the case may be-will be appointed and so it will go on in varying but ever-increasing numbers throughout the Dominion. Now if hon. gentlemen in this House, on whichever side they may sit, who honestly desire Civil

Service reform and the abolition of party patronage, will just visualize these things for a moment there can be no doubt as to the course they will pursue in connection with the measure now before the House. Besides that, Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should say to the hon. gentlemen who compose the Opposition sitting on this side that unless they are prepared, with their eyes open>
to place in the hands of the Government a weapon that will be used for their political extinction they should oppose this measure, not only now, but later on, with all the resources that Parliamentary procedure affords them and go to the length -not only now but later on-of obliging the Government of the day, which has gone back upon its professions and its practices in connection with Civil Service reform, to put any such measure as this through the House only by the application of closure.

Mr. Speaker, I shall only occupy a few moments of the time of the House out of consideration for one of the Progressive group who can hardly hold himself in check, and also by reason of the fact that I feel myself somewhat at a disadvantage in discussing this subject as against certain hon. gentlemen sitting opposite who have had advantages which I never expect to have. I refer to the hon. member for Gaspe and Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux), to my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Murphy), to the hon. gentleman who some time ago occupied a seat in the Government and sat on this side of the House, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and to the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), who also at one time in his distinguished career occupied a seat as a Cabinet minister. I say I am at a disadvantage in discussing this subject with those gentlemen because I cannot speak of the wrongs that were committed in times past in the distribution of patronage, and the horror which they now express is no doubt due to the workings of consciences which have long laid dormant. I can understand, for instance, the eloquence of the hon. member for Gaspe and Maisonneuve in regard to the wrongs and injustices committed in times past by Cabinet ministers when they held this patronage in their hands, but of course he has had experience in that particular which I lack.
But, Sir, I am consistent at all events in my opposition to the operations of the Civil Service Commission as carried on at present. Like my hon. friend from West

Toronto (Mr. Hocken), from the very first I expressed on the floor of the House my opposition to placing this power in the hands of a body of three men sitting here in Ottawa. I said that it was placing in their hands a power which was beyond their ability to exercise properly, and as time has gone on I have become fully convinced that my criticism was fully justified, for we have any amount of evidence throughout the country that no body of men sitting here in Ottawa can exercise the powers which have been conferred upon these men and exercise them justly and fairly. My hon. friend from West Toronto in my judgment was perfectly justified in referring to specific cases of lack of efficiency, if you like to put it in those words, either on the part of the Civil Service Commission or of the secretary of that commission. Some exception was taken by the hon. member for Marquette to his placing those facts before the House. But, Sir, I would like to call attention to some evidence which was placed on Hansard within the last week or ten days in answer to a question of mine, and inasmuch as that question was answered by the Civil Service Commission I think I shall be quite justified in making reference to it. I asked a certain question in regard to an appointment made some time ago in Paris, when it was made, whether by competitive examination, the salary paid, and how many persons competed. In due time the question was answered by 'the Civil Service Commission. It gave a list of some ten or twelve persons who had been applicants for the position, it stated the date when the competitive examination was held, and it also gave the name of the person holding the office, and the date of his appointment. That date was just seventeen months prior to the holding of the examination! That is very clear evidence, it seems to me, that things are not working as smoothly and properly as some hon. gentlemen would have us believe.
I could refer to a number of cases which have been brought to my notice, and which prove very clearly to my mind the utter impossibility of three men sitting here in Ottawa-I do not care how able they are- properly carrying on all the work which is thrown upon the shoulders of this Civil Service Commission. They have given evidence themselves time and time again that they cannot do the work. And when you talk of taking the patronage away from the members' of Parliament who, after all,
are held responsible if any inefficient servant is appointed, you are simply transferring that patronage from men who are held responsible by the people to men who have no responsibility at all and who snap their fingers in the! face of the people. What happened a few years ago? A certain position was advertised and several hundred applications came in to the commission. I forget the nature of the position, but that does not matter; I will guarantee that my statement is correct. The commission looked at the bunch of applications and exclaimed, " Oh, my goodness, we cannot handle that work, we have not got time," and they selected a number of men from the city of Ottawa to assist them.
I only remember the name of one of them, Mr. P. D. Ross, the editor and proprietor of the Ottawa Journal.

That was
for a publicity office.

I have forgotten the nature of the office, but a bunch of 300 or 400 applications came in and the Civil Service Commission referred them to two or three men. These men also were appalled by the magnitude of the task, and they shot their hands through the pile, threw two-thirds of the applications haphazard into the waste-paper basket, and went through the remaining eighty or a hundred applications. When they reached a conclusion they recommended to the Civil Service Commission that John Jones, we will say, should be appointed. Of course, we are told that the Civil Service Commission made the appointment of John Jones for that position. What an absurdity! Instead of the responsibility resting upon the commission it really rested upon Mr. P. D. Ross, the editor of the Ottawa Journal, and his two colleagues to make a proper selection. We might, of course, expect that gentleman to feel that it was incumbent upon him to exercise his best judgment in making a selection-a selection requested by a certain commission appointed by the Government which had been so kind to him in the way of giving him hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of printing and advertising, and that sort of thing, renting a portion of his building and making him rich-in that respect he might feel a certain amount of gratitude and be impelled to do his very best in making a proper selection. Who was exercising patronage there? The editor of the Ottawa Journal and one or two who were associated with him were exercising patronage. And what

responsibility had they? If the person selected by them and appointed to the position proved to be inefficient, who was called to task for it? The Government of the day would be called to task because of the inefficiency of that man. Will it answer before the public for the Government to say in such a ease: We had nothing to do with the appointment of this man; we agree that he is not efficient; we agree that he should not be there, but we are absolutely helpless; we did not appoint him; do not blame us. Will hon. gentlemen opposite take that attitude? Will they refrain from blaming the Government if any man appointed by the Civil Service Commission or by men selected by them proves inefficient? Not on your life; but they will utilize every moment of their time throughout the country in pointing to the inefficiency of this man and blaming the Government because of his inefficiency.
Now, the hon. member from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) thinks it would be a terrible thing to go back to patronage, but he has never expressed any great alarm about the attitude of his friends in the Government at Toronto. The Drury Government have not given up party patronage, though before election they were loud-mouthed in their expressions against it. Ever since they have been in office they have exercised patronage right to the hilt. What did Mr. Morrison say in that regard when comment was made with reference to a certain appointment made not very long ago? He said: "We are just human-we are showing that we are human in giving these positions to our friends." But there has been no criticism or condemnation from the hon. member for Marquette on that account. Not a word will he say about the Drury Government giving out a tender for $100,000 or $115,000 worth of motor trucks in about fifteen or twenty minutes to a friend of one of the ministers, without asking for tenders. Oh, no, that does not strike horror into the' heart of the hon. member for Marquette. That is perfectly fine in his estimation, just as are a great many other things that that government has done; and he will still go on lauding that government to the skies as absolutely perfect.
Now, with regard to other remarks passed by the hon. gentlemen opposite, especially by those who are lined up. along the front benches, if I had any doubts before coming into this chamber whether this Bill was a move in the right direction, they would all have been removed by the

attitude of certain of those gentlemen. Mr. Speaker, you can take it from me as absolutely true, as beyond any question of doubt, that when you see dyed-in-the-wool Grits like the hon. gentlemen opposite percetly satisfied with this commission and the way they are handing out patronage, there is something wrong in the state of Denmark. The member for West Toronto showed to what extent the secretary of the commission was carrying on. I do not know how close hon. gentlemen opposite are to the secretary of that commission, but I have a kind of suspicion that they are a great deal closer to him than I, am and that they can exercise a greater influence over him in regard to making of appointments than anybody on this side can. If they could not and were not exercising that influence, they surely would not be so well satisfied with the conditions as they appear to be.
I want to say right here that the fault I have to find with this Bill is that it does not go far enough. In my estimation the Bill should take the Outside Service entirely out of the hands of the Civil Service Commission. That, of course, is only my own opinion, and I do not expect that it will prevail. But I believe that as time goes on it will be demonstrated that the Outside Service should be taken out of the hands of the Civil Service Commission, and even then I think that the commission would have, in looking after the Inside Service alone, more work, perhaps, than they could properly attend to.
Can you imagine anything more ridiculous, Mr. Speaker, than the Civil Service Commission, sitting here in Ottawa, appointing rural postmasters? Hon. gentlemen say that the object of those who favour that particular clause of the Bill is to return to patronage; that they are animated by the desire to have the pleasure of handling the patronage-of naming postmasters now and then. But hon. gentlemen who represent rural constituencies know that in recommending the appointments of postmasters they would not have occasion to name more than two or three persons in the course of a parliamentary term, so that I do not think that patronage amounts to very much. But there is this feature to be considered, Mr. Speaker: in connection with the appointment of rural postmasters the member is merely the representative or mouthpiece of the people living in the section concerned. Any man who has any political shrewdness will, in making recommendation of a rural post-

master, consult the people in the locality where the appointment is to be made, and in that way the appointment is really made by the people. That is the way the appointment had always been made before the matter was placed in the hands of the Civil Service Commissiion. No member would fly in the face of public opinion in his county and recommend for appointment some person whose appointment would not meet with the approval of his people. At least, if he did he would seem to be lacking in political shrewdness. The method of making appointments to these minor positions was, under the old system, the most democratic method possible, for I say it was really the people who made the appointments; the member was merely the mouthpiece for the people.
Can you imagine anything more ridiculous, Sir, than this? Two or three years ago a little dredging was being done along that part of the Rideau Canal which runs through my constituency. The work was only to last for two or three weeks and they wanted a few labourers. What happened? They had to apply to the Civil Service Commission in Ottawa to appoint three or four men to act as labourers on that work for two or three weeks. Can you imagine anything more ridiculous? How did they know whom to appoint? How did they find out? They wrote to the postmaster or to some other person living in that locality and asked him to send the names of two or three men. Who was distributing the patronage? The one man in that locality who suggested the three or four names. WThat responsibility did he have? None whatever.
In the appointment of a postmaster vhat is the practice? We were told by one hon. member that when a rural postmaster was to be appointed, the inspector for that postal district went out and ascertained the man who should get the appointment. They do not do anything of the kind. When a vacancy occurs and a postmaster has to be appointed in some rural locality, the Civil Service Commission writes to the inspector of the district asking him to make a recommendation. What does he do? I do not know how he gets the names, but he ascertains the names of one or two persons in that locality, and he writes to them asking them to submit the name of a man who would fill the office of postmaster. On the say so of one or two gentlemen, the inspector passes the name on to the Civil Service Commission, and the Civil Service Commission makes the appoint-
182i
ment. Supposing the wrong man is appointed, supposing some person is appointed who is not efficient. What happens? At once the community finds fault with the member and holds him responsible for the appointment of an inefficient person. I heard of a case of an office that was to be filled along the Welland canal. It required a man of clerical ability, and preference was going to be given to a returned soldier. A written test was made, and the man who showed up best by his handwriting and the way in which he answered the questions was a returned soldier. On the result of that test, the Civil Service Commission made the appointment. No sooner was the appointment made than the people of that locality were up in arms, and to whom did they go? They went to the member of that particular constituency and they found fault with him. What was the burden of their complaint? They said that this man was an ex-convict and was out on parole, who enlisted and went overseas, who came back and fulfilled the conditions of being a returned soldier; but he was given preference over men who were thoroughly qualified and who had always been good respectable citizens. The people of that locality did not feel that that was right, and I think if I had lived there, I would have taken the same view that they did. The Civil Service Commission made the appointment with nothing to go by except the handwriting of this man and the arrangement of words in sentences in the examination paper. That shows at once that they made a mistake and a mistake which they had to rectify and did rectify by putting the man out of office. When the mistake was made, the people of that locality showed their lack of confidence, if you like, in the Civil Service Commission, by carrying their complaint at once to the member for that constituency. They held him responsible', and where the responsibility is held by the member, it is no more than right that he should be consulted in making sudh appointment.
In my judgment, the proper thing to do as regards the Outside Service is to put the patronage in the hands of the sitting member for the constituency, no matter which side of the House he sits on. I know that some take the view that if patronage is restored, it should go to the member supporting the Government and to the defeated candidate in constituencies which are supported by the Opposition. I do not hold that view; I say that when a man is elected to this House as a supporter

of the Government or not, he is here representing the people; the responsibility rests upon his shoulders, and I would listen to that man in regard to the patronage of his constituency. He will consult with the people who sent him here in making any recommendations to the commission, and I believe that the public service will be thoroughly safeguarded if that is done.
Party patronage came into disrepute in this country, not so much on account of the appointment of officials as on account of favouritism that was shown in letting contracts. I have had more or less to do with public life for quite a long while, and I can remember, when a certain party was in power and contracts for supplies of this or that kind were to foe let, there would be a list of supporters of the party in power and only those who were on that list could tender on that particular contract. I know that that has been the case, and that is something to be condemned and the public generally do condemn it. I do not know whether that obtained when the Conservative party was in power; but I do know that it obtained when the Liberal party was in power, and that only those who were associated with the Liberal party were allowed to tender for certain supplies. I am not going to say that it did not exist when the Conservative party was in power, but I am not aware of any cases. I am aware of cases when the other party was in power and, perhaps, some hon. gentleman can supplement my knowledge with regard to the actions of their party by referring to something that was done by the party with which I have been identified. I said that it was that sort of thing which brought patronage into disrepute and not the appointment of officials to little positions like country postmasterships and positions of that kind. I do not think there was ever any outcry in the country against that sort of thing, nor do I see that the passing of this measure is going to interfere with promotion on merit. I do not see why it should.
As )regards the cases referred to in the Bill, it is quite certain that the postmasters who are referred to in one clause are mostly country postmasters. No person in the Civil Service is going to ask to be promoted from a job which he has in Ottawa to be a country postmaster drawing $50 or $60 a year. There are not going to be any complaints along that line, and the same is true as regards day labour. I do not see how that is going to interfere

in any way with promotion by merit. The matter of appointments to the Outside Service could be properly safeguarded by an examination test such as we had before, the Outside Service was placed in the hands of the Civil Service Commission. I do not think it is necessary, nor do I think that the Civil Service Commission should feel that when a person gets up in this House to express his convictions along this line, he is making an attack on members of the commission. I have known two of the members of the commission for a number of years, and while I have respect for their ability, I never thought, even with all my regard for them, that they possessed any ability above that of the average member of ithis House, for instance. I never credited them with being supermen, and that is what you have to credit them with being if you entrust them with or say that they are capable of carrying out the work which has been laid upon their shoulders. As the system is carried on now, it is open to very severe and justifiable criticism, because of favouritism which has been shown, because of appointments which have been made evidently without the knowledge of the Civil Service Commissioners at all, through the efforts of the secretary of the commission, and because appointments have been advertised which were filled many months before. All that justifies the reference of this matter to a committee which will bring out all the facts in connection with the case.

Mr. Speaker, I shall detain the House only for a few minutes, as it is now past midnight. I have listened with very close attention to the speeches made by hon. members on the other side of the House, and it is quite evident from their speeches, with perhaps one exception, that they want to go back to the flesh pots of Egypt, to taste the old party patronage system. The hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) 'made a very vigorous speech-more vigorous than logical. Summed up in a few words, it amounted to this: Let us go back to the old party patronage system that was in vogue when I came into the House in 1911 and 1912. What was that patronage system, Mr. Speaker? I have been told by an hon. member who was in the House at that time that 10,000 civil servants were dismissed, or compelled to resign and that their places were filled by-what? By 23,000 untrained men and women, that is the spoils system. That is the system my good friend from Simcoe wants to restore.

I want to ask a question. Did that same gentleman also tell the hon. member that I read a list of 7,000 civil servants who were dismissed in the first few weeks after Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power?

I do not consider that a question at all. My good friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) made a very bitter attack, an unwarranted attack, I think, at least an unfair attack, upon one member of the Civil Service Commission in particular. He wants this House to believe that the actions of the Civil Service Commission have been such that power should be taken out of their hands, and that appointments have been made before positions were advertised. Now I want to speak of the Civil Service Commission as I have found them. Even after I ceased to be a constant supporter of the Government, I found no difference in the commission when I would recommend a returned soldier for a position that was vacant. I have no special axe to grind;
I am simply speaking of the commission as I have found them. In regard to the secretary, Mr. Foran, I have always found him a gentleman; he has always treated me courteously. The Civil Service Commissioners are Tory appointees, I believe, and it seems strange indeed that they would not treat well birds of their own feather, or at all events treat them a little better than their opponents. I remember very well in the campaign of 1917 the right hon. the member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) and two of his ministers toured the West. One of them has since gone to his reward; I refer to the late Right Hon. Arthur A. L. Sifton. The other minister who accompanied the ex-Prime Minister was the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), who was in the Cabinet at that time. My hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) was also on the platform that night in the city of Calgary. The three gentlemen I have named stated distinctly that the Union Government had abolished the party patronage system. Now I presume that the present Government is the successor of the Union Government of 1917, led by the right hon. the present member for King's. That being the case, why do they go back on their pledge? Was it merely a plank adopted for the purpose of getting the vote of the western farmers for the Union Government, because our good friends very well knew that one of the strong planks in the platform of organized agriculture in the West was Civil Service reform. I do not believe that that was in the mind of the ex-Prime Minister, and I am sorry that this Government proposes to take a retrograde step and go back to the old system of patronage and corruption.
* I do not contend that the present system is altogether perfect. There is room for reform, but a step in the right direction has been taken. There is one thing I have noticed, and that is that the Civil Service organization strongly support the present system of leaving appointments to the Civil Service Commission; they are strongly in favour of the competitive system of appointment, and the principle of promotions on merit. If we are to reverse conditions there will be no incentive for men in the service, because they will know very well-many of them were in the Civil Service under the old patronage system- what would happen. We need only recall the conditions that obtained in the Printing Bureau before 1918. Since that time hundreds of employees of the Printing Bureau have been pensioned off. Why? Simply because a great many of those employees were put there, no doubt by both parties, because they were good party heelers, but so far as the Printing Bureau was concerned they were misfits, and had never been trained to the printing business. Their appointment was the reward for political service in political campaigns. Surely we do not want to go back to that system, and I sincerely hope we shall not.
It seems to me from reading this Bill, as a layman, that this proposal would destroy our Civil Service system, because I find that it provides that everything which the Civil Service Commission would do must be referred to the Governor in Council. As I read it, that means that the power is taken from the commission and reverts to the Government. It means that we shall have corruption as we had it in the olden days, when thousands of civil servants were dismissed to make place for party heelers of the Government then in power. We have seen something of this in the West; perhaps it has not been as bad out there as in the East, but it has been bad enough.
I shall have much pleasure in supporting the amendment introduced by the senior member for Halifax.

I
shall not detain the House very long. I believe that in the constitution of the Civil Service Commission the Government went

too far and too fast. I do not think the country was ready for such a radical change involving such a tremendous work as was thrown upon the commission when they undertook it. I do not think that the commission was then, or is now, properly manned and equipped to take care of the work undertaken by it over the whole extent of the Dominion of Canada, particularly in connection with the Outside Service. So far as the commission is concerned, while I have not had much personal contact with them, I have been obliged to send letters on to them that were directed to me by mistake; and though I would hardly venture to make any recommendation, I have always found a ready response and a reasonable action in connection with all correspondence I have sent them. I think it is fair to give credit both to the secretary and to the members of the commission, so far, at any rate, as I am personally concerned, in regard to anything that I have asked them to do. Of course, I have never had the temerity to recommend people for positions, as my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) is in the habit of doing. I should be afraid to attempt to do anything of the kind, and I have a rather higher conception of my position as a member of Parliament than to dare to do anything so bold as that.

I said a
returned soldier. I am very much surprised that my hon. friend would not recommend a returned soldier for any position.

I do not know that even that, under the circumstances, is a good excuse. It is the best one the iton. gentleman could find, but I did not hear him say that it was only returned soldiers in Whom he took an interest. However, that is by the way. Now, the reason I support this Bill being sent to the committee springs out of the abstract statement I made at first:	I do not believe the Civil
Service Commission can manage the whole public service of the country. Let me give, in illustration, an Ontario case in connection with the Marine Department. I am informed on excellent authority that the commission undertook to institute an organization for steam boiler inspection at Toronto, and, after much deliberation, the commission recommended three men, named Evans, Stewart and Arnold, for the purpose. Now, Evans at the time had been placed on the retired list; Stewart was said to be competent; and Arnold had been dead for about six months. That case can be

verified, and it is due to the Civil Service Commission that it should be stated in this House, so that before this committee gets to work they can prepare an answer to show whether or not there was efficiency in connection with this matter. There is an Ottawa case also. "A" wrote an examination for inspector of immigration in June, 1920, and passed fourth highest in all Canada. Observe, this was in June, 1920. Last week he heard that five appointments were to be made. He made inquiry of the commission and was told that he must know the French language. He replied: "I do; I understand it almost .perfectly." He got past that point; he told them: "My papers show that I understand the language. If you had read my papers you would have seen that I understand the French language." They then told him that he should see someone else on the staff,-it is a sort of repetition of the story told by the hon. member for Toronto West (Mr. Hocken), another case of passing the buck. He went to this other Mr. So-and-So, who told him: "Well, you know, we must fill these positions with returned soldiers." Well, this gentleman replied:	"I went over early in the war
and did not return until after the armistice, and my papers show that fact too." Now, I say that these two cases show lack of consideration, lack of knowledge, lack of proper manning, lack of capacity; they demonstrate that the work is too big and too extensive to be allotted to any single board, at least until the Inside Service has been under way for years, and has been properly crystallized, and until efficiency is secured in regard to the public service. This efficiency is possible if half of the service is undertaken by the commission instead of the whole thing at once. Before the Pensions and Re-establishment Committee the other day appeared Mr. Dobbs. He was sworn, and took up the case of Christian Nelson, a double leg amputation case. Nelson was a heavy man, and had applied for a position. The evidence states:
This man applied for a position, I was given to understand at the time, on December 17 last, [DOT]that there was a vacancy for a switch board operator in the Post Office in Toronto. He made application on December 17, and I helped to make out his application. . . . Finally, Colonel Ross, the chief superintendent, recommended this man as a stamp vendor, which position I believe has gone through. I learned that only this morning. But on consultation with them this morning we found there was neither his application for the position nor any correpond-ence on the file previous to March 24. Where it has gone I do not know.
Mr. MacNeil: Was it sent to the department? Mr. Dobbs: To the department or the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is not in order in referring to evidence taken before a standing committee which has not reported to the House.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and will read no further. But this man, this double amputation case,_ as can be proved, on making his application, could not, get the position which he desired, but they advised him in a letter from the Civil Service Commission to apply for the post of letter carrier,-without any legs to carry letters on!

(Quebec South): After hearing the remarks made by some hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly the member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie), the member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), and the member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy),
I have been wondering whether the criticism of the Civil Service Commission, and particularly of the secretary, would have been so bitter had this gentleman paraded on the same day as some of these hon. members. I would say to these hon. gentlemen that, while criticising the secretary, they might have helped their case to a considerable degree by showing their impartiality at the same time in a strong criticism of the other members of the commission. After all, the secretary is only the servant of the commission, and if the three commissioners are not competent to manage the business of the commission, then I should think that hon. gentlemen opposite should ask, first, for the dismissal of the commissioners before advocating that of their paid servant. If the commissioners are incompetent, the secretary should be commended for having taken so much of their work upon his own shoulders. If, on the other hand, they are competent, then they should be in a position to keep the secretary in his place.
It was not for the purpose of stating this, however, that I rose at this late hour; it was merely to correct a misapprehension under which the hon. gentleman from North Simcoe seems to be labouring. I am sorry the hon. gentleman is not in his seat at this moment. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I could not catch your eye at an earlier period in the evening when my hon. friend was present. The hon. gentleman, speaking on behalf of the returned soldiers seemed to wish the House to be under the impression that they were in favour of the present Bill and, generally speaking, of the abolition of the Civil Service Commission.
I do not know whether or not the hon. gentleman gets his information from individuals who, at meetings presided over by him, made references to the Prime Minister of Canada of such a character that it was said that members of the Government refused to meet one particular speaker. I do not know whether the hon. member for North Simcoe gets his information from individuals such as those. As for myself, Sir, I go to what I consider the best authority that I know of in connection with returned soldiers. I go to what I consider the organization of returned soldiers that is most truly representative and which, as a rule, most sincerely and most clearly expresses the views of the great mass of returned men-I refer to the Great War Veterans' Association. Consulting the Ottawa Citizen of Friday, under the heading "Veterans Opposed to Patronage Bill"
I read the following:
The G.W.V.A., however, will vigorously oppose the Bill. Mr. C. Grant MacNeil, Dominion Command Secretary, stated that the G.W. V.A. was wholly and totally opposed to the new Bill.
