So that on the first occasion when the Government had an opportunity of doing away with patronage and so improving the lot of the returned soldier, it filled less than half of these posts by the appointment of returned soldiers. Surely no hon. gentleman opposite will rise in his seat and say that in his constituency no returned soldier was fit to hold such a position. I am sure that no hon. gentleman will say that, and if he does not do so how can he explain the reason for the appointment of comparatively few returned soldiers who, in a large number of instances, are responsible members sitting in this House.
Now, Sir, we have been told by the hon. memiber for North Simcoe that at the time this Act was introduced he asked that a returned soldier be appointed on the commission. If that is true I think the returned soldiers will thank him for his interest in their behalf. I should have thought, however, that he would have had sufficient influence with his colleagues to have insisted upon the appointed. I have come to the conclusion, however, that a Cabinet professedly formed in the interests of the returned soldiers which could not give a returned soldier a place in its ranks could not be expected to give a returned soldier representation on any other body.
I have only this much further to add-that should this project ibe carried	into execution we	will beface	to	face with this	situation:
Hon. gentlemen opposite were carried into power on one of the basic principles of their platform,-reform of the Civil Service. For four years they allowed the Civil Service to be reformed in order not to meet their responsibility of making appointments when such appointments would have been difficult to make. As any member who has had anything to do with patronage knows, during the lull between one election and another members are confronted with serious difficulties in relation to the exercise of patronage. Hon. gentlemen opposite did not take the courageous course when they had an opportunity to do so, but now on the eve of a general election, when it is possible to employ hundreds of thousands of men throughout

the country, they are only too glad to seek this belated opportunity to exercise patronage in the hope that by so doing they may obtain votes which otherwise would be lost to them. It hon. gentlemen opposite wish to obtain an honest judgment on their misdeeds, if every hon. member wishes the people to express their opinion fairly and squarely on the questions of the day, it is their duty to oppose this measure in every way they can and to the utmost limit provided by the constitution.
I should like to ask the hon. member if he approves of the system of keeping a returned soldier in the Civil Service for two, three and four years without making his position permanent?

I do not understand
what the hon. gentleman says.
I asked him if he approved of the system followed by the Civil Service Commission of keeping a returned soldier for years in the Civil Service without making his appointment permanent.

I do not know whether the Civil Service Commission ever did that; hut if the commission kept a man in the service for that length of time without making his appointment permanent because he was not qualified to fill the position, I do not want him in the Civil Service, whether he is a returned soldier or not.
You are backing up on it.

Mr. Speaker, when the Government made its appeal to the people in 1917 one of the planks of its programme was the abolition of patronage. In the West that was a popular cry, and the people generally responded to that appeal. Shortly. after the Government came into power they redeemed their election pledge. I am not here to criticise severely the operations of the Civil Service Commission. I believe that in large measure the appointment of that commission has been attended with a very reasonable amount of success and that on the whole it has worked fairly satisfactorily. But having said that, I do not mean to insinuate for one moment that complaints have not been made of serious defects in the working out of the Act. The work undertaken was of great importance and diversity, and it was only reasonable to expect that we would not get perfection in the operation of the Act. The Government has now reached the point where they find that these complaints have crystalliged into
a certain amount of opinion that has made it necessary for them to take action with a view to removing the defects complained of, and in order to do that they have introduced in skeleton form a Bill to he submitted to a committee of this House for consideration and recommendation.
The serious defect as I see it, looking on as a novice, I might say, is that men experienced in political matters have been able to read into the recommendations that have been made by the Government in this tentative Bill what I have not been able to discover myself, namely, that the Bill contains suggestions for the abolition of the Civil Service Commission. The Prime Minister some days ago stated distinctly that this was a measure to bring before hon. members certain suggestions in order to secure recommendations that would he beneficial in helping us to reach conclusions for the adoption of a better system than that which we now have. The statement was made to-day that this Bill simply meant the introduction of patronage. I do not see it in that light. Surely this Parliament is capable of looking into and correcting any defects in the present Act and giving us a measure that will have less blemishes. Possibly the old parliamentarian is able to see what the novice does not, and consequently, to express forebodings regarding the return of patronage, but I think it would be safer for us at this late hour to submit gracefully to the recommendation of the Government to place all the facts before the committee for consideration and recommendation, and surely our hands are not tied by taking this course. If the recommendations then made are such as to vindicate the fears that have been expressed, that will be the time for us to lay bare these troubles and to take action with a view to correcting them. I see no reason why we should not submit this matter to a committee which will have all the facts before them and which will submit a report for the consideration of the House.
Reference has been made by the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) to an appointment made in the city of Winnipeg and to the general satisfaction which attended that appointment. I wish to corroborate what he said in that regard; I believe that general satisfaction was( expressed in that appointment by the people of Winnipeg. But I want to put beside it a matter that came to my notice only last week. I was brought face to face with a person who made a statement which showed that there was serious lack of con-

sideration somewhere in connection with appointments that were to be made in Ontario and where the very principle complained of by members on the opposite side would seem to have thrust itself into the forefront and to have been the cause of a misunderstanding and bad administration. Cases of this kind ought to come before this committee and out of those cases there ought to be evolved some plan by which the difficulty would be overcome and a better system obtained than that which we now have. Let us trim up the weaknesses in1 the system. The principle is right; we want to stand by that principle as we have it.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. M. M. TWEEDIE (West Calgary) :
speechtext:
Notwithstanding the protests of some of my friends round about me and the anxious looks of some gentlemen opposite, I would like to make a few observations in regard to this Bill. The discussion seems to have proceeded upon the basis that this is a Bill to abolish the Civil Service Act which was passed in 1918 and to return absolutely to the patronage system as it existed prior to that time. The hon. member for Halifax has discussed the matter in great detail and has laid much stress upon tfye calamities which might result if this Bill passes. His first point was that there would be wholesale dismissals-this point was supported by the hon. member from Mackenzie (Mr. Reid)-and that party heelers would be placed in the positions thus vacated. But the hon. member for Halifax had more to do with the drafting of the Civil Service Act as passed in 1918 than any other member of the Government, and the power of dismissals under the Bill which is introduced to-day is exactly the same as that which was incorporated in the Bill which he piloted through the House. The power of dismissal of civil servants depends not upon this proposed legislation, but upon section 28 of the original Act, and if it is wrong to place in the hands of the Government the power to dismiss civil servants, then the member for Halifax is more than any other person chargeable with the responsibility of giving the Government any such power. If hon. members will take the trouble to read that section they will see exactly what the power of the Government is in that connection.
The hon. member for Mackenzie and the hon. member for Halifax would have the members of the House believe that if this legislation passes, every appointment in the Civil Service may be made by the Gov-

ernment. But there has been no change in the principle of the Civil Service Act except in respect to appointments enumerated in the first section of the Bill. These are limited to manual labourers, postmasters and professional, scientific and technical men. The hon. member from Halifax, when he was protesting to-day so strongly against this Bill, did not say that manual labourers should be appointed by the Civil Service Commission. He acknowledged that there were grave doubts whether the course taken under the Act of 1918 should any longer be followed; he admitted that that was a defect in the Act which required to be remedied. But rather than take the responsibility of attacking the difficulty which arises in connection with the Act the hon. gentleman would allow an ineffective law to drift along and have appointments made by the Civil Service Commission in cases with which they should have .nothing to do. In reference to country postmasters, while it looks as though postmasters who receive a percentage of the revenue may be appointed by the Government, the real test in connection with the appointment of all these postmasters is the fact that before they become permanent employees of the Government they must receive a certificate from the Civil Service Commission. The necessity for this provision must be apparent to every hon. member who represents a rural constituency. In a remote section of the country a postmaster receiving $50 or $75 or $100 a year may die and it is necessary that an appointment be made immediately so that the duties of the office may be carried on without undue interruption. But in the past these offices have been kept vacant; for months the vacancy has remained unfilled simply because it has been necessary to have the appointment made by the Civil Service Commission in Ottawa. In this respect I think the Bill is quite justified; power should be given to the Government to enable the Post Office Department, through its inspectors, to make the appointment at once, and after that appointee has been there for six months or less he must get a certificate from the Civil Service Commission if he desires to become a permanent employee.
With regard to the third class mentioned, professional', scientific and technical men, I think the commission itself has realized that to follow out the Act strictly is not feasible. If the Government assumes the responsibility of making these appointments, who is responsible for giving them

that power? In order to do that it is not necessary that we should amend the Act as provided in this Bills, because section 38 of the Act passed in 1918-for which, as I say, the hon. member for Halifax is largely responsible-provides that in any event, where the commission decides that it is not practicable to apply the Act to appointments to any position or positions, the commission, with the approval of the Governor in Council, may make such regulations as are deemed advisable describing how such position or positions are to be dealt with. It is in connection with technical, scientific and professional men that the Civil Service Commission have found it necessary to depart from the Civil Service Act and to provide regulations for appointment.
In connection with practically all appointments to professional or technical positions in the Government service there has to be another commission appointed by the Civil Service Commission to do the work which the Civil Service Commission are unable to do. They engage the services of three or four professional lawyers or engineers or chemists, and so on, and to them they delegate the power of selecting the men who shall fill these professional, scientific or technical position. The Civil Service Commission have demonstrated ab-salutely, by the manner in which they make those appointments, that the Civil Service Act is not applicable to those positions. They have found it necessary to have other regulations passed, and the question in connection with those appointments is: Should the Civil Service Commission have the power to delegate their authority, or should the authority be exercised by the Government in making those appointments? I believe in the best interests of the service, the Government should make the appointments of those professional, technical and scientific men. The Government are in close touch with the deputy heads of the departments, and in the matter of making these appointments, I believe they are absolutely sincere in their desire to get the highest grade of technical men who may be employed in this country.
The Bill goes a little further, and what objection can be taken to any clauses in it? The whole argument which we hear is that the provisions of the Bill lead one to believe that it places the power absolutely in the Government, so that they may, without consideration of other parties, make any promotion which they see fit. But on
a closer examination of the Bill, it is perfectly evident that the Government will receive no such power as this; that if a promotion is to be made in the service, it cannot be done by the Government or by the Governor in Council on their own responsibility. That promotion must be made in conjunction with the deputy head of the department in which it is to be made, in conjunction w'ith the Civil Service Commission which administers this Act, and when the promotion is made, there must be a certificate from the Civil Service Commission as the result of an examination which may be oral or written. That certificate must be issued by the Civil Service Commission, and the power ultimately rests with the Civil Service Commission and no other body as to the promotion to be made.
As regards the question of transfer from one department to another, we find that the procedure as set out in the Bill is practically the same. The Government have no authority under this Bill, nor have they any authority under the Civil Service Act to make any transfer unless they have the recommendation of the department from which a man is to be transferred, the recommendation of the department to which the man is to be transferred and the certificate of the Civil Service Commission as the result of an examination, be that examination oral or written. When the Government have that, then the transfer may be made. The real determining factor in connection with those transfers is the Civil Service Commission, because they are the body which must issue the certificate.
For those reasons, I think that this Bill should be sent to the committee to find out whether or not any valid objections may be set forth by the Civil Service Commission or by any of the deputies to the operation of it. I would be the last man to wish to see the old patronage system brought hack again. My hon. friend said that if we pass this measure, then the railway employees will all he under the thumb of the Government. He also stated that the administration of the Government railways in this country was absolutely free from party patronage. I had the privilege and honour of living in the same province in which he lived; I had occasion to use and associated with others who used the Intercolonial railway, and I never knew of any organization or institution in this or any other country in which there was more political patronage used than was used in

connection with the administration of the Intercolonial railway in the Maritime Provinces and Quebec. But he need not have any have any worry about the administration of the railways in this country, because the railways themselves are manned by their organizations and brotherhoods, and there is not a single member in this House, there is not a single politician, I believe, in this country who would dare lay his fingers, as regards political patronage, on the securing of appointments or promotions in connection any of the Services connected with the operation of our national railways.
I have just one further remark to make which is occasioned by a remark of the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), when he stated very broadly his views regarding the removal of the Outside Service from the operation of the Civil Service Act. He said that he would advocate that the whole Outside Service be removed. My judgment is that this Government should not lay its hands upon the Outside Service any more than it does on the Inside Service, and that the Outside Service of this country should be allowed to remain under the operation of the Civil Service Act. I am sure that the Outside Civil Service in Western Canada want to remain under the Civil Service Act, and it would be an unwise act, a retrogade step for this Government to undertake in the slightest degree to remove the Outside Service from the administration of the Civil Service Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
I submit that it is
wholly unreasonable to ask the House to go into Supply at this hour of the morning. We have been sitting here since three o'clock on Monday afternoon; it is now a quarter-past one on Tuesday morning. The business we have been discussing is business that the Government has brought before the House. There has been no attempt to prolong the discussion in any unreasonable way, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the public business cannot be carried on six days of the week by this Parliament, as a deliberative assembly, in the way it should be carried on if the Prime Minister insists on holding sittings after midnight and on to two, three and four o'clock in the morning. I think the attitude of the Prime Minister in trying to force the business of the country at this hour of the morning is not. only unreasonable so far as members of the House are concerned, but it is also wholly unfair to the public.
The public have a right to know what Parliament is doing. They want to know what is being said and done here, but it is impossible for reports to go out to the public of the proceedings of the House after half-past one or two o'clock in the morning. The public have a right to know what is being done in the way of expenditure of public money, and it is that part of the business of the country which the Government now proposes to take up. I might also say that the members pf the House have committees to attend. There is not a single member who has not some public business to attend to in the morning, and it is impossible for hon. gentlemen to attend to their business, particularly on committees, if they are to sit here until two and three o'clock in the morning.
I would also like to say a word on behalf of the officers of the House. There are the members of the Hansard staff, who have a very difficult task to perform. They have to take down what is said here line by line, and word for word, and it becomes physically impossible for men to do that class of work after they have been subjected to the strain of very tong hours. There is not an officer of this House who has not duties of a responsible nature to discharge. Every one of these men is subjected to a strain that should not be imposed upon him.
I might also mention the Printing Bureau. There is a large staff of employees who are entitled to at least some consideration. There is the Press, represented in the Gallery by different correspondents. They have very responsible duties, which they are anxious to discharge in a faithful and efficient manner, but with continuous late sittings it is wholly impossible for them to discharge their duties in a way that is fair and right. I submit that night after night we have had to tolerate this condition of affairs in the discussion of public business in a way that is not befitting a deliberative assembly charged with the high and responsible duties which this Parliament is called upon to discharge.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have no desire to enter into any controversy as to the wisdom of sitting much later to-night, and I rise merely to lay before the House in a simple way the only idea that was in my mind in calling for Supply. The House knows, of course, the rules of Parliament whereby we are compelled to enter into Supply of every department on Monday, Tuesday or Wed-

nesday; otherwise that department is not available for Thursday or Friday. Almost invariabley this session we have been met by one motion or another on the motion for Supply, a debate, protracted very often far into the night, has ensued, the motion for Supply has not been reached until early in the morning, and then the motion has been met with a protest that it is not fair to hon. members or to anybody at all to go into Supply at that hour. That has been the process throughout this session. To-day we 'have had a debate on a simple motion to refer a question to a Special Committee of Parliament, which Parliament has already appointed, and notwithstanding the assurance of the Government that the whole question, irrespective entirely of the specific terms of the Bill would be submitted to the House for further consideration, a debate has taken place which has occupied the whole day. It is now one o'clock in the morning and we are asked to abandon the day and not even get into committee, so that we may be able to proceed on Thursday and Friday with Supply. Now, I suggest to hon. gentlemen that we go into Supply on one of the departments which we have not so far entered upon, so that we may take up Supply on Thursday and Friday. We do not even ask that an item be passed; we simply ask that we have this day count in Supply in one of the departments. There are five or six departments that have not yet been touched, and we shall not get through at the rate of progress we are making unless we can at least utilize Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday to go into Supply. The only suggestion I make now is that we go into Supply, take up an item, and then rise and report progress so that we may relieve the terrible strain upon the officers of the House, upon the press, and upon the Printing Bureau.

What the Prime Minister says is all very well in regard to this particular moment, but I submit that Monday has been considered Private Members' day and it is not customary for the Government to appropriate that day for Government business as early in the session as had been done this year. There is no reason why the Opposition, or members of the House generally, should be deprived of the privilege of taking up any matter they please on the motion to go into Supply before certain departments are called. The right of hon. members in that regard should be preserved, and I do 
not think we should be asked in any way to concede what the Prime Minister has requested at the present moment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We intend to move into Supply every day, so that the hon. member will have any opportunity he desires to move an amendment again. He will have that opportunity to-morrow, and for that matter he has it now, although I do not want to suggest that to him. Surely it is not unreasonable on the part of the Government that we should seek to have one department a day. The object of the rule was to see to it that there was a motion to go into Supply for each department on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. We are complying with the rule and will go into Supply to-morrow and the next day too. We could, when we are in Supply, comply with the rule and call one department and then another. The Chair has so ruled.
When was that ruling made?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Some weeks ago.
Not yet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That ruling was given, but we need not discuss the point now. How is it unreasonable on my part to suggest that we merely go into .Supply, then rise at once, and move into Supply both to-morrow and the next day?

I am not going to offer further objection, but I would point out to my hon. friend and to the country that we are forced into the position of discussing these matters at halfpast one in the morning, for no reason other than that the Prime Minister and the Government saw fit to bring on the session much later than it should have been called and are now seeking to get through the public business as speedily as they possibly can.
Carried.

If hon. gentlemen think that they will get away any the sooner by creating a disturbance at this hour, they are mistaken. If there is one protest above another which we have a right to make it is that, so far as this Parliament is concerned, it is ceasing altogether to be of the nature of a deliberative assembly. We are having matters brought forward day after day and rushed through without an opportunity of considering their significance, or their importance. We had

Grand Trunk legislation introduced a day or two ago, which was given the first and second reading,-
Carried.

I just wish to point out to the Prime Minister that what he refers to as a ruling by the Chair with regard to going into different departments when in Supply is an opinion which he himself expressed. No ruling was given by the Chairman this session on this question.
